title: Before the Roar podcast: Previewing Lions vs. Jets
description: Detroit Lions vs. New York Jets Week 3 Preview: ‘Before the Roar’ breaks down the matchup and biggest storylines.
fullText:
Now that it feels like it has been close to a month since last Thursday, it's time for the Detroit Lions to get back on that horse in a Week 3 matchup where they will be hosting the New York Jets. Familiar faces abound, with Jets coach Aaron Glenn and defensive coordinator Brian Duker making their return to Detroit. To break everything down, myself and my good friend Meko Scott are back with another episode of "Before the Roar," where we preview the matchup.

As usual, we we set the table by going over some of the changes that the Jets made in the offseason, including bringing in veteran coach Frank Reich as offensive coordinator. They also upgraded their quarterback room by bringing in journeyman quarterback Geno Smith in an effort to unlock a strong group of skill players that includes Garrett Wilson at wide receiver, Breece Hall at running back, and rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq.

Flip to the other side of the ball where the Jets like to hang their hat and you will find a front-seven that is stocked with top-end talent. At the edge rusher position alone, they have Kingsley Enagbare, Will McDonald IV, and second overall pick from the 2026 NFL Draft David Bailey. Combine that room with the addition of All-Pro linebacker Demario Davis and you get a potent mix of youth and veteran leadership for the Jets' defense.

After discussing both sides of the ball, we breakdown some key matchups, and give our predictions at the end of the show. You can watch the entire episode right here.

If you haven't already, please be sure to like and Your support allows us to reach other Lions fans around the world.

title: 2026 WNBA playoffs schedule, first-round matchups and how to watch
description: The schedule for the 2026 WNBA playoffs has been announced, with the eight teams starting their championship pursuit on Sunday, Sept. 27.
fullText:
The 2026 WNBA playoffs schedule is set, with the eight teams poised to begin their quest for the championship on Sunday, Sept. 27.

The top-seeded Minnesota Lynx, who were the first team to clinch a postseason spot, will host the No. 8 seed New York Liberty to kick off Sunday's action at 2 p.m. ET.

The afternoon slate continues with the defending champion Las Vegas Aces, seeded No. 3 and aiming for their fourth WNBA championship in franchise history, hosting the No. 6 Indiana Fever.

The evening matchup features the No. 4 Atlanta Dream, who secured their playoff berth with a crucial win over Phoenix, hosting the No. 5 Washington Mystics.

The nightcap will see the No. 2 Golden State Valkyries traveling to face the No. 7 Dallas Wings, who are making their first playoff appearance since 2023.

Here is a look at the WNBA first-round playoff schedule.

title: Report: Chelsea and Liverpool are in the race to sign Serie A defender
description: Chelsea Join Liverpool in Alessandro Bastoni Race as Inter Milan Set £70m ValuationChelsea’s long-running search for the right defensive profile has brought Alessandro Bastoni back into focus, with...
fullText:
Chelsea's long-running search for the right defensive profile has brought Alessandro Bastoni back into focus, with TeamTalk reporting that the Inter Milan defender remains firmly admired at Stamford Bridge. Liverpool and Manchester City are also in the picture, while Barcelona continue to monitor the situation, giving this the feel of a major transfer battle that could build across the coming windows.

Bastoni, now 27, has been regarded for some time as one of Europe's elite centre-backs. The key detail in this latest update is the price. Inter previously held out for "close to £70million" and there is nothing to suggest their stance has softened. For any interested club, that immediately turns admiration into a serious strategic decision.

From a Chelsea perspective, the attraction is easy to understand. The report states that the Blues "remain admirers as they continue to shape their defence under Xabi Alonso". That line matters, because it points to a specific tactical fit rather than a general appreciation of quality. Chelsea have "moved towards a back-three system", and there is said to be a belief internally that they "could still be short of the ideal central figure to operate in that structure".

That is where Bastoni stands out. He is comfortable defending wide spaces, composed when stepping into midfield zones, and progressive in possession. TeamTalk notes that "Bastoni's ability to defend in a back-three, while also possessing the technical quality and passing range to contribute in possession, would make him an obvious fit for Alonso's system." It is difficult to argue with that assessment. Few defenders combine left-sided balance, aerial authority and build-up quality at his level.

If Chelsea are going to make another major move in the market, it makes sense that it would be for a player capable of improving the structure around him rather than simply adding numbers. Bastoni looks like that type.

Chelsea are far from alone. Liverpool are described as another club with serious interest, and the reporting is particularly striking on that front. TeamTalk says Liverpool "have already done significant work on Bastoni" and "continue to view him as an option as they prepare to move on from Virgil van Dijk". That frames Bastoni as part of a longer-term defensive succession plan rather than a short-term opportunistic target.

The Merseyside club are said to be "looking at a number of defensive targets ahead of 2027 and Bastoni remains a player firmly on their radar". In transfer terms, that usually suggests groundwork has been laid, even if the conditions for a deal are not yet in place.

Manchester City's interest also deserves attention. The report explains that City "continue to retain an interest in Bastoni" and adds that their position "could become particularly interesting if Ruben Dias were to leave the Etihad Stadium". With Saudi Arabian interest in Dias mentioned, there is a possible chain reaction here. Should City need a high-end replacement or a fresh defensive leader, Bastoni would naturally enter that conversation.

Barcelona's role in this story should not be overlooked either. Bastoni was apparently close to joining the Catalan side previously, and "the player prioritising the move as negotiations progressed" is a significant detail. Yet the move collapsed because "Inter's determination to secure close to £70million for their star defender ultimately proved a major obstacle."

That said, there is no sense that the door has closed. Barcelona are "considering their options ahead of the next transfer windows" and could yet revisit the market in defence if they can create room through sales. Bastoni "remaining a player of significant interest" keeps them relevant in what may become a crowded chase.

Crucially for Chelsea and the Premier League clubs, TeamTalk adds that Bastoni's previous preference for Barcelona "should not be interpreted as a reluctance to move to England." In fact, "intermediaries have made it clear to the interested Premier League clubs that Bastoni is very much open to a move to England." That changes the dynamic. If one of Chelsea, Liverpool or City decide to push hard, there appears to be encouragement on the player side.

Inter's position remains strong. They are "under no immediate pressure to sell one of their most important players", and that is often decisive in cases like this. It means any buying club will likely have to meet a premium fee and move on Inter's terms. The "previous valuation of close to £70million" is the clearest guide available and would probably be the starting point for negotiations rather than the end.

For Chelsea, the question is whether Bastoni becomes the priority signing in defence or simply one of several elite options under review. The profile fits, the availability is not impossible, and the player's openness to England is a major positive. The obstacle, as ever, is cost and competition.

As things stand, this looks like a situation to watch closely. Chelsea's interest is real, Liverpool's homework is advanced, Manchester City are in the background, and Barcelona have not gone away. Bastoni remains one of the standout defensive names in the market, and Inter know it.

From a hopeful Chelsea fan's point of view, this is exactly the sort of report that gets the imagination going. Bastoni feels like the kind of signing that could elevate the whole defence in one move. If the club truly believe they are "short of the ideal central figure" for this system, then there are not many better candidates on the market.

What makes this exciting is the fit. A left-sided defender who is elite on the ball, experienced at the top level, and naturally suited to a back three sounds tailor-made for where Chelsea are heading under Xabi Alonso. Plenty of centre-backs can defend their box. Bastoni looks like someone who can control games, help the team play higher up the pitch, and give real balance in build-up.

Of course, £70m is a huge fee. That part cannot be ignored, especially with Liverpool, Manchester City and Barcelona all hovering. But if Chelsea are serious about competing for the biggest trophies again, then eventually they need to win races like this. Not every top target can be a developmental signing. Sometimes you need to go for proven class.

The most encouraging line in the whole report may be that Bastoni is "very much open to a move to England". If Chelsea have a clear plan, can show him a central role in Alonso's project, and are willing to pay what Inter want, there is every reason for supporters to dream about this one becoming real.

title: After three straight 100-loss seasons, the improbable White Sox are headed back to the postseason
description: The White Sox clinched no worse than one of three AL wild-card spots with the rout in Kansas City.
fullText:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. — After becoming the first team in major league history to follow consecutive 100-loss seasons with a playoff berth, nobody would have begrudged the White Sox for spilling over the dugout railing and celebrating wildly on the field in Kauffman Stadium.

Instead, they matter-of-factly formed a handshake line, as if their 9-1 win over the Royals was any 'ol mid-summer matinee.

They were saving the party for the clubhouse.

The White Sox clinched no worse than one of three AL wild-card spots with the rout in Kansas City, and in the plastic-draped visiting locker room, the bottles of Moët were stacking up quickly. Miguel Vargas was drenched, Munetaka Murakami was beaming and a team expected to finish last in the AL Central was relishing in a most improbable postseason appearance.

"This means a lot for us," Vargas said. "We've been chasing this moment for a long time. It's special for us. It's special for the whole organization. This is a special group of guys, and this is the most fun we can have."

That might be a bit of hyperbole. The White Sox could be replicating — or, one-upping — the celebration this weekend.

That's because they still have their sights set on a division title. The White Sox are just a game back of Cleveland. Chicago is home for three games against last-place Colorado, while the Guardians are in Kansas City to wrap up the regular season.

Maybe that's why the White Sox showed some restraint in celebrating their postseason berth right in front of the Royals.

They could still use a little help from them.

"They know what this is about," White Sox manager Will Venable said. "This comes with the expectation that this was going to happen, which is really cool. They're definitely letting loose right now, we'll have a fun plane ride, but then back to business tomorrow."

It was a charmed all-around day for the city of Chicago. Just as the White Sox were securing a postseason pass, the Cubs were tying up a 2-1 win over the Marlins, clinching a wild-card spot of their own in the NL playoffs. Both Chicago teams reached the postseason for the fourth time after 1906, 2008 and 2020.

The Cubs made it last year, too, when the White Sox were busy losing 102 games and seemed to have little reason to hope.

It wasn't just that the White Sox were two years removed from losing 121 games, setting a post-1900 record, or that no team had made the playoffs after consecutive 100-loss seasons — let alone three in a row. But even midway through April, they were making good — err, bad? — on most folks' expectations, starting 6-13 and looking every bit the part of a perennial loser.

But then their youngsters starting slugging, and the White Sox started piling up wins.

Murakami, who signed a two-year, $34 million deal in December — after the White Sox paid a $6,575,000 posting fee to the Yakult Swallows — has 33 homers and drove in his 74th run. Vargas has been receiving some MVP hype after hitting 33 homers of his own and driving in 92. And Colson Montgomery, who tied Mark Reynolds' season record of 223 strikeouts, has masked all those whiffs by hitting 31 homers and driving in 87 runs.

"W's are all that matters," Montgomery said, Champagne and beer dripping from his goggles in the middle of the pandemonium. "You see this? This is all that matters. Whatever I can do to help the team, that's all I care about."

Chicago's trade of left-handed ace Garrett Crochet to the Red Sox in December 2024 also has paid long-term dividends.

Three players that the White Sox landed in the deal — Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Braden Montgomery — were in the lineup, and all played a big role in helping the White Sox clinch the 12th postseason appearance.

Teel homered, reached base five times and scored three runs. Meidroth had a couple of hits, extending his on-base streak to 15 games. And batting last in the order, Montgomery had a hit and scored during a three-run second inning that broke open the game.

It was 6-0 after two innings and 8-0 after four. And pretty soon, plastic tarps were going up in the visitors clubhouse, an almost unfathomable party just 90 minutes away.

"This is what the White Sox is. We come together," Murakami said, "and this is not the end. We're going to start from here."

title: 76ers' LeBron James reportedly had done deal to join Cavaliers before signing with Philadelphia
description: LeBron James went to the Philadelphia 76ers. It turns out he had original plans to join the team he started his career with.
fullText:
76ers' LeBron James reportedly had done deal to join Cavaliers before signing with Philadelphia originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

LeBron James was undoubtedly the biggest storyline of the summer, as it was the first time he hit free agency in almost a decade. James had spent the previous eight seasons with the Los Angeles Lakers.

The four-time NBA champion was set to hit free agency but could have signed back with Los Angeles. His agent, Rich Paul, notified the Lakers that James would not be returning for the 2026-27 season.

"LeBron James will return for an unprecedented 24th season in the NBA -- but it won't be with the Los Angeles Lakers. James has informed the Lakers that the franchise can move on without him because he will play elsewhere, Klutch Sports CEO Rich Paul told ESPN's Shams Charania on Tuesday," ESPN wrote.

The 41-year-old then went on to have the longest offseason of his career. He would eventually sign with the Philadelphia 76ers on the smallest deal of his career.

"LeBron James is signing with the Philadelphia 76ers for his final run at another NBA championship, he announced Friday," ESPN's Dave McMenamin wrote. "James, 41, is signing a two-year, $8 million contract with a player option, Klutch Sports Group CEO Rich Paul told ESPN's Shams Charania."

It is very clear that James felt like the 76ers had the best roster to compete for a championship. However, The Ringer's Bill Simmons still reports that James had a deal done with the Cleveland Cavaliers before pulling an audible.

"Listen, he was going to [the Cleveland Cavaliers]. I don't know what happened. I can't wait for the story. Something happened," Simmons said.

While there is nothing else to confirm this, Simmons is standing by what he reported during the summer as factual. If true, James almost returned to the place where he started his historic career.

There is no doubt that Cleveland would have welcomed him back with open arms, and there is no telling what could have changed his mind. His heart is in Philadelphia for the next two seasons. However, it turns out that it was once going to be in Cleveland.

title: Trump admin using AI to deny medical care for seniors in disastrous experiment
description: Vendors rolling out AI have an "incentive to deny as many claims as possible."
fullText:
In January, the Trump administration rolled out a pilot program that uses artificial intelligence to authorize or deny certain types of care for patients with Medicare—a federal healthcare program for seniors that previously hasn’t required doctors to get any such pre-approval, called prior authorization.

Not long after, media outlets began relaying the disastrous outcomes: technical difficulties, long delays in decisions and care, puzzling denials, frustrated doctors, and patients suffering in pain. Those reports were largely confirmed earlier this month when the Electronic Frontier Foundation released a tranche of federal documents about the program, called WISeR, that the group obtained amid litigation. The documents included feedback from healthcare providers, including one who called the program “a disgrace to the human race” and reported seeing patients crying in pain as they waited for care.

Amid the worrying reports, lawmakers have been trying to get answers and shut the program down. Meanwhile, the Government Accountability Office determined in May that Trump officials did not follow proper procedure in setting up the program, calling its legality into question. Still, it appears to be moving ahead unabated, with plans to expand in the years to come.

Last week, Rep. Suzan DelBene (D-Wash.) called a committee vote to try to get the Trump administration to release more documents about WISeR, but Republicans voted the effort down.

“It’s clear why the administration is doing everything they can to conceal these documents,” DelBene said in a statement. “The more that Americans learn about WISeR, the more outraged they get at the Trump administration for jeopardizing their care and trying to privatize Medicare.”

WISeR, which stands for Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction, aims to use AI and machine learning to ensure “appropriate Medicare payment” for select services while benefiting taxpayers “by decreasing fraud, waste and abuse.” It was rolled out in January in six states—New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, Arizona, and Washington—and intends to run until the end of 2031.

So far, the program requires prior authorization for around a dozen medical services, including nerve stimulation, epidural steroid injections for pain, cervical fusions (permanently connecting bones in the neck), skin substitutes for wounds, and treatments for incontinence and impotence.

According to the documents released by the EFF, the program’s implementation was rushed, and the technology wasn’t ready. One vendor, Innovaccer, was so unprepared that it asked the government to delay the rollout, and when it didn’t, the vendor set up its program to automatically approve all requests temporarily.

“[A]uto-affirming is the only path available that avoids creating a backlog of unprocessed prior authorizations and claims while we finalize, validate, and deploy the full rules-based solution,” Innovaccer wrote, according to a letter it sent to government officials.

But others carried on. One vendor, Zyter, had data discrepancies for months because it apparently didn’t understand the difference between Medicare Part A, which covers inpatient/hospital care, and Part B, which covers outpatient services. Zyter’s CEO, Sundar Subramanian, told Ars Technica in a written statement that the company is now “fully functional across Medicare Part A and Part B claims.” The company is working closely with federal partners and the healthcare providers to “enhance the experience,” Subramanian said.

Another vendor, Virtix, was found to be denying more prior authorization requests than it was approving. According to a weekly report on March 30, Virtix had reviewed 6,096 pre-authorization requests. It approved 2,863 of them, denying 3,233 (53 percent).

In addition to a questionable number of denials, decisions from the various contracted companies often took too long. WISeR is intended to provide authorization decisions within 72 hours, but many have taken weeks, some even months. The documents from EFF reveal at least one request was still pending after 83 days. In a survey, one healthcare provider said it “had a surgery pushed back almost two months due to zero communication.”

It was revealed in June that Virtix was put on a Corrective Action Plan (CAP) by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) for “noncompliance” with the 72-hour window. In a statement to Ars Technica, Virtix confirmed it was on a CAP but said it has since “reduced its average turnaround time for prior authorization to 1.18 days and prepayment review determinations to 1.17 days, well within the WISeR Model’s 3-day requirement.”

Virtix said the CAP ended on August 14.

It’s unclear if any other vendors have been put on a CAP. The CMS and the Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to Ars Technica’s request for comment and a list of questions related to WISeR in time for publication.

In its comment to Ars, Virtix said that it “understand[s] that any delay in care is difficult for patients, and we do not take lightly the impact that the prior authorization process can have on people who are in pain and seeking relief.”

That said,” the company continued, “the WISeR program uses long-established [National Coverage Determinations] and [Local Coverage Determinations] set by CMS, not by Virtix Health, to evaluate the medical appropriateness of each requested procedure.”

Virtix encouraged providers to consider resubmitting authorization requests and ask for peer-to-peer discussion about denials.

The suggestion to reach out for support is unlikely to assuage many providers who have experience with WISeR. From their perspective, technical snags, delays, and unexpected denials have led to real misery, and many providers have reported only radio silence from program vendors when they sought support.

The reality of WISeR’s implementation may best be captured by feedback from one healthcare provider in Ohio, which was working with Innovaccer, the vendor that initially auto-approved requests. In a survey response, the provider wrote (in all capital letters) about patients trying to get a minimally invasive surgery to treat compression fractures in their spines, saying:

I HAVE HAD TO WATCH 3 PATIENTS CRY AT BEDSIDE FOR NOT HEARING BACK ON THEIR PRIOR AUTH FOR KYPHOPLASTY/VERTABRAL AUGMENTIATION PROCEDURE. THESE PATIENTS ARE IN DEEP PAIN. SO MANY OFFICES OF MY PHYSICIANS ARE NOT HEARING BACK FROM INNOVACCER… THERE IS NO WAY TO GET A HOLD OF A HUMAN TO TALK TO… WHAT A DISGRACE TO THE HUMAN RACE IN AMERICA. THIS IS THIRD WORLD.

Another Ohio provider expressed similar frustration with Innovaccer about delayed care and lack of communication, writing in a survey response that the experience has been “extremely disappointing”:

A 3–4 day delay for necessary pain procedures is already difficult for vulnerable patients, but when providers cannot obtain answers for weeks, the situation becomes unacceptable… The lack of accessible support, accountability, and timely communication is deeply concerning. Programs affecting patient access to medically necessary procedures must have reliable provider support systems. Currently, that standard is not being met. Patients deserve better. Providers deserve answers. And systems designed to improve care should never result in preventable suffering.

Innovaccer did not respond to a request for comment from Ars Technica. In a statement to Stat News, Innovaccer said its technology is now “fully live” and that the company has “worked closely with all of our partners to refine and improve the program since its launch and we will continue to do so with the spirit of putting patients first.”

In a Senate hearing last week, Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) raised questions about WISeR to Chris Klomp, Trump’s nominee for Deputy Secretary of HHS, a position that requires Senate confirmation. In her questioning, Murray wasn’t focused on WISeR’s calamitous rollout; she was instead interested in how the program was designed to work.

“Do the contractors in the model—who are the private companies conducting the prior authorization assessments—make more money if they deny care? Just ‘yes’ or ‘no,’” Murray asked in her opening question.

“My understanding is no,” Klomp replied.

Klomp’s understanding is inaccurate, which is notable given that he has been working as the deputy administrator of CMS and has been directing Medicare since last year. CMS documents, included in the packet obtained by the EFF, clearly explain that the companies implementing WISeR are financially rewarded for denying requests for care. CMS’s planning documents describes it as a “novel payment approach where the model participants are compensated based on a share of averted expenditures.”

CMS documents written as a guide for WISeR participants explain further that for every denied request, CMS will determine what the regional benchmark cost for that care would have been and then pay the company 25 percent.

Murray further quoted the CMS Office of the Actuary, which explained bluntly in a memo that “model participants will have an incentive to deny as many claims as possible.”

“And what do you know,” Murray said. “In the first three months of this year, the Washington state contractor denied more requests than they approved.”

Klomp defended the program, saying, “My understanding is that when they deny care, if they do so inappropriately, there are significant financial penalties and that CMMI [Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation] is carefully watching their performance and has the ability to terminate [contracts]. My understanding as well is that [CMMI] will be producing a report or a report card of something shortly that will show an accounting by vendor in the six trial markets… to drive an accountability.”

According to the CMS documents, Klomp was referring to the “Aggregate Quality Score,” a percentage-based score calculated for each company implementing the WISeR model. The score is partly based on whether companies appropriately deny or authorize care requests, and it’s then used as a “quality adjustment” to payments to disincentivize inappropriately denying care.

But the CMS documents reveal that this adjustment penalty for denying legitimate requests is small. A company that earns an AQS score of between 100 percent and 85 percent will be paid all 25 percent of the “averted” costs from denied claims. If a company’s score falls between 84 percent and 60 percent, it will be paid 95 percent of the 25 percent of averted costs—just a 5 percent drop in profits. If it scores below 60 percent—a failing grade by school standards—it will get 90 percent.

Companies won’t be paid if an authorization denial is appealed and overturned, but data suggests few people go through the appeal process. In Medicaid Advantage, for instance, only 11.5 percent of care denials are appealed—though 80 percent of appeals result in the denial being overturned.

While Klomp claimed that there would be accountability for companies wrongly denying care, Murray seemed to dismiss the assurance. She said she had already heard from seniors in her state—one of the six in which WISeR has debuted—who have suffered for weeks in pain as their doctors “battled with these contractors for approval.”

Hospitals in the state have said the situation has not gotten better since its rollout in January.

“I already know CMS is planning to expand this to oncology,” Murray said. “I am going to do everything I can to stop this. It is really hurting patients.”

According to the CMS documents, the Trump administration plans to expand WISeR’s prior authorization system from cancer treatments to air ambulance transport, advanced imaging (such as MRIs), cardiac catheterization, pacemakers, Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillators (ICDs), and genetic and molecular lab tests.

title: Biolinq's color-coded glucose sensor patch nets FDA clearance
description: After raising $100 million in venture capital funding earlier this year, Biolinq has obtained a groundbreaking green light from the FDA for its needle-free continuous glucose monitor.&nbs | After raising $100 million in funding, Biolinq has obtained a groundbreaking FDA clearance for its Shine needle-free continuous glucose monitor. The Shine system, which also tracks activity and sleep data, will first be aimed at people with Type 2 diabetes.
fullText:
After raising $100 million in venture capital funding earlier this year, Biolinq has obtained a groundbreaking green light from the FDA for its needle-free continuous glucose monitor.

The Shine system, which also tracks activity and sleep data, will initially be targeted at individuals with Type 2 diabetes. The reader employs microsensors placed in the topmost layers of the skin, which the company describes as being up to 20 times shallower than filament-based CGMs that require a subcutaneous introducer during placement and setup.

Biolinq also bills its sensor as virtually painless and autonomous, with the coin-sized forearm patch providing real-time feedback on glucose levels via its own color-coded LED display, allowing it to be used without a paired smartphone app.

The agency’s de novo clearance pitches the Shine sensor as providing a more qualitative view of the user’s glucose ranges and trends—not as a CGM that supplies the quantitative measurements used to calculate insulin doses.

“Biolinq Shine is a first-of-its-kind biosensor designed to support metabolic health for people with diabetes who are not dependent on insulin,” Biolinq Chairman Dan Bradbury said in a statement. “By automatically tracking glucose levels, physical activity and sleep information, this technology offers meaningful insights that can encourage healthier choices every day.”

“The entire Biolinq team is thrilled about this regulatory milestone, which is a testament to the outstanding work by our team,” added CEO Rich Yang. “We are grateful to the FDA for its rapid and rigorous review in establishing a new category of wearable biosensors.”

In April, the San Diego-based company announced a $100 million series C round, stating that it would help launch its commercialization plans. Biolinq has also been developing an electrochemical microsensor array that tracks lactate and ketone levels, in addition to glucose monitoring—however, the initial FDA clearance only covers glucose monitoring.

“As long-standing supporters and investors of Biolinq, Alpha Wave remains confident in their ability to deliver on a bold, innovative vision for biowearables,” said Rick Gerson, chairman of Alpha Wave Global, which led the company’s series C as well as a $58 million round in 2024. “Biolinq is on the path to redefine how society thinks about cardiometabolic health and wellness, driving the next wave of innovation with a profound multi-analyte biosensor platform.”

title: The end times fascists are plotting their escape from our world
description: An unholy alliance is working toward an apocalyptic future from which only a chosen few will emerge unscathed. It’s becoming clear how we stop them
fullText:
When Jeff Bezos announced his plan for an opulent Venetian wedding in early 2025, many locals found the idea offensive, even obscene. A growing number of residents were struggling to find secure and affordable housing in a city overrun by tourists and Airbnb, and the billionaire was planning to, in effect, rent out the municipality for three days, forking over an estimated $50m for festivities that would clog central canals and block well-trafficked streets. Worse, Amazon’s carbon emissions were soaring, thanks to artificial intelligence and the datacentre build out – and that’s personal in Venice, where the streets already flood dozens of times a year.

Marta Sottoriva, a 35-year-old high school teacher, told us that she first heard about the wedding plans just when Bezos’s rocket company, Blue Origin, was grabbing headlines. Bezos had sent a “crew” of female influencers and celebrities, including his fiancee, Lauren Sánchez, and the pop singer Katy Perry, to the suborbital edge of space in a seemingly pointless publicity stunt. “The idea that you are so rich and powerful that you can use space as a 10-minute trip,” Sottoriva recalled, only intensified the “feeling that our city was being taken away from us in such an arrogant way”. Federica Toninello, another young activist, agreed, telling us that it felt as if both space and Venice were being “colonized”.

Colonizing space is exactly what Bezos hopes to do. Blue Origin, Bezos claims in his well-rehearsed sales pitch, will secure humanity’s survival by allowing a trillion people to one day spread across the solar system. The unbearable horror he imagines himself saving our species from? The threat of what he calls a “civilization of stasis”, otherwise known as having to contend with real ecological limits and devising a way to share the planet’s finite resources. To avoid this reckoning, Bezos imagines a future in which “Earth will be zoned residential and light industrial” and set aside as a sort of preserve out of reach for most of its native inhabitants. The vast majority of humans will pursue the nebulous benefit of “exponential growth” in the forbidding void of space, trapped on Blue Origin spacecrafts. It would seem that Bezos believes the prospect of humanity living sustainably and peaceably on our precious, singular home is a nightmarish possibility unworthy of his consideration.

Predictably, it turned out that most Venetians would rather continue living in magnificent Venice. Unlike Bezos, they don’t fret about hypothetical civilizational stagnation; they worry about economic stagnation as a result of government divestment, a lack of jobs and opportunity, and being forced out of the city and country they love. Young Italians often have little choice but to emigrate to find work; over the last decade, more than 1 million citizens have moved, a third of them between the ages of 25 and 34.

To date, the precarity and anger many Italians feel has mostly benefited the neofascist right. But those same forces also drew people to the anti-Bezos cause, helping to coalesce a budding, self-consciously antifascist movement.

The spirited, disruptive “No Space for Bezos” campaign tapped into wells of outrage against billionaires, climate breakdown and militarism – and it also gave the organizers a megaphone to broadcast ideas for different, less lethal ways we could choose to live together. Activists printed posters and stickers showing Bezos’s head on a rocket blasting into space. They made a dummy of Bezos clutching fistfuls of fake money while clinging to a giant buoyant Amazon package, then set it free to float down the canals. They unfurled banners from Venice’s iconic buildings and bridges and across its piazzas: “Tax the rich to give back to the planet.” And they chanted that the money for the wedding would be better spent rebuilding Gaza. For days, they caused gleeful chaos and relentlessly poked fun at the groom and his star-studded guest list, which included his billionaire bunker neighbors Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and a gaggle of Kardashians.

Not long before the wedding, officials announced that the event was being moved to a less central location due to the protests. Even Bezos’s two yachts, Koru and Abeona, were denied permission to dock locally. Organizers declared victory and celebrated. The international press devoured the visual-rich showdown. And the online right didn’t know who to root for: the Davos elites spraying one another with foam on a superyacht, or the leftist riffraff making agitprop?

Like Donald Trump’s enormous ballroom, Bezos’s extravagant wedding epitomized the obscenities of our networked gilded age. For the Amazon founder, it wasn’t enough to be part of one of Europe’s most beautiful cities – he needed to consume it and swallow it whole. A year later he would do the same with New York City’s Met Gala, sparking similar outrage and grassroots creativity.

The Venice protests, which dwelled on Bezos’s dreams of outer space at the expense of Earth, pointed to something fundamental about the age of end times fascism – a concept at the center of our new book, referring to an unholy alliance working toward an apocalyptic future from which only a chosen few will emerge unscathed. Today’s battle lines are not simply between people who struggle to survive under increasingly degraded and costly conditions and an oligarch class thinking of ever more ludicrous ways to waste their wealth. They are more cosmological than that.

On one side are those of us who have no escape plan, no bunker in the sky or underground, and who therefore are committed to staying right here, in the complexity of our earthbound reality, with one another. We know we need to do what is necessary to make “here” – this planet and all of its ecologies and communities – and safer for the multitude of beings who rely upon them, fully aware this is our one and only home.

On the other are those with rapturous plans to shield themselves and their families from the political and ecological fires burning our planet, whether those plans take the form of heavenly ascension, earthly bunkers and fortressed nations, or fantasies of colonizing space and merging with machines. Instead of improving conditions for actual people on Earth (or even pulling back from pouring fuel on the fires), end times fascists are plotting their escape, indifferent and oblivious to all that’s worth saving.

Bezos’s fixation on space gets at something else that is key to understanding end times fascism and its fixation on bunkering and abandoning our shared world: the apparent inability of the people driving this project to marvel at, or even notice, the wonders that surround them.

That was glaringly apparent in 2021, when Bezos sent another crew to space. This time William Shatner, best known as Star Trek’s Captain Kirk, was on board (to fulfill one of Bezos’s boyhood fantasies, of course). “Space. The final frontier,” Shatner had said at the start of each episode. But as the now 90-year-old actor watched our blue-and-green planet recede from the window, he was suddenly flooded with terror. “The contrast between the vicious coldness of space and the warm nurturing of Earth below filled me with overwhelming sadness,” he later recalled, explaining that he had gained a much deeper appreciation for our planet’s sublime and fragile gifts.

“Every day, we are confronted with the knowledge of further destruction of Earth at our hands: the extinction of animal species, of flora and fauna … things that took five billion years to evolve, and suddenly we will never see them again because of the interference of mankind,” Shatner wrote. He took the trip expecting to be awestruck by the universe and instead he longed for home the minute he left: “I discovered that the beauty isn’t out there, it’s down here, with all of us.”

Perhaps Shatner’s insight about our precious imperiled planet resonates with the Amazon founder, but the billionaire’s plans for space colonization and his company’s large expansion of carbon-spewing data centers both suggest otherwise. And among tech oligarchs, Bezos is all too typical. Peter Thiel, for one, once revealed that his three best ideas for achieving true freedom are “cyberspace”, “outerspace” and “seasteading” (the idea of building new countries on floating oil rigs). In other words, this man, whose enormous wealth affords him access to the most spectacular settings our planet has to offer, actually believes these three cold, dead places are superior to the Earth we have, verdant and alive.

Something similar seems amiss with Elon Musk, a man who seems to look up at the wonders of the night sky and see only opportunities to fill that inky unknown with his own space junk. The venerable novelist Joyce Carol Oates highlighted these apparent limits in the fall of 2025 when she roasted him ruthlessly on his own platform, X. “So curious,” she wrote, “that such a wealthy man never posts anything that indicates that he enjoys or is even aware of what virtually everyone appreciates – scenes from nature, pet dog or cat, praise for a movie, music, a book (but doubt that he reads); pride in a friend’s or relative’s accomplishment; condolences for someone who has died; pleasure in sports, acclaim for a favorite team; references to history. In fact he seems totally uneducated, uncultured. The poorest persons on Twitter [X] may have access to more beauty & meaning in life than the ‘most wealthy person in the world.’”

The observation clearly got under the tech baron’s notoriously thin skin: he called her “a lazy liar” and began posting approvingly about various movies to prove Oates wrong. Yet in Musk’s euphoria on the day his aerospace company, SpaceX, went public, he made no attempt to hide his boredom with our blue planet and its challenges: “We want to solve [problems] here on Earth and we should solve them. But there also have to be things that get you excited about the future, that make you glad to wake up in the morning because you can’t wait to see what happens next.” It would seem that only abandoning Earth provides that thrill.

Most people have the capacity for awe, to gasp at the jeweled beauty of a songbird or the otherworldliness of a whale’s exhalation or the intricate latticework of an ancient holy site. Children have the capacity for pure awe; so do 90-year-old actors in suborbital space. To experience awe is to dissolve into the swirl of the universe, to feel small in the best way. This sense of interconnection is also why we grieve when we witness strangers suffering, and feel the great sorrow of extinction. The fact that this capacity seems to be missing from the men who hold our collective fate in their hands is a personal loss for them – and an existential crisis for the rest of us.

One dangerous part of the tech oligarchs’ world-abandoning project is that the tools they are building are designed to remake us in their own broken image. Popular platforms and apps train us to share Silicon Valley’s dream of discarnate freedom, perpetually nudging us to forsake real places and in-person connection in favor of simulations – and to view Earth, our bodies and our relationships as prisons to hack and flee. Altman, for one, has made it clear that he sees “certain advantages to being a machine”, and he has repeatedly insisted that his own children will never be smarter than AI, as though intelligence can be reduced to no more than computation. Like similar services, ChatGPT is trained to hijack our empathic response systems so we, too, will elevate machines and imbue them with more significance than they deserve.

The inability to appreciate this planet and its marvelous cast of characters helps explain why they are so prepared to sacrifice it. Indeed, the tech right’s willingness to eliminate our life-sustaining labor and replace human relationships with synthetic ones cannot be separated from their indifference to what little remains of the planet’s fast-vanishing wildlife and plant diversity. They don’t seem to know how to love this place, to savor the pleasure of other people’s company, or to marvel at the mysteries presented by other species.

In short, we are up against an ideology that has given up not only on the premise and promise of liberal democracy but on the livability of our shared world – on its beauty, on its people, on our children, on other species. There is something treasonous in this. Treasonous not to an abstraction like a flag or a nation, for we are not nationalists. But treasonous to the unspoken pact made with the web of life that sustains us.

They are traitors to creation, to the wonders of here.

There is no cut-and-paste formula for fighting end times fascism. Whether it’s Venetians taking on Jeff Bezos or Albanians telling Jared and Ivanka Trump that their country is not for sale or a small town in Kentucky organizing against a sprawling datacentre, every front in this fight takes on the character and texture of its place. There are, however, some guiding principles that are beginning to emerge across locations, and Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for mayor of New York City – and his approach to governance since his election – embody many of them. Start from love of place, then conjure a radically inclusive future where everyone can afford dignified lives, embrace common goals across difference, get outside and gather offline and in person, take on the powerful joyously, draw on history and don’t be afraid to stir the soul.

Mamdani has pounded away at his core policies to make the city more affordable, and has made good on many of those promises in his pursuit, for example, to lower rent and expand universal childcare. But he has also done something more sublime, dwelling on the boisterous, charming corners of the city that are the reason so many people choose to endure the pressures pushing them to leave.

As Mamdani’s star was rising, fascists and neofascists across the country and around the world did what they do. They sorted and separated, ranked and expelled. They sowed confusion and division by claiming Mamdani wasn’t a real American, and blamed the left for every social problem and grievance. They held up multicultural New York as a supposedly terrifying example of what happens when the “great replacement” succeeds. JD Vance spoke out in defense of people’s right to not want to live next to people from “a totally different culture”, and Stephen Miller railed on X: “NYC is the clearest warning yet of what happens to a society when it fails to control migration.”

As the fascists drew their rigid lines – in versus out, protected versus disposable, “heritage” versus. invader – the campaign to elect Mamdani threw a year-long party that celebrated one of the most racially and ethnically diverse places ever known, five boroughs shaped by wave after wave of new immigrants who have made their homes on Lenape lands. With its every action, the campaign asserted that shared identity can be forged not just by ancestry but by a commitment to a shared home, and to a shared set of values about how to live together in that home.

New York is a city of people carrying countless hyphenations and keeping myriad cultural practices alive. But as Mamdani put it: “No matter what you eat, what language you speak, how you pray, or where you come from, the words that most define us are the two we all share: New Yorkers.”

So Mamdani explained the complexities of ranked-choice voting in the Democratic primary using a line of mango lassis as props. He canvassed for votes at queer clubs, shouted out Haitian revolutionary history at the massive Bayo concert, shared his favorite bagel order, and broke fast during Ramadan over biryani in the Bronx. Once in office, he also turned the now legendary Knicks playoff run and the 2026 World Cup into a summer-long party few will forget. In these ways and others, Mamdani re-enchanted a city that had faced relentless vilification from Washington as dangerous, dirty and dysfunctional.

It was a perfect encapsulation of “hereness” – an idea developed by the Jewish Labour Bund, a Yiddish socialist group that was founded in the 19th century and grounded in fierce commitment to place and community not based on bloodlines. Molly Crabapple, a proud New Yorker and artist who recently published a bestselling history of the Bund, made the connection in a piece published in the Guardian. “Like New York itself, Mamdani’s campaign was multicultural, multiracial, polyglottal,” she wrote. “When Andrew Cuomo tried to bait him as un-American, he released ads in Spanish and Bangla, Hindi and Arabic. He ran a campaign devoted to class-first politics that sought to speak to everyone in their own idiom, while never once apologizing for who he was.

Amid all this celebration of difference, Mamdani’s campaign also emphasized the kinds of daily experiences and anxieties that are common and unifying for nearly all New Yorkers, lingering in the ordinary places that are too often overlooked or reviled. Mamdani rubbed shoulders with commuters on packed subway cars, paid homage to the glories of the Staten Island Ferry, and visited countless bodegas, approaching the strangers he met with nonjudgmental curiosity and a smile so wide it became a punchline on Saturday Night Live.

But the campaign was not only antifascist – in the myriad ways that it celebrated the unruliness that makes New York lovable, it was also the antithesis of fascism. More than a rejection of hate, it was an invitation to kindness, to a world in which we avert our eyes from no one. That meant lifting up and honoring the very people fascists are most eager to eject and discard: the working-class, immigrant workforce that keeps the city functioning. The campaign shined a spotlight on delivery workers getting ripped off by platforms such as DoorDash, on Amazon warehouse workers fighting to have their unions recognized, and on taxi drivers in line at LaGuardia, one part of a nocturnal workforce that makes it possible for New York to boast of being the city that never sleeps.

Faced with the prospect of a fairer city funded by marginally higher taxes, some prophesied a billionaire exodus. Hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman threatened to leave along with other high earners and Fox forecast a “Mamdani Migration”. Luxury real estate agents reported being bombarded with calls from clients wanting to sell their penthouses and move to Palm Beach.

The threats of defection only underscored the mutually reinforcing nature of the two core themes of Mamdani’s campaign – the joyous love of here, even if here is kind of a wreck, and the concrete plans for repair and improvement. Because the more devoted you are to a place, the easier it is to put in the resources and energy required to improve it. It’s a politics based not on wanting to escape this earthly realm, whether our cities or our animate bodies, but on a deep desire to stay, and to protect all that is irreplaceable, human and alive.

This is the very same spirit that we’ve seen motivating people to protect their air and water from sprawling datacenters and to defend their immigrant neighbors from ICE. While reporting on the weeks-long uprising in Minneapolis, the journalist Adam Serwer memorably described the guiding ideology of the resistance as “neighborism”, or the “commitment to protecting the people around you, no matter who they are or where they came from”. It was an openhearted, welcoming ethic that united huge numbers of ordinary people to do something deceptively simple: protect the most vulnerable members of their community from what looked very much like an invading army. That meant everything from braving bullets, to cooking dinner to opening up spare rooms to families who were no longer safe at home.

In these and countless other ways, Minnesotans rose up to insist that their neighbors were already where they belonged, whether they were, as Serwer put it, born in Minneapolis or Mogadishu.

The human networks that neighbors are building, block by block, group chat by group chat, are about more than refusal. In our time of serial shocks and intersecting crises, they are also the basis for a different kind of survivalism. But while the various strains of fascists build bunkers for the few, ours are survival networks grounded in the principle that every one of us, without exception, deserves to live and thrive. They are also bound by a belief that keeping one another safe when the inevitable shocks arrive is a sacred duty. Part of that involves telling new stories, stories that are truthful and inspiring enough to help our depleted fellow humans fall back in love with our one and only home and defiantly recommit to defending it with all they’ve got.

Those stories cannot be about returning to something called “normal”, to what passed for calm before Brexit and Trump and Silicon Valley’s authoritarian turn. Those were the years during which too many problems were allowed to compound and fester: fascism is always a warped response to real crises. And end times fascism is a response to real planetary-scale crises, including ever-concentrating levels of carbon in the atmosphere and wealth in the hands of the super-rich. The responses it proposes – mass sacrifices of humans and non-humans alike – are monstrous and must be purged from our midst.

To achieve this, we will have to figure out how to address the underlying crises contemporary fascism feeds off of. Because boundaries are being crossed. Limits are being exceeded. Walls are being hit. Fascists want us to believe that what is hitting the wall is the human story: it’s over, so make sure you are among the chosen who transcend to the next world. Pray to your God for salvation. Implant the chip, merge with the machines. Militarize and purify your bunkered nation. Arm yourself to the hilt and hide behind your fortune. Don’t worry about the humans, the animals, the trees, the rivers and reefs that won’t make it.

But they are wrong. It’s not the human story that is hitting the wall. Rather, it is the story we have been trapped inside of. The one about how greed must be the engine of civilization. About how growth can go on for ever. About how there are always more efficiencies to be found, more workers to be rationalized, more resources to be sacrificed, more people, places and planets to colonize. These myths are hitting the wall of reality and much will have to change as a result.

The logics that must be abandoned should be clear by now. Unlimited violence. Unconstrained exploitation. Insatiable wealth. Unchecked dominance. Those are the drives that make coexistence impossible. Looking forward, two paths beckon. We can abandon and betray this world, or we can break with capitalism and build new economic and political systems that honor life and prioritize care and repair.

Thankfully we are not starting from scratch. Our movement ancestors have left us maps to earthly Zions where everyone is welcome, to inclusive futures where peace and safety are core principles. Not the post-human future desired by end times fascists, but a post-capitalist and pro- (all of) life one. Deeply democratic, socialist, feminist, multiracial, multispecies, internationalist, generous, courageous and animate. Embodied and sensory, proudly earthbound.

And that, fundamentally, is the prospect that terrifies end times fascists more than anything else. It’s why Thiel denounces anyone attempting to regulate fossil fuels and AI as the antichrist; and why Trump and Vance smear nonviolent Minnesotans defending their neighbors as “domestic terrorists”. What keeps these men up at night is … us. It’s the possibility that a popular and vigorous movement will rise up and defend this planet and the many life-forms who call it home.

We didn’t choose to be born into a fight quite so fateful, but we have reached a choice point. We can either follow end times fascists into oblivion, or we can commit to building the unruly, boundary-crossing movement they so deeply fear. One that wrests away their weapons, holds them accountable for their crimes, and defends the paradise of here.

This essay was adapted from the book End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, out 15 September via Farrar, Straus and Giroux

Naomi Klein is a Guardian US columnist and contributing writer. She is the professor of climate justice and co-director of the Centre for Climate Justice at the University of British Columbia

Astra Taylor is a writer, organizer and documentary maker and a co-founder of the Debt Collective

Illustrations by Sophy Hollington

title: Jevmem – automatic project memory for Claude Code, built on Jev
description: Automatic project memory for Claude Code. Also works with Cursor and Codex. - Avinash-jetwani/jevmem
fullText:
Automatic project memory for Claude Code. Also works with Cursor and Codex.

init creates JEVMEM.md, jevmem.config.json and a gitignored .jevmem/ folder, and registers two Claude Code hooks in .claude/settings.local.json, which it adds to .gitignore (details).

What is automatic and what depends on the agent:

MCP add_memory goes through the same gate as the hook. Client configs: docs/mcp.md.

Tiers, questions, policy, contradictions, recall and audit: docs/how-it-works.md.

66 held-out turns, all seven deciders given the same state, 2026-09-23 (method, regression set, pricing, p95, retries):

The 0.30 s is the Jev API decision; through a real Stop hook process, Node start-up included, it is 0.6 s end to end (cost and latency).

On 66 held-out turns, jevmem's median decision took 0.30 s, against 2.8–4.3 s for six current LLMs.
Its accuracy was within the LLMs' range: 98.5% save/skip (tied with GPT-6 Astra for highest) and 95.5% save+kind, against 90.9–98.5% for the LLMs. GPT-6 Astra (98.5%) and Claude Opus 5.5 (97.0%) were more accurate on save+kind; Claude Fable 5.1 tied; GPT-6 Luna, Gemini 3.8 Flash and Grok 4.7 were less accurate. It found 5/5 contradictions, as did five of the six LLMs.
GPT-6 Luna was cheaper ($0.000089 against $0.000127) but less accurate (93.9%) and about 10× slower.
This is a single run, and differences of one or two turns are within run-to-run noise. If the most accurate decision matters most, GPT-6 Astra or Claude Opus 5.5 are better, at about 40–60× the cost per decision and 9–12× the latency. jevmem is for when you want a fast, cheap decision on every message.

Exactly what is sent, stored and scrubbed: SECURITY.md.

Every command accepts --help. Set JEVMEM_VERBOSE=1 for a one-line latency/cost summary after every hook run.
