fullText:
Residents in Hawaii have been told to prepare for hurricane conditions as Nolo intensified into a hurricane on Thursday, threatening Hawaii's Big Island with potentially catastrophic flooding.

Some areas of the Big Island are expected to see up to 35 inches of rain, with life-threatening flash flooding possible, according to the National Hurricane Center.

Nolo is one of three storms currently brewing in the Pacific.

A second, the Category 5 Hurricane Polo, is off Mexico's Pacific coast and is expected to approach Baja California Sur on Monday, according to the NHC. A third storm, Hurricane Odalys, strengthened into a Category 3 storm but is churning over open water far from land.

Hurricane Nolo is expected to remain south of the Big Island through Saturday before turning west and moving away from the island, the NHC said. Tropical storm conditions are expected to begin on the Big Island on Friday night, with hurricane conditions possible Saturday, particularly in areas of steep terrain.

John Bravender, a meteorologist for the National Weather Service in Honolulu, said of the projected heavy rainfall, "That by itself could cause catastrophic flooding, but when you put that on top of grounds that we've been raining off and on for the last couple of months … that rain could cause even more damage."

In a video message on social media, Hawaii County Mayor Kimo Alameda told residents, "This is a very serious situation. We do believe that the rain is going to come. It's coming already."

Community Organized Relief Effort (CORE) said it is responding to the storms, providing tarps, headlamps, camp stoves, and other supplies critical for preparing people for possible destruction or displacement.

Activity in the Pacific Ocean is partly being fueled by a "supersized" El Niño climate pattern.

El Niño affects hurricane severity in both the Atlantic and the Pacific. This year's particularly powerful  El Niño conditions, which the UN's World Meteorological Organization has said could become the strongest on record, have led to fewer hurricanes in the Atlantic (particularly the Caribbean) and 

Weather changes fast. Get real-time alerts for your area on the new Yahoo Weather app.

Here's the location, path and status of each of the storms:

The National Hurricane Center said Hurricane Nolo was expected to remain south of the Big Island through Saturday before turning west and moving away from the island. Residents were urged to follow the advice of local officials, including evacuating if told to do so.

Nolo was located 240 miles south of South Point, Hawaii..

It had maximum sustained winds of 80 mph.

It was moving north-northeast at 5 mph.

Heavy rain is expected to increase in coverage and intensity on Friday and continue across the Big Island and Maui through the weekend. Some areas of the Big Island could see up to 35 inches of rain, and parts of Maui could get up to 15 inches. The rainfall could produce life-threatening, catastrophic flooding and mudslides, especially in steep terrain across the eastern and southern portions of both islands.

A Hurricane Watch, meaning that hurricane conditions are possible within the watch area, in this case, within 48 hours, is in effect for:

A Tropical Storm Warning, meaning that tropical storm conditions are expected somewhere within the warning area within 36 hours, is in effect for:

A Tropical Storm Watch, meaning that tropical storm conditions are possible within the watch area, generally within 48 hours, is in effect for:

Large and damaging waves are likely along parts of the Big Island's coastline into the weekend. A tropical storm watch is in effect for Maui County, where tropical storm conditions are possible beginning Saturday.

According to the National Hurricane Center, Hurricane Polo regained Category 5 strength early Friday and is expected to approach Baja California Sur on Monday. Polo is expected to begin weakening by Saturday.

Polo was located about 250 miles south-southwest of Cabo Corrientes, Mexico.

It had maximum sustained winds of 160 mph.

There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect, but interests in Baja California Sur were urged to monitor the storm.

Swells from Polo will continue to affect southwestern Mexico and spread toward west-central Mexico and Baja California Sur through the weekend, bringing life-threatening surf, rip currents and coastal flooding.

The National Hurricane Center said Hurricane Odalys strengthened into a Category 3 storm but posed no threat to land. There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.

Odalys is expected to turn north over the next couple of days and gradually weaken heading into the weekend.

Odalys was located about 985 miles west-southwest of the southern tip of Baja California.

It had maximum sustained winds of 115 mph.

It was moving northeast at 5 mph.

title: Allies back Saudis as Houthi attacks threaten key oil route
description:
Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani military chiefs are to discuss help for Saudi Arabia as it faces attacks by Yemen's Houthis, while Iraq further curtailed Iranian flights on Friday, in line with US pressure, and an Iranian official threatened retaliation. 
   The Houthis have launched strikes on the Saudi-backed government ‌in Yemen and repeatedly fired into Saudi Arabia, disrupting oil flows from the world's largest energy exporter, as part of a wider Middle East war that began with US and ‌Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28. 
   The military escalation continued this week despite a push during the UN General Assembly in New York to revive diplomacy to end the conflict, which quickly spread to Lebanon and the Gulf in March before escalating ​in Yemen in recent weeks. 
   With talks stalled and during a lull in direct fire by the US and Iran, Washington had shifted tactics to extend financial sanctions by targeting companies from third countries that do business with Iranian firms through "secondary sanctions". 
   Iranian airlines were barred from neighbouring countries including the United Arab Emirates and Oman on Thursday in response to new US sanctions, the first big impact of the shift.
fullText:
CAIRO/DUBAI Sept 25 (Reuters) - Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani military chiefs are to discuss help for Saudi Arabia as it faces attacks by Yemen's Houthis, while Iraq further curtailed Iranian flights on Friday, in line with US pressure, and an Iranian official threatened retaliation.

The Houthis have launched strikes on the Saudi-backed government ‌in Yemen and repeatedly fired into Saudi Arabia, disrupting oil flows from the world's largest energy exporter, as part of a wider Middle East war that began with US and ‌Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.

The military escalation continued this week despite a push during the UN General Assembly in New York to revive diplomacy to end the conflict, which quickly spread to Lebanon and the Gulf in March before escalating ​in Yemen in recent weeks.

With talks stalled and during a lull in direct fire by the US and Iran, Washington had shifted tactics to extend financial sanctions by targeting companies from third countries that do business with Iranian firms through "secondary sanctions".

Iranian airlines were barred from neighbouring countries including the United Arab Emirates and Oman on Thursday in response to new US sanctions, the first big impact of the shift.

On Friday, the three other Iraqi airports that operate flights to and from Iran joined Baghdad airport in suspending them, sources and state media said.

A flight ban, if sustained, could deepen Iran's isolation and worsen an economic crisis in the ‌country, which is already facing a US blockade of its seaports.

Mohammad Mokhber, ⁠an adviser to Iran's supreme leader, accused regional countries of "alignment with America" for blocking flights.

"If Iran does not have the possibility to fly and receive airport services, then no country in the region will have this possibility either", he said in a social media post.

The war, which US President Donald Trump ⁠launched alongside Israel, has killed thousands of people and disrupted global trade and energy supplies, adding to inflationary pressures.

While the fighting between the US and Iran has been stop-start, Iranian allies have mobilised, with Hezbollah attacks triggering an Israeli invasion of Lebanon and the Houthi advance in Yemen prompting a new humanitarian crisis.

Iran and its allies have significantly squeezed oil exports from Saudi Arabia, a US ally. The Houthis have disrupted ship traffic at the mouth ​of ​the Red Sea, while Iran has limited tanker traffic at the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for 20% of ​the world's oil exports before the war.

On Thursday, the Houthis said they had ‌fired dozens of missiles and drones at Saudi targets, while Saudi authorities said they had intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Houthi fighters.

Later, Saudi Arabia's Grand Mufti, the kingdom's top religious authority, called on soldiers to be ready to lay down their lives to fight the Houthis until the group was ousted from power.

Amid the fighting, the Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish foreign ministers met on Thursday for discussions under a defence pact signed in August.

They condemned attacks targeting the holy Saudi city of Mecca and other civilian sites, while affirming Saudi Arabia's right to defend itself and planning a meeting between chiefs of staff on ways to assist the kingdom.

Turkey's defence ministry said Chief of General Staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu was travelling to Saudi Arabia on Friday to meet his Saudi and Pakistani counterparts.

Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan said the defence pact, which ‌stipulates that an attack against one country be considered an attack against all, could lead to intelligence, logistical or ​ammunition support.

"More advanced military support could also be considered depending on the scale of the threat," Erdogan said in written ​responses to Newsweek.

The speaker of Turkey's parliament, which has yet to ratify the pact, said ​it could be expanded into a broader alliance "for the Muslim world", including Iran.

In New York, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told reporters on ‌Thursday that Tehran had conveyed a proposal to the US via intermediaries ​under which the Strait of Hormuz would be reopened ​if Tehran's conditions were met.

Under Iran's proposal, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon, within seven days. The US would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran's frozen funds and waive its oil sanctions, he said.

"The Strait of Hormuz will be reopened on the last day," Araqchi said, adding that talks with the US on other issues, including Iran's nuclear issue, ​would then start.

A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Wednesday that Tehran was ‌reviewing Washington's response to its peace proposals.

Oil prices fell on Friday as markets weighed the possibility of a truce, despite the number of ships recorded transiting the Strait of ​Hormuz dropping to nine on Thursday, half the 10-day average.

title: Americans navigate 'wild West' of health insurance after dropping Obamacare plans
description:
When Stacy Cox, a self-employed photographer in Kanab, Utah, dropped her Obamacare health insurance plan this year, routine preventive care became a financial dilemma. Now she finds herself weighing $1,200 for a mammogram against survival of her business.
"It's scary," the 49-year-old Cox told Reuters. "Every month we come to the table and we have a discussion. Is it ‌time to close a business?
fullText:
Sept 25 (Reuters) - When Stacy Cox, a self-employed photographer in Kanab, Utah, dropped her Obamacare health insurance plan this year, routine preventive care became a financial dilemma. Now she finds herself weighing $1,200 for a mammogram against survival of her business.

"It's scary," the 49-year-old Cox told Reuters. "Every month we come to the table and we have a discussion. Is it ‌time to close a business? Is it time to seek employment somewhere in the hopes of gaining health insurance?"

Cox is at high risk for breast cancer due to family history and has ‌an autoimmune disease requiring regular medications.

She is among 3 million Americans who dropped out of the Affordable Care Act marketplace, created by President Barack Obama and often called Obamacare, due to sharp increases in premiums and deductibles at the beginning of 2026.

The plans, which offer subsidies ​based on income, covered 19.2 million people as of February, according to government data. Expiration of enhanced COVID-era premium tax credits at the beginning of the year contributed to sharp cost increases.

Cox is one of nearly a dozen Americans who told Reuters they shifted to skimpy, short-term health plans that provide less comprehensive coverage, or have joined health-sharing programs, where members pool monthly contributions to help pay each other's medical bills. Many Americans have opted to go without health insurance altogether, a situation that the ACA was originally meant to address.

Several hospital operators have flagged rising costs tied to treating uninsured patients, including Universal Health Services, a Pennsylvania-based hospital system with more than 500 facilities. In July, its ‌CEO said it seemed most patients who had dropped ACA coverage were now ⁠uninsured.

Enrollment data on short-term coverage remains limited.

A spokesperson for the US Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said these plans, which are primarily designed to help fill a temporary coverage gap, such as when someone is transitioning from an employer-based plan, are one of several options available.

In the ACA marketplace, insurers have proposed a median premium increase of about ⁠15% for 2027, according to health policy research group KFF, marking the second successive year of double-digit hikes.

Enrollment for ACA plans opens November 1 and runs until January 15. UnitedHealth, Elevance, Centene and Molina Healthcare offer Obamacare plans. Some insurers, like UnitedHealth, also offer short-term plans.

Ryan Shapiro, 56, from Frederick, Maryland, plans to wind down his photography business by year end and help his wife run her interior design business, in part due to the rising cost of healthcare.

Shapiro dropped his ​ACA ​coverage for this year because his monthly premium was set to more than double to over $1,000. He instead chose a ​short-term plan that costs roughly $600 a month and covers hospitalization and critical illnesses.

Under current ‌federal rules, short-term plans are generally limited to three months, plus a one-month renewal. After CMS said last year it would stop enforcing that limit, several states allow longer coverage duration.

"It's half the cost of full-blown health insurance," Shapiro said. "It's a way for us to kind of minimize our expenses should a health crisis happen."

Several people interviewed said they had postponed or skipped preventive care, annual checkups and other treatment because of high premiums and deductibles, opting to pay out of pocket for urgent care when necessary.

"What do we do if one of us gets sick?" said Cox, who has skipped regular cancer screenings. "Do we just die? Because we sure can't afford to fight it, and that's a really scary place to be in."

High deductibles have been another pain point, forcing patients to pay thousands of dollars out of pocket for medical services before insurance coverage kicks in. Some also ‌said their plans offered a narrow choice of doctors.

Some people have turned to health-sharing programs, often organized by religious groups, ​that typically do not provide consumer protections.

Cristin Connelly, a 53-year-old public relations consultant in Atlanta, joined Zion HealthShare in 2025 after dropping ​her ACA plan. She pays $480 a month for herself and her young adult children, which includes an ​annual preventive doctor's visit for each family member, one mammogram a year and a colonoscopy every other year, among other services.

Her plan has a minimum spend of $5,000 for submission, ‌a de facto deductible Zion refers to as an initial unshareable amount individual members ​must pay before medical expenses become eligible for the ​community sharing pool.

Zion HealthShare, which has more than 78,000 active members, has no religious requirements.

"My experience with insurance is it's such a hassle to get things paid. They deny claims all the time and then say they're only paying a portion of it," said Connelly. Her health-share experience "so far has been that when I ask for a self-pay rate for anything, it's much less."

She said she hopes ​to move off the health share in the long run.

Experts say health-sharing arrangements and ‌other non-traditional products carry significant limitations.

Many states do not adequately police aggressive or deceptive marketing practices, said Sabrina Corlette, a research professor at Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms, leaving consumers ​vulnerable.

"There really and truly is a bit of a wild, wild West out there with respect to these products," Corlette said. "Some of them are legit, some of them not so legit, ​very much buyer beware!"

title: Trump and Xi toast 'peace' but Taiwan, trade and AI divides remain
description: Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go?
fullText:
US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping exchanged warm words at a lavish White House state dinner but gave little indication of progress on pressing issues.

Xi stressed that they should ensure AI remain "under human control" and act "as responsible major countries", while Trump toasted a future of "harmony, peace and success" for both nations.

But tensions remain despite the diplomatic niceties, including over Taiwan - with Xi urging Trump earlier in the day to take the "correct position" on the self-governing island which Beijing claims, amid a weapons package paused by Trump.

Billionaire business leaders and US tech CEOs joined the leaders at the extravagant dinner late on Thursday.

Their arrival was marked by protesters shouting from just outside the White House gates, some of whom were arrested.

Trump lavished praise on Xi during his first visit to the US in over a decade, telling those attending the dinner that while the two countries had "different systems", they had "never gotten along better".

Xi meanwhile welcomed the "historic juncture" in US-China relations - and said both leaders' ambitions could "surely be mutually reinforcing".

"China and the United States must act as responsible major countries to meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times, and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other," he said.

While Xi said he and Trump had shared "in-depth exchanges and reached common understanding on many issues", little mention was made of the crucial matters which divide the leaders of the world's two most powerful countries.

China believes the US is trying to contain its rise as a superpower, and it wants Washington to stay out of its way - particularly when it comes to trade, technology and Taiwan.

Trump has meanwhile been expected to aim for deals around trade and tariffs during the visit – like lowering Chinese tariffs on American goods, increasing imports of Chinese rare earth minerals, and increasing exports of US agricultural products.

Back at the White House after the dinner on Friday morning, Xi said he believed he and Trump were "charting the course for the great shift of China-US relations".

He also confirmed that the two men would meet two more times by year's end, at the end of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, or Apec, leaders' meeting in Shenzhen, China in November and again at the G20 held in Florida in November.

Trump has been blunt about his ambitions for artificial intelligence (AI) - and clear that he considers China to be the US's main rival for its development.

But beyond Xi's reference to AI remaining under "human control", little indication was given of what progress the two leaders may have made on the issue during their talks.

The dinner also came just hours after Chinese state media reported Xi had, behind closed doors, advised Washington to handle "with prudence" its approach to Taiwan. Washington is yet to comment publicly on the remarks.

The US is legally bound to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, but Trump delayed approving a $14bn (£11bn) arms package for it after Xi in May warned that mishandling the issue could cause the two countries to "collide or even enter into conflict".

At the time, Trump called it a "very good negotiating chip" with Beijing.

The evening marked a continuation of the lavish welcome Xi has so far received in the US.

Trump presented the Chinese president with a sculpture of a bald eagle - America's national symbol - saying it embodied "the free and soaring spirit of America". First Lady Melania had participated in its design, Trump added.

Others in attendance included key White House figures, such as Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, chief of staff Monica Crowley, and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

They were joined by scores of US officials, as well as conservative broadcasters, tech industry bosses, social media CEOs and corporate executives.

Apple's Tim Cook and Nvidia's Jensen Huang were seated at the same table as Trump and Xi, as was Elon Musk, who previously worked in Trump's administration leading the effort to shrink government.

OpenAI's Sam Altman, Google's Sundar Pichai, and Amazon's Jeff Bezos were also present, as were Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Yass, the American billionaire who owns a share of TikTok.

The leaders of companies including General Motors, Visa, Paramount Skydance and ExxonMobil could also be seen in the room.

"Everybody wanted to be there," Trump said ahead of the event. "I would say you have the entire tech world, the entire banking world, and a lot more."

One notable absence was Anthropic - one of the biggest and most valuable AI firms in the world. The BBC has asked Anthropic if it was invited, or if they chose not to be there.

The office of the First Lady Melania Trump, which planned the event, said the dinner menu would showcase "American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence".

The first course was yellow squash, wild mushrooms and crispy pancetta. The guests ate off red tablecloths - red being a symbol of luck and good fortune in China.

For their main course they dined on a sesame-crusted sea bass, braised bok choy and roasted eggplant.

Dessert featured the two leaders and their fellow diners tucking into vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit, with an accompanying ice cream "made with harvested White House honey".

The wine chosen by the first lady included Schramsberg Blanc De Noir - a nod to President Nixon's 1972 "Toast to Peace" with former Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai, when they used a bottle from the same vineyard.

Trump and Xi began the final day of their visit on Friday with tea at the White House's Red Room with their wives.

The group then headed to the US National Archives for a tour of the building and its exhibits.

Formally called the National Archives and Records Administration, the building holds some of the most important documents regarding the founding of the United States - including the US Constitution, the Declaration of Independence and the Bill of Rights.

Xi and his wife are expected to depart Washington later in the day.

title: Internal DOJ charts show agency bleeding staff as caseloads surge
description:
A drastically diminished Justice Department workforce is struggling to keep up with its civil side caseloads, according to documents obtained by The Hill and NewsNation.
A series of charts, apparently inadvertently shared and then recalled, show how the number of attorneys within the civil division has plummeted under the Trump administration.
The charts substantiate a dynamic long suspected: that the Department of Justice (DOJ) would not be able to swiftly replace a crew of veteran attorneys after a wave of firings and resignations.
fullText:
A drastically diminished Justice Department workforce is struggling to keep up with its civil side caseloads, according to documents obtained by The Hill and NewsNation.

A series of charts, apparently inadvertently shared and then recalled, show how the number of attorneys within the civil division has plummeted under the Trump administration.

The charts substantiate a dynamic long suspected: that the Department of Justice (DOJ) would not be able to swiftly replace a crew of veteran attorneys after a wave of firings and resignations.

Stacey Young, who founded the DOJ alumni group Justice Connection, described the staff turnover as a “massive exodus.”

“The workload has skyrocketed, particularly in the civil division offices that have lost the most lawyers. So what we’re seeing is that the lawyers who are left are overworked, stressed out, many have lost those who led their office because they were pushed out by this administration. And because of the difficult circumstances under which they’re working, I expect that the rate of departures won’t slow down anytime soon,” she told The Hill.

“Putting out this data seems to me like a desperate cry for help. It seems like the civil division knows how badly it needs more funds to hire more lawyers to make up for the purge of longstanding experts that they caused.”

According to the Office of Personnel Management, the Justice Department has lost roughly 10,000 workers since the start of the Trump administration, a metric that includes component agencies like the FBI and the Federal Bureau of Prisons.

In graph after graph, the charts track data from the start of the Trump administration through August, showing a significant decline in civil division staff as caseloads have steadily ticked up.

DOJ defended the workload, saying it has hired new staff.

“The Civil Division is working every day to advance and defend the President’s agenda in court, and it is winning. Since the start of this Administration, the Civil Division has hired over 200 new attorneys with many 

“Civil Division attorneys have achieved countless wins in courts across the country and secured billions of dollars in fraud recoveries for the American people,” they added.

One chart reviewing impact on each branch within the division detailed how caseload was skyrocketing — with work for the commercial litigation branch jumping a whopping 84 percent per attorney, while lawyers in the Office of Immigration Litigation saw their workload jump 63 percent.

Attorneys who work on appeals saw their caseloads jump 54 percent while lawyers in the federal programs branch — those who work on defending executive orders among other administration priorities — saw their workloads jump 44 percent.

The number of attorneys in the federal programs branch dropped from 113 to 71 just within the first few months of the Trump administration. A jump in cases has largely settled to around 1,000, but they are being handled by a diminished team.

Jennifer Ricketts, a former Justice Department attorney who led the federal programs branch, said the swift exodus shows how many longtime attorneys who defended presidential priorities across administrations likely began looking for a new job as soon as President Trump won the election.

“They were aware of how much in the first Trump administration they tried to stretch the law and put us in positions where we struggled to make sure we satisfied our professional responsibilities and folks did not want to have to go through that exercise again,” she said of the branch.

“You don’t get jobs really quickly. So they had already started looking after the election, so it was not tied to any specific decision. It was the anticipation of what they may do, especially given how aggressive they said they were going to be and how aggressive we had seen them be in Trump one …. I think folks knew maybe not the scope of what was coming, but they knew none of it was going to be pleasant.”

One of the other most significant declines in staffing — combined with one of the highest rises in cases — was in the Office of Immigration Litigation, which has seen cases surge amid Trump’s pledge to carry out the largest mass deportation operation in history.

The Office of Immigration Litigation handles both individual immigration cases being heard at the Board of Immigration Appeals as well as immigration matters brought in federal district court, such as habeas corpus cases brought by migrants being held in detention. Habeas petitions have soared alongside detention rates as the administration has largely cut off access to bond hearings.

One former staffer from the immigration office noted the steady decline in staff in that branch, with attorneys going from 320 down to 243 as cases climbed from roughly 7,700 to nearly 9,500.

“We never had attrition like we’ve had. There’s been a lot of reasons for that,” the former staffer said.

Early in the administration, the Justice Department moved the branch’s leader to a new sanctuary city task force, and the Justice Department later made headlines for firing Erez Reuveni, a longtime Office of Immigration Litigation staffer, after he acknowledged in court that Kilmar Abrego Garcia had been mistakenly deported.

“When our colleague Erez Reuveni got fired, I think there were a lot of people that were saying, ‘If that could happen to him that could happen to any of us,’” the former staffer continued. “And I think that people just started looking, and you know, workload’s gone up. The office has sort of tried to recover from those blows … But it’s been increasingly challenging for people to do that. I think there’s a lot of unhappy people.”

“With caseload going up and the resources going down, it just makes it challenging,” they added.

Also surprising is the attrition among appellate staff attorneys, though their ranks have been rising over the last several months.

“It’s a very plum section, very elite section, and if folks leave there, they would often go to the solicitor general’s office or some other very prestigious placement,” Ricketts said, referencing the team of attorneys for the solicitor who argue before the Supreme Court.

While staffing in that branch hasn’t dipped as much as others, their caseload has increased substantially because the Trump administration has been appealing so many of its losses in court.

Though now down six attorneys from the 61 it began with, the number of appealed cases went from around 780 at the start of the administration to more than 1,100 last month.

“They will appeal everything. I mean, it does not appear to be an administration that takes losses. They do not seem to be worried about creating bad law in the court of appeals. They seem to be pursuing a very aggressive interpretation of executive branch authority, and so they are willing to roll the dice and take it up,” Ricketts said.

“I think my sense is they have a sense that the Supreme Court is willing to accept more of those ideas, what would have been considered extreme ideas, than we ever imagined, and so why not?”

Similarly to the Office of Immigration Litigation, the commercial litigation branch has also seen a consistent loss in staff — dropping from 350 at the start of the administration down to 289 — while caseloads have jumped from around 13,000 to nearly 19,000.

It’s hard to know what has driven the surge in caseload in the branch, which handles a wide variety of matters from cases where the government has a financial interest to intellectual property to those who represent the U.S. in cases in foreign courts.

But it does include two areas where there has been more active litigation.

The commercial litigation branch includes fraud — a topic of great interest to the Trump administration as it probes entitlement programs.

It also handles cases before the Merit Systems Protection Board, the quasi judicial board responsible for reviewing federal employee workplace challenges, including wrongful termination cases that have surged as the Trump administration pushed to reduce the size of the government.

After the email with the charts was sent last week, it was quickly recalled.

Sources suspect the graphs are preparation for the next budget cycle.

“Somewhere along the line, somebody in the division or the department is going to use this data to justify asking for more resources,” the former Office of Immigration Litigation staffer said.

They noted that none of the graphs start its axis at zero, a choice that emphasizes the rise in cases and fall in staff.

“They ginned up the charts to make that visually apparent,” they said.

The Justice Department has already made efforts to recruit more staff. In May, the department promised something largely unheard of in the federal government — a $25,000 signing bonus to those joining the civil division.

But it’s unclear if that’s working.

“DOJ had never given signing bonuses to try to attract applicants. These jobs were some of the most competitive legal jobs in the field. The fact that they’re now having to provide financial incentives for people to apply shows you just how desperate they are,” Young said.

“And we know that job openings that used to attract hundreds or thousands of applications are now attracting almost none.”

The Justice Department took a number of actions shortly after Trump took office that flushed staff and prompted headlines.

In the criminal division, the Justice Department fired those who had worked on cases involving Trump. In the civil division, many branch leaders were reassigned to take on unrelated work. The U.S. pardon attorney lost her job after she refused to certify that actor Mel Gibson should have his gun rights restored. And still more attorneys sought and gained jobs outside the department or availed themselves of a government buyout spearheaded by Elon Musk.

At the beginning of the administration, the Justice Department also withdrew offers to recent graduates who had been given entry level jobs through the prestigious Attorney General’s Honors Program, cutting off a pipeline of young attorneys from top schools who then rise through the ranks of the department.

“It reflects what we’ve been saying all along. This situation is untenable when you have an office that is experiencing a surge of cases because of this administration’s lawless conduct at a time when lawyers are fleeing the department. The administration won’t be able to defend itself in court,” Young said.

“DOJ lawyers, in the best of times, are overworked. Their workloads right now have increased exponentially, especially when it comes to civil division lawyers, and as their workloads continue to increase, more will leave, and the problem will just keep getting worse and worse.”

title: Iran's president offers to dilute uranium and allow inspections in push for U.S. deal
description:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian flatly denied Thursday that Tehran wants a nuclear bomb while claiming Iran is willing to submit its nuclear program for international inspection, blaming Washington for the nearly seven-month war in the Middle East and accusing it of blocking diplomacy.
Asked point-blank during an exclusive interview on Fox News’ "Special Report," "Do you want a nuclear bomb or not?" Pezeshkian firmly rejected the premise.
"Not at all. Not at all.
fullText:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian flatly denied Thursday that Tehran wants a nuclear bomb while claiming Iran is willing to submit its nuclear program for international inspection, blaming Washington for the nearly seven-month war in the Middle East and accusing it of blocking diplomacy.

Asked point-blank during an exclusive interview on Fox News’ "Special Report," "Do you want a nuclear bomb or not?" Pezeshkian firmly rejected the premise.

"Not at all. Not at all. Our martyred, esteemed supreme leader had announced several times that, from a religious decree, it is unholy. It is illegal," he told Bret Baier, referencing religious edicts issued against weapons of mass destruction.

IRAN 'ALREADY AGREED' TO GIVING UP NUCLEAR WEAPON AMBITIONS, TRUMP REVEALS

The Iranian leader's public denial came amid long-term international scrutiny of Iran’s nuclear program and its enrichment of uranium to levels well beyond those typically used for civilian nuclear power.

This became President Donald Trump's central rationale for launching Operation Epic Fury in February.

On Thursday, however, Pezeshkian indicated Tehran would be open to lowering its enrichment levels and allowing outside verification as part of an effort to ease nuclear tensions.

"So, that weapon's mass destruction. We said we’re willing to dilute them. It’s not a big deal. We are willing to submit ourselves to verification," he said.

Pezeshkian also pointed to the failed memorandum of understanding, or MOU, signed by him and President Donald Trump in June intended to halt hostilities and establish a framework for a broader U.S.-Iran agreement.

The process was intended by Washington to lead to an end to Iran’s nuclear ambitions and included a 60-day process toward that final agreement.

"We have no problems. We did reach an agreement with your president," Pezeshkian said of Trump, who signed the agreement.

"That agreement was signed, and, based on that, we are willing and still wish to move forward.

IRAN NUCLEAR DEAL HINGES ON IAEA ACCESS TO LONG-BLOCKED ATOMIC WEAPON SITES, EXPERTS SAY

"And the framework was agreed upon. We had not closed the Strait of Hormuz; it was open without any legal justification or framework," he said.

"They attacked us. They assassinated and martyred our esteemed supreme leader, our scientists, our military commanders and government."

Pezeshkian then criticized Washington for the subsequent breakdown in diplomacy but insisted Tehran remains prepared to reach an agreement.

"The problem is that America, instead of conducting dialog, they descend into the arena by bombing us first, by blocking every pathway. We are ready," he said.

"This is not the way to conduct yourself on the world stage. They can have free access to see whatever we have, but not to put us under such pressure, under blockades, deny us access."

Pezeshkian also placed broader blame on Washington for the war.

"We do not seek to kill Americans, as shown by actions, demonstrable actions. America has sought to kill Iranians," Pezeshkian said. "What we know is that if we’re attacked, we must defend ourselves."

TRUMP BETS ECONOMIC PRESSURE CAN SQUEEZE IRAN AS REGIME’S OWN FAILURES DEEPEN THE PAIN

Addressing U.S. military strikes — including Operation Outcast — and increasing secondary sanctions, Pezeshkian said Iran would continue resisting Washington’s campaign.

"This is something that has been the doing of the United States," he said. "We will keep resisting. We will find ways, and the life of our country will continue. We will remain.

"Yes, we do have economic issues, certainly. But in order to remain, we will go through any hardship and endure.

"If America thinks that they can keep sanctioning us, we have nothing to do, nor do we consider any type of American elections. If the current American government, within international legal frameworks, wishes to reach an agreement, fine. If not, before the elections or after the elections, what difference does it make for us?"

Pezeshkian repeated that Iran does not want the war to continue, while blaming Israel for helping provoke the conflict and putting responsibility on Washington to bring it to an end.

TRUMP GIVES EVERY NATION AN EASY CHOICE: DO BUSINESS WITH AMERICA OR TERRORIST IRAN

"We will stand resolutely to defend ourselves. We never sought war. We do not seek war," he said.

"I deeply believe that humans should not cause the death of another human. But with the instigations conducted by Israel, they have imposed this war on us.

"But we do not wish to continue. It’s America that must choose whether it wants to end this or not."

The Iranian president also addressed reports that Iranian forces used Chinese satellite imagery to carry out a deadly strike on a U.S. base in Jordan. The attack resulted in the deaths of three U.S. service members.

When questioned about the reports, Pezeshkian denied direct knowledge.

"I’m specifically unaware of these purported images that you talk about," Pezeshkian said.

"Now, what do militaries do with one another between two countries? It is their own business within their own guidelines."

title: Inside Trump's plan for the 'biggest DOJ election observer effort in history'
description:
A voting booth sits at a polling station in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, in April 2020. - Thomas Werner/Bloomberg/Getty Images/File
President Donald Trump and his allies inside and outside his administration are aiming to blanket polling places with an expanding network of party and federal election monitors this November, intensifying scrutiny of the nuts and bolts of voting as Trump hunts for what he claims, without evidence, is widespread cheating and fraud in US elections.
Trump’s Justice Department says it will dispatch more than 1,000 monitors on Election Day in what Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon has called the “biggest DOJ election observer effort in history” — hundreds more than the Biden administration deployed in 2024. New records reviewed by CNN suggest that several DOJ monitors deployed during this year’s primaries helped challenge Trump’s 2020 election loss. Another pleaded guilty to illegally accessing a government elections website in 2016.
fullText:
President Donald Trump and his allies inside and outside his administration are aiming to blanket polling places with an expanding network of party and federal election monitors this November, intensifying scrutiny of the nuts and bolts of voting as Trump hunts for what he claims, without evidence, is widespread cheating and fraud in US elections.

Trump’s Justice Department says it will dispatch more than 1,000 monitors on Election Day in what Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon has called the “biggest DOJ election observer effort in history” — hundreds more than the Biden administration deployed in 2024. New records reviewed by CNN suggest that several DOJ monitors deployed during this year’s primaries helped challenge Trump’s 2020 election loss. Another pleaded guilty to illegally accessing a government elections website in 2016.

While most jurisdictions that hosted DOJ monitors during the primaries reported no issues with their presence, federal observers sent to Wyoming were accused of disruptive behavior by Republican officials in the state.

Critically, there is no evidence that the monitoring efforts will disrupt polling places or prevent anyone from voting in November. Justice Department monitors and partisan observers have long been part of Election Day.

Separately, the Republican National Committee is training new “special monitors” to scrutinize voting machines — recording serial numbers, inspecting security seals and photographing results tapes — and report any concerns or discrepancies to the party’s legal team through a special hotline, according to RNC training materials from Wisconsin that have not previously been reported on.

The effort comes as Trump and his allies intensify claims that voting machines are vulnerable to hacking and fraud, with some seeking to ban them altogether.

“Having you all on the ground, notifying us of issues, allows us to take direct action,” an RNC official told a group of special monitors in Wisconsin on a July training call. “And this leads to real outcomes that benefit Republicans across the state.”

It marks the latest expansion of a Republican election monitoring apparatus that has grown dramatically since 2020 and helped generate anecdotes, allegations and legal challenges questioning whether recent elections were run properly and transparently.

title: Trump Is Destroying Public Health. Democrats Need to Fight Back.
description: Gregg...
fullText:
If they win in the midterms, the party must move quickly and aggressively to undo the harm Trump and his cronies have caused.

It is truly difficult to keep up with the pace of OMB Director Russell Vought and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy’s Jr.’s assaults on public health, biomedicine, and science. Over the past week or so, Vought has decided that he must have control over grant funding at the National Institutes of Health. His larger attempt to put all federal grant funding under his thumb was sidelined by Congress, so he is getting President Trump to issue an Executive Order giving him this authority, whether it is legal or not. Over at Health and Human Services, RFK Jr. has seized control over the US Preventive Services Task Force, and is doing what he did to the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices last year: gutting it and filling the seats with cronies and crackpots.

The USPSTF is our nation’s premier arbiter of preventive services—overseeing everything from disease screening (e.g., mammograms and colonoscopies) to preventive therapies (e.g., pre-exposure prophylaxis against HIV infection). Insurers are statutorily compelled to cover highly rated interventions without cost sharing for all Americans. Now those ratings will be judged by the charlatans in RFK Jr.’s inner circle.

The damage these two men have done and will continue to do is without parallel in American history. Their actions will cost lives, make people sick, and set back research and innovation in the United States for a generation or more. And it is time to stop treating them like ordinary political actors. Vought and RFK Jr. are out-of-control zealots with no rational policy goals. To treat them otherwise is to invest their deep sociopathy with credibility. Trofim Lysenko, the Soviet agronomist whose policies led to the deaths of millions of Russians, didn’t “have a point,” and you didn’t have to “hand it to him” in his criticism of the orthodoxy of Mendelian genetics. You certainly didn’t have to find a way to “collaborate on shared goals” to make the USSR healthy again. He was a monster. These two men are too.

While I think it’s critical to catalogue what these men have wrought, it’s more important to try to stop them. To the credit of many working in public health, science, and medicine, there has been a growing resistance to Vought and RFK Jr. That pressure helped successfully tank Vought’s recent efforts to take over grant-making, while many professional societies have stepped up to offer alternatives to the lunacy of HHS’s public health recommendations and sued the federal government. There are also brave solo actors who have risked their careers in speaking out.

But there is an opportunity on the horizon to do much more to restore public health, biomedicine, and science in the US. If the Democrats win control over one or both chambers of Congress this fall, they must act decisively to reverse as much of the Trump-era damage as possible.No half-measures will be sufficient; the Democratic inclination for everything to be bipartisan needs to be weighed against the real costs in human lives and suffering that this kind of political deal-making entails. Otherwise, the Democrats will be complicit as deaths continue to mount from this Administration’s policies. We need to play hardball, even if it rubs the denizens of Capitol Hill the wrong way.

There is so much to do. We need to reverse the budget cuts that have decimated federal agencies. Then we should go down the list of Vought and RFK Jr.’s greatest hits and reverse whatever policies we can by statute. Democrats should use reconciliation, tie provisions to must-pass bills, and consider the nuclear option of changing the rules on the use of the filibuster in the Senate. Yes, Trump can veto bills and the usual horse-trading is still going to need to happen, but if you start negotiations at what you can agree on with this GOP, you are already conceding too much. And outside the legislative arena, control over the House and/or Senate offers ways to hold these men and their underlings accountable. Democrats should bring them to testify before committees, subpoena documents from agencies and the White House, and private actors who have been key participants in their efforts, and consider impeachment proceedings for the lot of them.

Perhaps this sounds too brazen, too far from the world of DC realpolitik, and members of Congress will think, “Oh, we couldn’t possibly do that,” or, “Well, we are really focused on affordability for 2028.” But this kind of reticence and evasion masks a fundamental misunderstanding of what has just happened in the US. Covid was a once-in-a-generation pandemic. It killed over 1 million of us here in this country. But Russell Vought and RFK Jr. are deadlier than a virus. The world of hurt inflicted on millions of Americans (and millions more around the globe) by this administration is a catastrophe. It demands an extraordinary response.

Between the reemergence of right-wing red-baiting and Donald Trump’s use of the chilling National Security Presidential Memorandum–7 to criminalize left political organizing, we’re seeing McCarthyism reborn before our eyes. 

This assault on democracy cannot be ignored or wished away. Resisting it requires bravery in the face of threats and repression, a steadfast commitment to the truth, and the unwavering belief that we can—and will—overcome this darkness.

We must have an independent media that sets the record straight, unearths corruption and abuses of power, and advances a politics of justice and dignity for all if we’re to win this fight.

That’s why I’m writing to you today. This September, The Nation needs to add 100 monthly donors to sustain our progressive journalism. Your contribution makes the next investigative report, the next truth-speaking column, and the next pathbreaking essay all possible. 

I hope you’ll support our work with a recurring donation today. If you donate $10 or more a month, we’ll send you a brand new “Hands Off the Free Press!” sticker to recognise your commitment to our cause. Please, donate today.

Onward,

Katrina vanden Heuvel
Editor and Publisher, The Nation

title: I Tried Snap Specs, and They Could Be the Future of Smart Glasses
description: Snap Specs put a standalone spatial display on your face.
fullText:
Snap was in the smart glasses game from the jump. The company’s original camera-equipped Spectacles debuted back in 2016, beating Meta to the market by five years. Meta’s Ray-Bans and Oakleys captured massive consumer mindshare anyway, while Snap’s smart eyewear has been less visible.

With Snap Specs, though, the company is aiming to make up for lost time by delivering smart glasses that go beyond a hidden camera and voice-activated AI. At the Snapdragon 2026 Summit, I got my hands (and eyes) on a pair of Snap’s soon-to-be-released spatial-computing glasses that overlay digital graphics onto the physical world.

There's a lot of tech packed into these black polymer frames. They're powered by two Snapdragon processors, with two full-color hi-res cameras facing outward; the tracking system supports 6DOF (six degrees of freedom) hand tracking for gesture controls; and it's all standalone, as there's no tether or wired puck handling the heavy lifting. With all that crammed into the frames, plus the battery to run it, you'd expect them to be heavy. At around 135 grams, they aren’t light, but Specs are surprisingly comfortable. The weight is distributed evenly, mainly across the frames, so for the brief time I used them, they remained ergonomically acceptable. Specs feel more like a pair of sunglasses than a bulky VR helmet. As for battery life, Snap promises four hours of mixed-use on a full charge.

In the interest of not alienating the people around you, Snap chose to make the lenses clear enough that your eyes can still be seen through them, but if you want to close out the world, there’s electrochromic dimming for quick transitions between clear and dark lenses. It both useful and a cool trick. Check it out:

The in-glasses display is surprisingly bright. Specs' visuals are powered by a proprietary liquid crystal on silicon (LCoS) display system, and even when used in a light-filled conference room, I could still clearly see the UI and its various apps. I tested out YouTube under these borderline abusive conditions, and it streamed high-def video in 16 million colors suitably.

The display offers a 51-degree field of view. It feels like having a large floating window hovering in front of you. From there, you can use simple gestures to launch apps, watch movies, play games, and do most other tasks you can’t do from your phone. But it was the context-aware, real-world spatial computing tasks that I wanted to try—the things you can't do from a phone or PC.

Snap plans to launch Specs with a full suite of both first-party and third-party apps that will do everything from improving your drawing skills to teaching you music. I tried out a golfing demo, and it made the possibilities of augmented reality glasses immediately clear. Instead of putting blindly toward a distant hole, Specs show you exactly which direction to swing the putter and adds a virtual flag to mark where the hole is. It’s anecdotal evidence, but my personal putting game improved immensely. Is it cheating? Probably, but it works.

A half-hour or so of testing a prototype isn’t enough time to really say whether these will be useful in a person’s real life, but I can say for sure that they’re very cool, and I’m looking forward to going more in-depth with them in the coming months as their release date approaches. Snap Specs are planned for release this fall and will retail for $2,195.

title: Wales out to prove they are no one-hit wonder
description: Wales and USA will both be looking to back up impressive WXV opening round victories when they go head-to-head at Cardiff Arms Park on Saturday.
fullText:
Resurgent, inspired, unrecognisable, brave - pick one. Each describes Wales' performance against South Africa in their WXV opener.

Sean Lynn's side scored eight tries against one of the rising forces in women's rugby in one of the best displays of their professional era.

But they know they cannot afford to bask in glory. Wales must now prove they are more than a one-hit wonder when they return to Cardiff Arms Park on Saturday.

The next - and even bigger - challenge is USA, who, like the Springboks, have rocketed up the world rankings and are now a top six team.

The Eagles looked down and out in Dublin, but scored 28 unanswered points to secure a remarkable comeback victory over Ireland.

So we have two teams with confidence and momentum and two teams who are backing themselves to back it up. It should make for an interesting contest.

Saturday, 26 September at 15:00 BST

Live on BBC One, iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app, with live text coverage

One of the few disappointments against South Africa is that Wales did not see more of the promising Keira Bevan and Seren Lockwood half-back partnership.

Lockwood failed a first-half head injury assessment which paved the way for Lleucu George to reclaim the 10 shirt, with Bevan moving back to scrum-half.

And that is what Lynn has gone with this week.

He has also recalled Carys Cox, who replaces Seren Singleton on the wing after the former's recovery from knee surgery in the summer.

Georgia Evans will win her 50th cap, while there are three new faces on the bench in Molly Reardon, Sian Jones and Nikita Prothero.

Wales recall George and Cox to backline for USA

Wales suffer scrum-half Lockwood blow for USA Test

USA have also had a bit of a reshuffle after their triumph in Dublin, with theirs being a six-day turnaround compared to Wales' eight.

Head coach Jack Hanratty has given Nina Mason a start at fly-half after impressing on her debut.

Mason's Life University team-mate Bella Vogel shifts to inside centre to accommodate Emily Henrich at 13, while Katana Howard joins the replacements.

Wales ended a run of nine consecutive Test defeats against South Africa and will be looking to make it back-to-back Test wins for the first time in the Sean Lynn era.

USA are on a decent run, having beaten Ireland and South Africa in their last two outings. They also enjoyed a convincing victory over Australia in the Pacific Four Series earlier this year.

Wales head coach Sean Lynn said: "We produced a performance against South Africa that demonstrated that we have moved the dial and all the hard work we put in during pre-season was there for all to see.

"We know we have to back that performance up against a fit, fast and athletic USA side which will turn up full of confidence after their win against Ireland.

"The Welsh public saw the style of play we are committed to building, and we play for them and want to make them proud.

"To have their noisy support and backing at Cardiff Arms Park on Saturday can only inspire this Wales squad."

USA head coach Jack Hanratty said: "A win can be massive for the group and although we were in a battle, the energy since (last week) has been vibrant. Not just because of the win, but because of the potential.

"We have the opportunity to go three international wins in a row, which is no easy feat but this is a real challenge.

"Wales showed massive dominance and look like they have a new DNA when they played South Africa last weekend - which are a team that we had a real arm wrestle with this past summer.

"The quick six-day turnaround for us, versus an eight-day for Wales, is big in preparation, so this week we have to get right."

Feaunati returns as England brace for Black Ferns

McLachlan & Wills back from injury to face Australia

BBC One Wales commentator Gareth Rhys Owen said: "Wales produced their best performance in a long time against South Africa, and the result was arguably even more significant than it might have appeared.

"Much of our commentary focused on explaining the level of the opposition. South Africa's women are not the equivalent of their all-conquering men, but they are a rapidly developing side who arguably went into the match as favourites. The manner of Wales' victory, therefore, was hugely encouraging.

"The same context is important ahead of the USA game. The Americans are a very good side, as they demonstrated by roaring back against Ireland, and will provide another significant test of Wales' progress.

"The question for Wales is a simple one: was South Africa a one-off, a rare bright light in a difficult period, or a genuine sign of things to come?"

title: Packers booed during 'butt-whooping' at home to Falcons
description: The Green Bay Packers' head coach Matt LaFleur says his team got a "butt-whooping" as they lost 35-14 at home to the Atlanta Falcons on Thursday.
fullText:
The Green Bay Packers' head coach Matt LaFleur said his team got a "butt-whooping" as they lost 35-14 at home to the Atlanta Falcons on Thursday.

The Packers were booed by their own fans as they were well beaten by a Falcons team that lost 34-3 at home to the Carolina Panthers on Sunday.

Although a depleted Green Bay opened the scoring at Lambeau Field, the Falcons hit back with 27 unanswered points.

Their 498 yards on offence included 242 rushing yards, while Green Bay's total 328 yards featured just 17 from nine carries.

"They had 500 yards of offence, we had whatever it was - it was a butt-whooping," said LaFleur.

"I'm not going to put it on one thing. We definitely have to respond better but that was at least a three-quarter butt-whooping right there."

The Falcons' offence struggled as they lost their first two games of the NFL season but quarterback Michael Penix Jr's return from knee surgery helped them bounce back.

Running back Bijan Robinson rushed for two touchdowns and 194 yards, and added 19 receiving yards, while Drake London racked up 194 receiving yards from just nine catches.

The Packers were already without defensive star Micah Parsons and running back Josh Jacobs but lost two offensive linemen to injury in last week's win at the New York Jets.

Although the hosts took the lead through a Christian Watson touchdown, the Falcons then took charge with Bijan Robinson, Austin Hooper and Brian Robinson Jr all getting into the endzone while Nick Folk added two field goals.

Matthew Golden's touchdown stopped the rot for the Packers but Bijan Robinson claimed his second score late on to seal an emphatic win for the Falcons.

Both teams now have a 1-2 record, with Green Bay visiting Tampa Bay next Sunday while Atlanta travel to divisional rivals New Orleans a week on Monday.

title: Transfer windows & drones among ideas to boost cycling
description: A new report from cycling's world governing body proposes a series of changes to boost the sport - and improve safety.
fullText:
Transfer windows, team budget caps and drones replacing convoy vehicles at races are three of the ideas to boost cycling in a new report from the sport's global governing body.

The Union Cycliste Internationale's (UCI) report, entitled "Future of Cycling", examined road cycling and heard from 55 stakeholders including professional teams, national federations, race organisers and some riders.

It aims to turn a "large but passive audience into active, loyal fandom", admitting cycling's under-35 audience was "under-represented" and there was a need to "strengthen its appeal".

"While the sport today enjoys strong and growing popularity across five continents, its media exposure and the revenue it generates for its stakeholders do not yet fully reflect its potential," it said.

Among the most frequently referenced recommendations were:

A more coherent race calendar based on geography with fewer overlaps

More predictable rider participation in races alongside transfer windows and fees

Simplifying the ranking and category system

A stronger second division with clearer pathways

Continued growth of women's cycling

A financial fairness mechanism, such as a budget cap on teams

The combined total budget of professional UCI tour teams in 2025 was £731m (850m euros), but individual team budgets vary.

Long-discussed budget caps, aimed at evening out the peloton and increasing "financial fairness", would improve the attractiveness of the sport for investors according to the UCI.

But it admitted any such mechanism remains the biggest point of difference for stakeholders and would be at the heart of upcoming discussions.

Meanwhile work on a new transfer system and rider-agent regulation was already under way, it said.

One of the main pillars of the report was safety. Its publication comes a month after the death of Welsh teenager Finlay Tarling who was in collision with a non-race vehicle at the Volta a Portugal.

The UCI said it had seen wide support for stricter, evidence-based course-design, minimum standards for barriers and protective infrastructure around climbs and descents, with several contributors calling for greater use of circuit-style finishes.

It recommended reviewing the number of convoy vehicles – especially motorbikes - and greater use of drones.

Also, it noted near-universal backing for GPS tracking and some interest in features such as brake lights.

UCI president David Lappartient said road cycling was "experiencing unprecedented growth".

He added: "That success comes with responsibilities.

"The first of these responsibilities is safety. It is not negotiable, and it will move forward at an even faster pace than the other parts of the reform."

The riders' union, the Cyclistes Professionnels Associes (CPA), has been approached for comment.

The 21-year-old is set to make her Test debut off the bench after impressing for Munster during the Women's Interprovincial Championship.

The United States staged a remarkable second-half comeback to beat Ireland in Tallaght on Sunday.

Ireland led 31-12 before four successive tries helped the Americans to a memorable success.

Ireland: Flood; Parsons, McGann, Higgins, Elmes Kinlan; O'Brien, Reilly; O'Dowd, Jones, Cahill; Wall, Tuite-O'Sullivan; Hogan, King (capt), Adams Verling.

Replacements: Buttimer, McGrath, Djougang, Clohessy, Moore, Lane, Dalton, Gallagher.

title: Red Roses struggle to meet fans' selfie demands - Hunt
description: England scrum-half Natasha Hunt says it is no longer possible to satisfy fans' post-match requests for selfies and autographs, given the Red Roses' success and growth.
fullText:
England scrum-half Natasha Hunt says it is no longer possible to satisfy fans' post-match requests for selfies and autographs, given the Red Roses' success and growth over the past decade.

Hunt, 37, made her England debut in 2011, when the team were regularly playing in front of three-figure crowds.

Even in 2019, an attendance of 4,674 at the Women's Six Nations game against France set a new record for a standalone Red Roses game away from a Rugby World Cup.

More than 50,000 tickets have been sold for Saturday's meeting with New Zealand at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium, a year on from a world record sell-out crowd of 81,885 who watched the Red Roses beat Canada to become world champions at the venue.

"I didn't think ever in my lifetime I would be in a position where we'd get crowds the size that we do," Hunt told Rugby Union Weekly.

"It is unbelievable and we definitely don't take it lightly.

"We're so appreciative and we absolutely adore our fans and love them and what they do for us and have done for us.

"But I do think we're in a tricky space at the minute where there's that expectation that everyone has to have a photo or a signature or something.

"Sometimes you go and you see people and they will say 'can you go get Ellie [Kildunne]? Can you go get Meg [Jones]?' And I really can't because they're probably being bombarded by 700 people over there.

"Some of the girls have had DMs saying 'it would have made our day, we're disappointed' and it breaks your heart because you want everyone to have the best time ever."

Saturday, 26 September, 15:00 BST

Live on BBC iPlayer and BBC Sport website and app, with accompanying live text commentary

The same issue has emerged in women's football, with Women's Super League club Chelsea banning their players from posing for photos and signing autographs after matches - saying that although it was a "tough" decision, it was "no longer safe or sustainable".

Former Chelsea and England defender Millie Bright previously expressed concern that players were become "collectibles" to fans, emphasising that "we are humans the same as you" in an Instagram post., external

Hunt says players' performances, possible injury concerns, recovery schedule and family commitments can all affect their ability to interact with fans after games.

"If one of the girls is injured or they've not had the best game, their capacity and energy to come to you and give back might be a little bit less than others on that day," she added.

"I'm not saying we don't want to have the photos and autographs, but there is a cap on the time where we have to be back in the changing rooms doing the recovery.

"And family is huge for us, let us see our families first.

"We'll do everything we can to make your day, but just be aware we're doing our best so please just bear with us."

Hunt says that in the early days of her Test career, it wasn't possible to imagine such a problem.

"It was everyone's parents at Esher Rugby Club back in the day," she added.

"I would have been out there for 20 minutes, signed everything twice over, everyone had a chat with me, then gone in [to the changing room]!"

The Red Roses have partly built their relationship with their growing fanbase by engaging as people, as well as players.

Captain Jones' openness about her grief for her parents, and star full-back Kildunne's willingness to talk about her body dysmorphia are just two examples.

A recent survey,, external carried out by The Good, The Scaz and The Rugby podcast, revealed a difference in what attracted different genders to women's rugby, with 62% of women, compared to 41% of men, saying they "watch women's rugby because I identify with the players' causes, interests or specific challenges that players face".

title: Premier League joins call for Fifa reforms
description: The Premier League joins three of its top European counterparts in calling for "fundamental" reform of the way that world football's governing body Fifa is run.
fullText:
The Premier League has joined three of its top European counterparts in calling for "fundamental" reform of the way that Fifa is run, claiming its president Gianni Infantino has "actively promoted exploitative ideas".

In a joint statement with Spain's La Liga, Germany's Bundesliga, and Italy's Serie A, the English top flight says it is speaking out "because we understand how Fifa's relentless expansionism affects everyone".

The four leagues say the shake-up is needed to make world football's governing body "transparent, objective, proportionate and inclusive" and claim that "our sport cannot grow globally if its foundations are undermined".

It comes days after Infantino proposed an external review of how Fifa operates amid the ongoing crisis over his failed plan to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors, which sparked a global outcry.

Referencing "one of the biggest abuses of power in Fifa's history", the four leagues say that "while football's stakeholders ultimately forced the withdrawal of the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, the conditions that led to FFE remain".

The statement added: "The Fifa president has now acknowledged the need for reform, but it is not enough for surface-level, process changes to be explored in the aftermath of FFE – fundamental governance reform is essential to restore clear constitutional boundaries within Fifa, including confidence that individual disciplinary matters remain demonstrably insulated from political interference."

That is known to be a reference to the cancelled suspension of United States forward Folarin Balogun at the World Cup after US President Donald Trump called Infantino asking for the striker's ban to be reviewed.

"Fifa's governance problem goes far beyond the role of one individual," the leagues added.

"The wider question is whether Fifa's president should simultaneously wield such regulatory, commercial and political power without effective checks and balances, including the agreement of affected stakeholders... governance that concentrates unchecked regulatory, commercial and political power in a single office, while relegating affected stakeholders to mere advisory status, is not fit for purpose."

Fifa has been approached for comment.

The four leagues call on Fifa to;

establish a permanent body representing key stakeholders, including leagues, clubs, and players from across men's and women's football which has "a meaningful role in [its] decision-making process".

ensure "evidence-based decision-making", with any major proposal subject to an independent assessment evaluating the impact on all stakeholders.

create a separation between Fifa's regulatory role and its commercial function via "robust institutional safeguards to preserve trust, legitimacy and accountability" with ethics, financial oversight and electoral bodies "that are genuinely independent of the Fifa administration and presidency".

Two years ago, Europe's top leagues - along with players' union Fifpro - filed a legal complaint against Fifa with the European Commission over what they claimed was an "abuse of dominance" by world football's governing body over the expansion of the international fixture calendar and an alleged lack of consultation.

Fifa denied that, and accused some leagues of "hypocrisy" and acting "without consideration to everyone else in the world".

They claim that their legal action "is a consequence of a flawed governance framework in which Fifa can use its regulatory authority to advance its own commercial objectives without accounting for the impact on the economic and social sustainability of national competitions that affect all stakeholders. This must change now for the sake of football".

Despite three confederations calling for him to step down, Infantino has said he will stand for re-election in March, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.

The four leagues want candidates to support their proposals and say: "Now is the moment to decide not only who will lead Fifa, but also how Fifa should be led. Leagues have a crucial role to play in this process, and we want to ensure that the voice of every league is heard."

The letter is signed by Richard Masters, chief executive of the Premier League, Marc Lenz, CEO of the Bundesliga, Javier Tebas, president of La Liga, and Luigi De Siervo, CEO of Serie A.

Last month Masters told BBC Sport that Infantino had "pressed the self-destruct button" by delivering "a self-inflicted wound" over FFE.

title: Liver transplant anniversary inspired team talk - Dyer
description: Southend United boss Kieron Dyer says the anniversary of his life-saving liver transplant inspired an "emotional" pre-match team talk.
fullText:
Southend United boss Kieron Dyer says the anniversary of his life-saving liver transplant inspired an "emotional" pre-match team talk at the weekend.

The former England midfielder, who played for Ipswich Town and Newcastle United, had the operation in 2023 after being diagnosed with primary sclerosing cholangitis in 2019.

Dyer, 47, said he addressed the Shrimpers' players and staff before their thumping 6-1 win at Gateshead which saw them go second in the National League.

"I said [to the players] that I don't want to put extra pressure on you, but I need the win - they executed that perfectly," Dyer told BBC Essex.

"I always speak to [his organ donor] at night before going to bed, so I said 'that one's for you'."

Primary sclerosing cholangitis is characterised by inflammation and scarring of the bile ducts and caused Dyer's eyes and skin to turn yellow.

"For me to be alive, someone's had to have their life taken away," Dyer added.

"I know some of his life. I know his name, I know he had a wife because his sister wrote a really powerful letter to me.

"I'm always grateful because not many people get second chances at life. I was on my death bed. I probably only had a few weeks myself to live.

"It [the anniversary] is always an emotional day. We do huddles in the changing room before games and I pick different members of staff to lead them... I thought Saturday's was a good one for me to do."

Dyer won 33 caps for England and also had spells with West Ham, QPR and Middlesbrough.

He was appointed as Southend boss in June, and has taken the Shrimpers to three points off the top of the National League after nine games.

"It [receiving an organ donation] was the most humbling thing and gives you a completely different perspective on life. You can't take any day for granted.

"I wouldn't want anyone to go through that but it does broaden your horizons when you think about life and how you have to cherish every moment."
