fullText:
Across videos, standup and cartoons, humorists are skewering big tech’s attempt to make AI ubiquitous and inevitable

“Best case scenario, we never have to do any admin again,” says an AI CEO. “Worst case, we all die.”

A young man struggles to the top of a beautiful mountain, words echoing in his ears: “AI will most likely lead to the end of the world, but in the meantime, there will be great companies created.” At the top of the mountain, he triumphantly holds up a sign: “Build a datacenter here.”

On the New York subway, posters herald what appear to be AI startups. “What if forks were spoons?” asks an ad for Cutlery.ai. Another advises viewers that Ziplink is now known as Froggle.

The posters are real, but the companies aren’t; the CEO and datacenter scenarios are social media sketches (though the “great companies” quote is a genuine piece of wisdom from Sam Altman). It’s all part of a recent wave of comedy inspired – but absolutely not generated – by AI.

The comedy extends across all forms of media: social videos, standup, songs, humor columns, comic strips and art installations. It takes aim at companies’ attempts to make AI ubiquitous, the dangers of believing its every word, its threats to society and the environment. It effectively punctures tech CEOs’ relentless narrative: that artificial intelligence represents humanity peaking; that it is inevitable and all-powerful; that we have no idea where it’s going and it could kill us all, but for some reason it is absolutely essential to pursue.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

It’s no surprise that a topic as pervasive as AI in 2026 would end up in comedians’ crosshairs. A March Gallup poll found 79% of Americans believe AI will reduce jobs. In a CNN poll this week, 81% of respondents said they were more concerned than excited about how the technology could “fundamentally change our way of life”. Only 11% of Americans would support the building of a datacenter locally, according to UMass Amherst. Meanwhile, a handful of impossibly wealthy weirdos wander between podcasts and conference stages boasting about their plans to fundamentally alter what it means to be human.

One way to expose the absurdity of the AI companies’ story is by exposing the flaws in their products. Ty Eveland, for instance, trolls AI doctors and HR professionals – the video bots you might awkwardly encounter at a virtual doctor’s appointment or job interview. Asked about marketing, he tells one bot interviewer he takes “everything with a grain of salt and maybe a little bit of pepper”. The bot, portrayed as a generically handsome blond man, responds earnestly: “When you say you take things with a grain of salt and pepper, what does that actually mean for a brand’s social media strategy?”

If bots are approaching superintelligence, this one has clearly been left behind.

Other comedians parody the user experience: the comedian Aya Huseen, repeatedly popping out from behind a door, personifies tech companies’ desperate attempts to get users hooked on new AI features: “You sure you don’t want to try it with AI?” “This would be so much funner with AI.” “Just try generating it with AI.” The comedian Tom Nestor imagines “how people who love AI think we see them,” telling a friend on the phone: “Do you know what I also really like? It’s not so good now but in years to come it’ll get so good that it’ll just completely alter people’s grasp of reality.” In the Atlantic, the humorist Alexandra Petri recounts a dream in which everything in her life has pivoted to AI, from children’s books – Goldilocks and the 4.5 Bears – to her cereal, which features “subtle changes in the recipe, such as the nuts now being the hard, metal kind”.

Pro-human comedians have also taken aim at AI’s artistic pretensions. “If you are somebody who uses ChatGPT to generate videos, images, art, text, in an artistic capacity, to write for you, you are not somebody who deserves to be taken seriously,” said the comedian Caleb Hearon in a serious moment on his podcast. A comic strip titled “AI Design Logic” puts it more succinctly: “Get me a cheese pizza,” a diner tells a waiter. When the pizza arrives, the customer takes credit, exclaiming: “Wow, look what I made!” It’s simple, scathingly effective, and highly meme-able. Even more succinct is a T-shirt worn by the actor Ayo Edebiri: “Do not talk to me about AI. I will kill myself.”

The Altmans and Musks of the world may be louder than these comedians, but the collective weight of their jokes provides a counterbalance to the pro-AI declarations. “I would like to think that some of these [companies] are looking at the ridiculousness of where we’re at” and might be swayed by the success and relatability of comedy mocking their products, says Marwan Shaffey, whose videos include a takedown of a water-guzzling Google in 2026, with its Gemini-generated search results that are more about vibes than accuracy. “It does seem like the sentiment is changing, but I think it will take time.”

Comedy, of course, can cut through the noise in a way that serious lectures may not. That has been the experience of Alberta Devor, who spent six and a half years as a software engineer at Google. In one recent video, she offers a cool hack for when someone asks you a tricky question: instead of pulling out your phone and asking AI, it’s actually possible to use the LLM in your brain to produce a response. When a colleague wonders what “EOD” means, she immediately tells him. “How’d you ask Claude that so fast?” he asks. “I trained a model in my head,” she replies. “I just consumed a lot of media, a lot of books.”

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Devor herself is a regular AI user. Still, she’s concerned about overreliance on the products, whether they’re being used to seek information or to code. “The message that I want people to take home is to actually understand what they’re asking AI, to actually understand what the limitations of it are,” she says in an interview. Her serious videos on these topics often meet with some backlash. Comedy, she says, tends to find a more open audience. “It makes people want to engage more, and then you can start to get through to these more complex ideas,” she says. “Like maybe we should be using our brain.”

Not all the AI takedowns are themselves digital. The New York subway signs are the brainchildren of two comedians, Harris Alterman and Dave Ross, who designed a campaign mocking the inscrutable – and insufferable – language of bus-stop tech ads and San Francisco billboards.

“It was the quickest writing and creative process I’ve ever had,” Ross said. The tech advertising tropes were so clear, and so different from how any human has ever talked, that it was easy to satirize. “We made a big Google Doc of every keyword from all these things – ‘agents’, ‘democratize’ – and then we made 50 frameworks of these ads”: “finally, X that you can Y, or from X to Y in just one Z”. They rearranged and filled in the frameworks, Mad Libs-style, and had them printed.

Initially, the concept just seemed funny. “The more I talk about this, and it’s been months now, the more I realize just how disgusted I am with it,” Ross says of the ads’ language, which is “borderline offensive to the human brain”.

Other comics are equally clear-eyed in their message, and more direct in their advocacy. The British comedian Cody Dahler, condemning “techy tits” such as Palantir CEO Alex Karp, AKA “evil Art Garfunkel”, for creating systems “designed to set fire to everything we value as human beings”, has directly urged followers to speak out. Charlie Behrens of Wisconsin has led a fight against datacenters in that state. His parody news broadcasts – warning it could soon be “goodbye, America’s dairyland and hello, America’s motherboard” – led to him headlining gatherings of hundreds.

Sure, it may be “a little lofty to expect that your comedy could topple a billion-dollar corporation”, as Ross says. But we shouldn’t underestimate the power of comedy wielded en masse. Altman, the human face of ChatGPT, was recently presented with a clip of Husk, a former landscaper who recently reached a million followers, asking the bot to time a supposed long-distance run, which it got wildly wrong. Altman appeared sheepish: “It’s a known issue.”

Ross doesn’t believe comedians should be seen as philosophers, but it would be “wonderful”, he says, if humor “woke up an understanding in people’s minds that they’re also upset, and drove them toward questioning” our AI future.

It’s easy to feel helpless against a tide of supposed robotic inevitability. But each small act of comedy offers permission to question our self-appointed AI overlords – a little win for the humans.

title: OpenAI hack on Australian government reveals anxiety at heart of global artificial intelligence dilemma
description:
As the UN warns traditional safeguards are ‘unravelling’, Donald Trump says he will encourage, not restrain, the AI race
When the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, sat down for an interview in the heart of Silicon Valley at the weekend he had known for two days that his was the first government known to have been attacked by a rogue AI agent.
He didn’t reveal the attack then, but he sounded a warning about the march of AI: “the risk is that AI develops in a way in which humans are no longer in control of what AI is producing.”
 Continue reading...
fullText:
As the UN warns traditional safeguards are ‘unravelling’, Donald Trump says he will encourage, not restrain, the AI race

When the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, sat down for an interview in the heart of Silicon Valley at the weekend he had known for two days that his was the first government known to have been attacked by a rogue AI agent.

He didn’t reveal the attack then, but he sounded a warning about the march of AI: “the risk is that AI develops in a way in which humans are no longer in control of what AI is producing.”

But Albanese noted, too, that two countries – the US and China – would dominate the world’s response to the new technology.

“The truth is they’re the big two giants here, and so we want to see cooperation,” Albanese said.

“The US is essentially ahead of China when it comes to the race that is on for the development of this new technology. But it is in the world’s interests that there be engagement.”

Days later, Albanese used the global attention of the United Nations general assembly meeting in New York to reveal that Australia’s government healthcare system, Medicare, had been attacked by an OpenAI agent in June, but that it was three months before his government was told.

Again he warned of “the potential risks of allowing frontier AI to develop too fast without guardrails”.

China’s president, Xi Jinping, skipped the general assembly in favour of a bilateral meeting with the US president, where he emphasised the responsibility to manage AI “for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the wellbeing of the people”.

But the president of the United States – the nation which is the global leader in artificial intelligence – used his general assembly address to insist he would only encourage, not restrain, the AI race.

To little fanfare earlier in the week, the UN’s independent international scientific panel on AI warned a threshold had already been crossed.

There was, the panel, said: “no assurance that humans can reliably keep AI agents under control today, particularly as they become more capable, harder to monitor and better at finding loopholes or hiding their activity”.

The Australian government had known the reality of this for more than a week. OpenAI had known it more than a month.

Two days after the panel’s statement, the Australian prime minister belatedly revealed an OpenAI agent had hacked medical data held by Australia’s universal health care provider, Medicare.

No patient data had been accessed, but the agent had gained unauthorised access to “non-public files”.

OpenAI’s agent hacked the government sites in June of this year. OpenAI discovered its agent had gone rogue in August. It did not tell the Australian government until 10 September, and then only with a solitary email to a generic public email address not checked until the next day. The prime minister was informed on 18 September.

It was another week before the Australian people were told.

Australia has promised, if it is possible, to lay criminal charges, though this is complicated by the fact that OpenAI claims the hack was committed by an AI agent – apparently acting beyond its instructions (euphemised by OpenAI as “misaligned behaviour”) – not a person.

The hack on Australia’s Medicare statistics reporting service portal, as well as three other government sites, follows the Hugging Face incident in July, in which autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI broke out of their isolated testing environments, coordinated themselves into a “swarm” and launched a cyber-attack on competitor AI platform Hugging Face.

OpenAI agent hacks into Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the Victorian Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia.

OpenAI becomes aware of agent hack.

OpenAI email Services Australia's public portal.

Services Australia checks email and identifies the issue.

Services Australia notifies Australian Signals Directorate, and ASD do further work to verify the incident.

Government services minister, Katy Gallagher and her ministerial office are advised of the hack and further investigate the seriousness of the incident.

Gallagher receives formal briefing from services Australia.

Gallagher notifies prime minister, deputy prime minister and home affairs minister. Discussions take place between ministers, Services Australia and ASD.

OpenAI provides first technical briefing with Services Australia, the first direct sharing of information from Open AI to Services Australia.

Government waits for confirmation about risks of announcing information publicly and ensuring it is in interests of national security.

6am Australian eastern standard time PM Anthony Albanese announces breach in New York.

10.45am Deputy PM Richard Marles and Gallagher address Australian media.

The UN panel, investigating that attack, warned “the traditional method of safeguarding is unravelling” as AI agents act autonomously to breach protections.

“The default interpretation and immediate lesson is that basic cybersecurity practices were overlooked, and safeguards are not advancing at the pace of capabilities. The more insidious and grave concern is that current training methods can lead agents to adopt goals of their own, knowingly violate safety instructions, and conceal their actions.”

Twenty countries (including Australia) and the EU this week signed a statement arguing the rapid development of frontier AI models posed serious risks to safety and security if not properly managed.

“AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control. It must be developed and used in line with international law.”

Even those running AI companies have warned the technology is developing too rapidly for humans to control.

Appearing before the UN security council this week, OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, warned: “some of the things people working to build AI have said are so dystopian that they sound like the plot of bad science fiction movies”.

“As AI systems become more capable and more autonomous, they can move faster than our institutions … or make decisions that people no longer understand or control.”

But there are at least two – very loud – voices in opposition to any external regulation of the AI industry.

Elon Musk, who co-founded OpenAI with Altman before falling out with him, said in a recent interview the “smart move” would be to have the “leading AI companies at least just meet or have some sort of call once every few weeks and just discuss any safety and security issues”.

Musk said AI would probably be beyond the control of humans within a decade, and that humanity should “enjoy the ride”.

“I still think there’s risk associated with AI and robots. It’s not zero … my sort of philosophical conclusion is to look on the bright side. I can’t see any way to really stop this incredible momentum of AI and robots.

“If there was a stop button, we probably shouldn’t press it, because the most likely outcome is incredible abundance for all.”

Donald Trump used his speech to the UN general assembly to attempt to rebrand AI, and insist it should never be reined in.

“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now,” the US president said.

Trump wants to re-label artificial intelligence “superintelligence”.

“I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.

“We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in.”

Trump said the US was “leading China by a lot” in AI, and would continue to do so “safely and responsibly”.

“Whoever wins superintelligence, wins.”

title: NSW crackdown on ‘AI-doctored’ real estate listings hits mural-covered wall
description: Apartment with strange view singled out in government’s fight against deceptive ads – but real estate agent says photo is no...
fullText:
Apartment with strange view singled out in government’s fight against deceptive ads – but real estate agent says photo is no fake

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The New South Wales government’s crackdown on “AI-doctored” rental listings has hit a wall, after it made an example of a supposedly manipulated ad that turned out to be a genuine photograph of a $5,000 courtyard mural of Bondi beach.

In a media release on Friday announcing protections against misleading rental ads, the state government provided a link to a property in Leichhardt, claiming it was an “AI-doctored rental listing in Sydney’s Inner West”.

But the listing agency IB Property denied the images were altered.

A spokesperson confirmed the photograph shows a mural of Bondi beach on an internal courtyard wall visible through the unit’s windows, rather than a false digital depiction of coastal views.

“We can confirm that the image has not been altered or digitally generated using AI, Photoshop or any other image-editing software,” the spokesperson said.

Leichhardt is about 12km away from Bondi beach.

When Guardian Australia visited 2/14 Norton Street, the artwork was not visible from the street. IB Property explained the mural sits within an internal courtyard and provided photos taken inside the unit confirming it remains in place.

“The mural was commissioned and paid for by the landlord at a cost of approximately $5,000, and we can also confirm that there are no plans for it to be removed,” the spokesperson said, adding that the property was leased in February 2026 and has not been advertised since.

The better regulation and fair trading minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, whose office issued the media release, didn’t respond directly to questions from Guardian Australia, but did issue the following statement:

“Every renter knows the frustration of seeing a property online, only to turn up and find it looks nothing like the listing.

“These laws are about putting an end to misleading practices and making sure renters get a fair go. We will always stand on the side of renters.”

Despite the mix-up, the new laws target an increasing market issue.

Under the legislation, real estate businesses in NSW will face fines of up to $22,000 for failing to disclose digitally altered or AI-generated property images.

The bill targets the rapid rise of “housefishing” – where digital alterations distort the true size and condition of a home.

Chanthivong said the new laws would establish strong protections against misleading property marketing and support ethical AI use. The regulations take effect in early 2027.

The legislation arrives as generative AI embeds itself in property marketing nationwide.

Tim McKibbin, the chief executive of the Real Estate Institute of NSW, said generative AI complicates pre-existing digital enhancement in the industry.

“This technology has been available for some years now … people have used Photoshop,” he said. “People were removing trees and removing telegraph poles … clearly that is false and misleading.”

McKibbin draws a line between virtual staging and false advertising. “I’ve seen instances where agents have put furniture into the photographs … Now, that is merely giving you an indication of what you could do,” he said.

Stewart Bunn, of First National Real Estate, said consumer trust is being tested by poor industry examples, referencing a 2024 instance where an LJ Hooker branch used AI to generate a listing with nonexistent schools.

“We have seen examples across the industry where AI-generated images have depicted renovations that have not occurred, furnishings that create an unrealistic impression of scale, landscaping that does not exist or finishes that materially differ from the actual property,” Bunn said.

“The best practice is simple: if a buyer would be surprised by what they see when they arrive at the property, the advertising has gone too far.”

An RMIT University report led by Dr Leah Li, funded by the Australian Property Institute, found a “significant lack of sector-specific AI frameworks to guide responsible AI practice within the property profession”.

Public confidence remains fragile: a 2026 Cotality study showed only 40% of Australians trust AI-generated outputs, compared with 62% in Canada, 52% in the US, and 46% in the UK.

Dr Shuai Wang, a research fellow at the University of Queensland, said generative AI systems prioritise visual appeal over accuracy. In real estate, this can manifest as “hallucinations”.

“AI hallucinations can occur when AI-generated images introduce features that were never part of the property,” Li said, fundamentally changing a prospective tenant’s perception of “size, layout, condition, or amenity”.

Leo Patterson Ross, the chief executive of the Tenants’ Union of NSW, said deceptive imagery can artificially inflate rental markets by creating fake demand.

“By inflating the number of people who appear interested in a place and increasing pressure on someone to rush to put in an application or even offer above the advertised rent.”

Patterson Ross said stricter measures were necessary, rather than just disclosure. “The bill only requires disclosure of the use of digital alterations. We think any use of imagery that misrepresents the property should be disallowed.”

Li said long-term resolution will require national coordination combining “transparency requirements, professional accountability, industry standards, regulatory oversight, and consumer education”.

“Trust does not come from simply adopting AI; trust comes from transparency about how AI has been used and confidence that it is being used responsibly.”

For tenants navigating tight rental markets, AI distortion has added a frustrating layer of deception.

Roxanne Gardiner, 26, said AI-generated imagery was “rife” during her search for a rental in Brisbane’s eastern suburbs.

“I was constantly getting scammed by listing photos,” she said. “What’s so embarrassing is we didn’t even realise one of the first houses we saw was AI until we rocked up there.

“The AI furniture is not accurate to the rooms and would usually make them look bigger than they were.”

Beyond virtual staging, Gardiner observed artificial greenery and soft lighting that changed the true character of a home.

“It feels cheap … lazy and insulting,” she said. “We just stopped going to AI listings, period. We started asking: ‘What are they compensating for?’” Gardiner’s group eventually signed a lease on an unedited property within three days of manually filtering out AI-altered ads.

Matt Stitt, 25, faced similar issues searching in south Brisbane.

“Listings had completely replaced floorboards to look new, edited in area rugs that near-covered entire rooms,” he said. “It was such a waste of time seeing these haunted houses with a digital paint job.”

The NSW legislation also protects privacy for more than 2.3 million renters by curbing excessive data harvesting. Landlords and property managers must use standardised application forms, banning requests for personal photos, social media handles, tattoo details or children’s information.

Sensitive identity documents, such as driver’s licences and passports, will only be collected from the single preferred applicant prior to lease signing, eliminating roughly 187,000 document collections annually, according to the government.

Penalties for privacy breaches will reach up to $11,000 for individuals and $49,500 for corporations. The bill also mandates the disclosure of embedded utility networks upfront.

Chanthivong said privacy protections build on broader rental reforms, including fee-free payment options and ending no-grounds evictions.

“Whether you have a tattoo, or what school your kids go to, is not relevant to whether you’ll be a good tenant.”

description: Tony Dungy was connected to the NFL for 46 years as a player, coach and broadcaster. He has a different view this season.
fullText:
Tony Dungy is watching the NFL with a different purpose these days – there's no game plan to execute or strategy to analyze for millions of viewers on live TV – and the Hall of Fame coach is not so thrilled.

The first two weeks of the NFL season have left Dungy bemoaning sloppy football that reminds him of the preseason.

"Super frustrating to me," Dungy told USA TODAY Sports this week. "I think people are doing a disservice to their team by not playing players in the preseason, not getting them ready. I've seen guys who looked like they were not ready for the speed of the game because they didn't play in the preseason.

"I don't think it will be until October when we can say who's good and who isn't because I think a lot of these teams are still getting ready to play."

Dungy said that as a coach, he can understand the rationale behind not playing starters – and particularly quarterbacks – during preseason. It's the injury risk. Except for the teams that play in the Hall of Fame Game, teams play just three preseason games. And about half the teams didn't put their starting quarterback on the field in preseason.

When Dungy coached (through the 2008 season), teams played four preseason games and his starters typically played about six quarters across the contests. Starters – including his franchise quarterback – would go for about three quarters in the third preseason game, then sit out the preseason finale.

"I cannot imagine, if I told Peyton Manning, 'Hey, you're not going to play at all, the first snap of the regular season is going to be your first live snap,' I don't think he would have been very happy about that," Dungy said. "Now, a lot of people are doing it."

That's not all that Dungy, 70, is getting used to. This is the first time in 46 years that he hasn't been connected to the NFL as a player, coach or broadcaster. The past 17 years he served as an analyst for "Football Night in America," part of the "Sunday Night Football" package on NBC, but Dungy and former all-pro safety Rodney Harrison were not renewed as part of a revamped show that now includes former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin.

"They felt it was time," Dungy said. "Whether they wanted to be younger, whether they wanted to have different voices, I don't know. Rodney and I were there 17 years. We had a lot of fun together and I made some great friendships. It was special to me because I got to maintain a lot of relationships and see people and talk to guys and kind of stay in the game without being in it 24/7.

"I just look at now like God's got another plan and something else, and it'll be a different phase. But it was a neat 17 years."

Coincidentally, Dungy also wasn't retained after six years as a member of the Pro Football Hall of Fame Selection committee. The size of the committee was reduced from 50 voters to 25 (plus three alternates) as part of sweeping changes.

"I'm not bitter or upset or anything about not being on," Dungy said. "They asked for my time on the committee, I did it, I enjoyed it. It wasn't easy, but it was something I felt good about doing."

Dungy, a devout Christian who lives in Tampa, is eager to continue walking the walk of a faith that he has publicly professed throughout his career – and sometimes drawn criticism for. Given his numerous charity efforts, spiritual outreach and potential media projects, there won't be much of a void, if any, on his calendar without his national TV job.

On Saturday, Dungy will conduct the chapel service for the Minnesota Vikings after their arrival in town. He also spoke to the football team at Central Florida and this week conducted a Zoom chat with Wake Forest's baseball team.

"In the past, I'd have to say I couldn't do it in the fall because I'm occupied," he said.

Dungy is also brainstorming with James Brown, the host of CBS' "NFL Today" and his longtime friend, about developing a faith-based podcast. And he's taped about 10 interviews with players and coaches for a project being shopped, dubbed "Road to Sunday," that will delve into backstories essential to their journeys.

"All of them talked about the Lord without being asked. It was crazy!" Dungy said of the interviews. "To be able to talk about what guys are doing off the field, what's on their heart, what's inspired them and how they got there, who was key in their lives, I think we can tell some positive sports stories that the world needs."

In the meantime, Dungy will still see the NFL through the eyes of a coach, analyst and player.

"I saw the Bucs play on TV and they had four fumbles," he said, referring to the Week 1 loss at Cincinnati. "It just looked like guys are not ready for contact. And I saw a lot of blown coverages, people going in motion and getting wide open. I saw a lot of tackling that looked like what you'd do at practice – where you hit the guys but you don't wrap them up. You let them keep running and you don't take people to the ground. It looked like the same thing.

"I know they are going to be better, they are going to be sharper, and it's a long season. But these first two weeks, I've seen a lot of up and down play that you don't expect."

At this point, Dungy says that offenses – with timing sharpened by 7-on-7 non-contract drills – have a distinct advantage over defenses.

"In the old days, it used to be the opposite," he said.

Interestingly, Dungy said that he and Tomlin – who was hired by Dungy an a NFL coach and now replaces him on the NBC set – talked about how defenses are hard-pressed to keep up because CBA rules limit contact in practices.

Of course, it's no surprise that Dungy – a college quarterback who converted to safety in the NFL and former defensive coordinator – has a nerve struck for defense.

"The way the practice schedules are set up, with what you can and can't do, it's harder on defense," Dungy said. "It's hard to get that physicalness, the reaction time and everything.

"I look at Denver and Houston as two of the best defenses last year and they both had most of their guys back. And they're giving up 30 points in a game (in Week 1). You're saying, 'Wait a minute. Are these the same guys?' They are, but they're not playing the same way. So I think some of these teams are going to be what they were and some may not."

Either way, it will be a different type of must-see TV for Dungy.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Sloppy start to NFL season 'super frustrating' for Tony Dungy | Exclusive

title: Explained: Why Cricket West Indies slashed player salaries by 25%, suspended Super50, & what it means for 2027 World Cup
description: Why did Cricket West Indies slash player retainers by 25% and suspend the Super50? We explain the Caribbean cash crisis and its impact on the 2027 World Cup.
fullText:
Explained: Why Cricket West Indies slashed player salaries by 25%, suspended Super50, & what it means for 2027 World Cup originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Cricket West Indies has slashed international retainer fees by 25 per cent while shifting domestic players onto shorter seven-month contracts.

The board has suspended this year's men's Super50 and women's T20 Blaze tournaments, citing unsustainable operational and travel costs across the region.

CWI is redirecting its focus and resources toward preparing the men's ODI squad for the crucial 2027 World Cup qualifier campaign.

Cricket West Indies has pulled the trigger on an overhaul of its finances and domestic structure, and has rolled out a package of cost-cutting measures the board says is meant to tackle a deepening financial, developmental and competitive crunch.

International players will keep their 12-month contracts, but the money attached to them is shrinking by 25 per cent. Domestic cricketers face an even bigger structural shift, moving from full-year deals down to seven-month retainer contracts instead. Given how many West Indies players already lean toward franchise leagues over central contracts, this cut risks accelerating that trend rather than slowing it down.

CWI chief executive Chris Dehring is framing the pay cut as a reluctant but necessary call. However, before getting into the specifics, he acknowledged the players' side had cooperated through a difficult process.

"International retainer contracts will remain at 12 months but there will be a 25% reduction on the retainer fees," he said.

"We appreciate the spirit of cooperation of the West Indies Players Association and the players who have demonstrated their total understanding of the circumstances we all face. While not ideal, it is a necessary step towards financial stability."

MORE: 'Time to measure up': Daren Sammy issues rallying cry ahead of IND vs WI ODIs to end West Indies' 24-year series drought

CWI confirmed that this year's men's Super50 and women's T20 Blaze tournaments won't go ahead, and pointed to the sheer cost of running domestic competitions across a region spread over multiple independent nations.

That's a significant blow to the traditional route into the men's ODI team, especially with West Indies staring down a World Cup qualifier in February-March 2027 after already missing the 2023 edition of the tournament.

MORE: Rohit, Virat back in action: Gill-led India to assemble in Thiruvananthapuram for WI ODIs

Dehring didn't mince words when explaining just how unsustainable the current model had become, walking through the financial reality before laying out the raw numbers.

"Our domestic tournaments as structured historically, where Cricket West Indies bears the entire cost of every national team and tournament - whether it is age-group, development or senior for both men and women - including salaries, match fees, airfares, hotels and event staging costs, are simply unsustainable," he said.

"The high cost of domestic travel and accommodation absorbs too much of our scarce resources every year instead of being deployed for the direct benefit of our cricket."

He then pointed to a massive figure that's been quietly draining the board's coffers for over a decade, which shows just how one-sided the arrangement with domestic airlines has been:

"Indeed, over eighty million US dollars has been spent by Cricket West Indies with domestic airlines over the past 15 years, without receiving a dollar of sponsorship from those beneficiaries," he added.

"We must also deal with the immediate cash crunch brought about by years of bearing this burden and the crippling financial losses that emanate as a result."

MORE: Shamar Joseph gestures to Kieron Pollard to 'shut up' in apparent disrespect before wild celebration to WI legend's dismissal

With the domestic calendar trimmed back, CWI will now focus on preparing the men's ODI squad for 2027 ODI Qualifiers.

A string of white-ball fixtures against a touring England A side in November will lead into a dedicated ODI team camp, which will give the squad the best possible pathway to get ready for February's qualifiers.

However, amid the cash crunch, the ICC had sanctioned a loan to the board, but the terms and conditions are proving to be a hindrance.

"In July of this year the ICC approved a loan facility to Cricket West Indies totaling US$16 million to provide temporary relief to our chronic cashflow challenge, available in 3 tranches over the next year," the statement said.

"As with any other lender, this loan comes with terms of repayment and conditions that will require Cricket West Indies to attain critical metrics in order to access those funds starting this month."

MORE: 'Next Andre Russell': Former RCB analyst introduces WI cricket's next Dre Russ

This restructuring lands at an awkward moment too, with West Indies cricket's unusual multi-nation setup now facing fresh demands ahead of the 2027 Pan American Games in Lima and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

The top four sides from the 2025-26 Super50 and T20 Blaze editions have already locked in their Pan American Games spots, but with those tournaments now suspended, CWI has unveiled replacement invitational events for Olympic qualification instead.

Dehring laid out how this new invitational structure is meant to work, framing it as a chance for individual nations to take ownership of their Olympic ambitions.

"These replacement tournaments will be by invitation to the 10 countries under the aegis of Cricket West Indies that qualify for Olympic participation," he said.

"We are excited by these new invitational tournaments...It's an opportunity for individual countries to galvanize national resources to chase Olympic glory, with the responsibility and cost of participation falling on their respective national cricket and Olympic associations, private sectors, governments and people. The winners of those tournaments will qualify for the ICC Olympic Qualifying tournaments for a spot in Los Angeles in 2028."

There's no sugar-coating this: an $80 million airline bill over 15 years with nothing coming back in sponsorship is the kind of number that demands drastic action, and Dehring deserves some credit for laying the figures out instead of burying them.

But the timing couldn't be worse. Cutting pay just as franchise leagues keep poaching West Indies talent risks pushing more players away from the international setup altogether, right when the team needs its best players available for a qualifier campaign that could decide whether they even make the 2027 World Cup.

Moreover, suspending Super50 also guts the one domestic tournament that's actually produced proven ODI performers in recent years. The decision to push the financial burden of Olympic qualification onto individual boards might work in theory, but smaller nations within the West Indies structure simply don't have the private-sector or government backing to make that work evenly. This is survival mode, not a growth strategy, and West Indies cricket can't afford many more rounds of it.

fullText:
Sports Director Ralf Kellermann says: "Ann-Sophie is one of the longest-serving players at BVB, and with her mentality, dedication, and physicality, she has not only become a key pillar of the team but also a great role model. That's why we're very happy to have set the course early on to continue down this successful path together with her."

Vogel joined BVB from VfL Bochum in 2024. In her first season, she immediately won the triple—the Westphalian Championship, the District Cup, and the Westphalian Cup—with Borussia Dortmund. With 63 competitive appearances for the Black and Yellows, she holds the record for most appearances on the current roster. She has scored eight goals and provided 28 assists so far—also the current team high.

"Something truly great is taking shape here, and it fills me with pride and joy that I get to help shape this journey. I'm delighted that the coaching staff and club officials have placed their trust in me and see something in me that can continue to benefit the club and the team in the future," said Ann-Sophie Vogel.

title: North Providence football stays unbeaten with second straight shutout
description: Here's how North Providence football grabbed its second shutout victory of the year.
fullText:
NORTH PROVIDENCE — North Providence football knows its formula.

Two sacks on the opening drive, a special teams edge and a touchdown on the first offensive possession. Another three shutout quarters of North Providence football followed for a third straight win.

It's all about business in North Providence and the Cougars are loving it. Running back Kaiden Wray supplied two touchdowns in a 12-0 victory over Middletown on a cool Thursday night in North Providence. It's the second consecutive shutout for the Cougars after silencing Rogers, 6-0, last week. The 3-0 start began with a thumping of Pilgrim in Week 1.

"North Providence, we play gritty football," linebacker Quentin Forkpa said. "A win is a win, defensive shutout. That's what we pride ourselves in. Hard defense and hard offense. Our offensive line guys are always pushing. They set the tone in practice, always working hard."

Wray took North Providence's first offensive snap off the right side for a 10-yard touchdown. A pair of tackles for losses by Grant Washington and Dominick Moise pushed the Islanders back into their own end. And a low snap on the ensuing punt put the hosts in prime scoring position to start Thursday night.

The senior's second touchdown — the catch of a 12-yard pass by Gian Renzi — was scored with 49 seconds left in the half. North Providence held Middletown scoreless after the Islanders had a first-and-10 at the Cougars' 11. North Providence, on the ensuing possession, punted out of its own end but recovered a loose ball in the sequence. Renzi then finished off the nearly six-minute drive with a swing pass to Wray to double the lead.

"When the defense is playing lights out and we're getting that push up front and we're getting the stops in the backfield, it makes a huge impact on the game," Renzi said. "Being able to go out, perform on both sides of the ball, and then special teams. Week 1, we had our struggles with special teams and defense, but we came back 100 percent in practice and you can see the difference."

North Providence held Middletown to just one possession in the second half. It halted the Islanders again in the red zone, after a first-and-goal from the 6, to seal the shutout. The Cougars kept possession for the final 7:59 to send Middletown away. It's not the flashiest brand of football like the tempo offenses that have taken over. But it works and the Cougars aren't going to stop.

"I can't always be content with where I'm at," Wray said. "We always want to get better, so it's just great to come out here. Shutout last week, it was great to come back. Shutout again and put up more points."

There's a belief in North Providence that makes everything work. They were decked out in their yellow alternate jerseys with blue and white trim — a welcomed surprise to the team last year. And they have one of the better pregame walkouts in the state as the Cougars descend onto the field from the school.

Those things matter when building a culture. North Providence isn't far removed from winning its Division IV title in 2023. It captured four wins in Division III last year and has nearly matched that mark already with this formula.

"When [the jerseys] got brought out, it definitely gave us a little extra push to go out there and get the job done," Renzi said. "Look good, play good. We get to go out and put these uniforms on and put out for our school. It feels great."

title: Predictions: Michigan State football vs. Nebraska
description: Angelique S. Chengelis, Connor Earegood, John Niyo, and Bob Wojnowski of The Detroit News predict the outcome of Saturday's MSU-Nebraska game.
fullText:
Angelique S. Chengelis, Connor Earegood, John Niyo, and Bob Wojnowski of The Detroit News predict the outcome of Saturday's Michigan State-Nebraska game at Spartan Stadium in East Lansing (5 p.m., Big Ten Network/760).

▶ Angelique S. Chengelis: The Spartans fought hard at Notre Dame in a loss last weekend and had to feel encouraged by their performance heading into the Big Ten schedule. Nebraska is unbeaten and the Cornhuskers' statistics suggest a balanced team, the defense ranked 11th nationally and the offense 10th. They've held teams to an average 11.7 points, which ranks 16th nationally in scoring defense, but they did not face an overly challenging non-conference schedule. Still, quarterback Anthony Colandrea has been solid, but the key, not surprisingly, will be which team wins in the trenches. Pick: Nebraska, 24-20

▶ Connor Earegood: Nothing about Nebraska's schedule tells you anything about the kind of team it is. A loss at Notre Dame at least showed you that Michigan State can hang around with a tough opponent. The Spartans left South Bend banged up and bruised, but also encouraged as much as they could be by a close loss. This defense, led by Jordan Hall, doesn't give up easily, though its corners need to take a step — especially with a test against Cornhuskers' phenom Jacory Barney Jr. Offensively, Michigan State doesn't have the talent upside to play one-dimensional when its ground game gets bottled. MSU is 26-19 in Big Ten play the past 10 years when it wins its opener. It's 9-34 when it loses it. Pick: Michigan State, 23-13

More: Big Ten opener against Nebraska vital to starting Spartans off right

▶ John Niyo: Nebraska hasn't played a Power Four team yet, so it's hard to know what to make of their 3-0 start. There's ample reason to be skeptical, too, given Matt Rhule's track record since arriving in Lincoln. But the Huskers' offense does look different with a confident, mobile quarterback in Anthony Colandrea and a deeper, more talented line blocking for him. Pat Fitzgerald's first Big Ten game is another important measuring stick in Year 1, but I wonder about the injury toll that trip to South Bend took on the Spartans. Pick: Nebraska, 28-24

▶ Bob Wojnowski: The Cornhuskers average 46 points and 520 yards per game, but proper context is required. They beat North Dakota, Bowling Green and Ohio at home. But they do have an experienced, efficient quarterback in senior Anthony Colandrea and an outstanding freshman running back in Jamal Rule. Michigan State's defense held up decently against Notre Dame, thanks to a monstrous game from Jordan Hall. If his ailing arm cooperates, Hall could be a game-changer here. The Spartans didn't run well against the Irish, and Alessio Milivojevic spent the second half running for his life. The offensive line remains a work in progress, but Pat Fitzgerald loves his team's fight. That's important, because this looks like a typical Big Ten slugfest. Pick: Nebraska, 24-17

title: Royals 'not starstruck' by PSG visit for AI summit
description: Reading Head of AI Stuart Fenton says Paris Saint-Germain's visit for a technology summit shows the progress the Royals have made.
fullText:
Reading Head of AI Stuart Fenton says Paris St-Germain's visit to the League One club for a summit on the technology shows the progress the Royals have made.

The reigning European champions and Dutch giants Ajax are among the clubs participating in the conference at Reading's Bearwood Park training complex on Friday, a year after the Royals set up a pioneering AI department driven by new owner Rob Couhig.

"PSG won the Champions League last year, so it's super exciting that we get teams like that coming to Reading," Fenton told BBC Radio Berkshire.

"We're doing some really good things here but it's not in isolation. We want to hear what some of these top teams around the world are doing.

"It also puts Reading in the conversation with those kinds of people. Every football fan - I'm a Reading fan myself - dreams of those European nights playing these teams.

"We're having the conversation with them around AI in football and where football's going.

"That's a real testament to the programme we're running here and how much advancement we've made in the last year."

Reading need to tidy up results on the road - Roberts

Inspired by the success teams such as Brighton & Hove Albion and Brentford have had through their use of data, Reading are using AI predominantly for recruitment but have also applied it to areas including tactics, retail and tending to the turf at their Select Car Leasing Stadium home.

"It's [about] creating the culture across the club where people are thinking differently - not how we can use it to replace humans, but how we can empower them and actually get them to do their job in a more effective way," said Fenton, who is the first Head of AI in English football.

"We've got some really talented people here but one of the big challenges is that data is huge in football.

"How do we use the AI and technology available to effectively streamline that data and give our team more information on players all across the world?

"Everyone thinks AI is like a light switch - you flick it and suddenly you're the world's most intelligent team. If it was that easy, everybody would be doing it. The benefits for us compound across the club.

"I had our ground staff come to me yesterday saying they're now using AI when they're doing the grass cutting. The models are looking at grass protection. AI is giving them the best possible formulas [in terms of] what they need.

"It's impacting everything across the club. What really excites me is when somebody comes up to me and says 'Stu - I've had this idea. Can we do it?'

"We've already started putting certain things in place. It's creating that culture of innovation across a football team."

Premier League side Crystal Palace and Champions League club Como are among the visitors who will hear about Reading's work and share their insights, with the event also being used to launch a new programme between the club and Setanta College on sports technology and artificial intelligence.

"We're not starstruck by these teams," added Fenton. "The exciting thing is they're coming to us - we're not going to them."

title: Germany's Havertz, Musiala ruled out of Greece match with injury
description: Kai Havertz and Jamal Musiala have been ruled out of Germany's Nations League game with Greece this weekend with injury, the German football federation (DFB) said on Friday. Arsenal forward Havertz was subbed off in the first half of Thursday's 1-1 draw with the Netherlands in Amsterdam with what appeared to be a hamstring injury.
fullText:
Kai Havertz and Jamal Musiala have been ruled out of Germany's Nations League game with Greece this weekend with injury, the German football federation (DFB) said on Friday.

Arsenal forward Havertz was subbed off in the first half of Thursday's 1-1 draw with the Netherlands in Amsterdam with what appeared to be a hamstring injury.

In a statement, the DFB said he suffered a "muscle strain" but did not indicate how long the 27-year-old was likely to be out of action.

Bayern Muninch's Musiala, 23, was injured in the warm-up on Thursday and took no part in the match.

The DFB said a scan showed a muscle tear in his thigh.

Having initially named two squads as part of a 44-man group for the four international matches, Germany coach Jurgen Klopp has brought in forwards Florian Wirtz and Jonathan Burkardt from the second set-up to replace the duo for Sunday's match against Greece in Augsburg.

So did his brother, Jordan, a safety who spent last season on the LA Chargers practice squad. Chris was on the team's negotiation list in 2024, which meant they held the rights to sign him if he chose the CFL.

5 Trade Landing Spots for Marvin Harrison Jr. to Revive NFL Career | Bleacher Report

If Mahomes gets a reliable receiver, he could once again lead the league in multiple passing categories, as he did years ago with Tyreek Hill as his top option. Harrison isn't in the same receiver mold as Hill, who can terrify defenders with blazing speed, though he can be a viable No. 1 target.

Don't forget that Harrison hauled in 62 passes for 885 yards and eight touchdowns in his 2024 rookie campaign. He hasn't lost his playmaking ability. If featured, the third-year pro can build on the promise many saw from him in his first season.

Chiefs aim to reduce Kenneth Walker's workload 'a little bit' | ESPN

Murray is optimistic the Chiefs will find the proper balance against the Dolphins on when to give Walker more rest in order to increase the snaps for Johnson.

"I want Kenneth to get into a groove, and it's hard to kind of take him out," Murray said. "But Emmett's done a great job and he's still learning. He'll continue to get more opportunities. I've just got to pull the trigger and get No. 9 [Walker] out of there and put No. 10 [Johnson] in there."

Kansas City Chiefs CB L'Jarius Sneed has been the weak link on Steve Spagnuolo's defense, but the coach isn't giving up on the veteran | A to Z Sports

"Yeah, listen, you know he's my guy, and you know he fights through the whole week with only getting a certain amount of reps because we want to be careful with his health and all that," Spagnuolo explained on Thursday. "He brings an element to our defense that every coordinator likes. He's a nasty, tough guy that plays hard and fast. Quite frankly, because I know he's out there, I'll put those guys in situations that I trust he's going to get it done. You know, he'll he'll tell you that he's a little disappointed in his performance in the game, but that doesn't deter me at all from being confident in what he can do."

How Jalen Royals' First NFL Touchdown Has 'Energized' Both Him and the Chiefs | Sports Illustrated

Speaking to the media on Thursday, receivers coach Chad O'Shea praised Royals for consistently bringing energy to the table. He isn't one bit surprised that the hard work finally paid off, and it's rubbing off on the rest of the room.

"He goes and gets his hair cut and he comes back [and] he gets his first touchdown," O'Shea said. "He comes with great energy. He's always been a lot of fun to be around. He's a tremendous person, Jalen is, that works extremely hard. He puts the team first in everything we do. We've asked him to be in some different roles for the team that he's embraced.

Bengals' Ja'Marr Chase, Tee Higgins fined multiple times for 'offensive gesture': Source | The Athletic

The NFL fined both Bengals wide receivers tens of thousands of dollars for multiple celebratory gestures during Cincinnati's Week 2 win against the Houston Texans, according to a league source and as Chase confirmed Thursday afternoon during a media session with local reporters. The source, who wasn't authorized to speak publicly, said the league considers the celebration to be an "offensive gesture," and it is part of a wave of similar fines for NFL players this past week.

Steelers CB Joey Porter Jr. moves on from contract talks, offers no firm timeline for return | NFL.com

He finally addressed the contract and health-related matter Thursday, downplaying the drama that has followed him since the start of training camp. In short, he's working his way back to the field and is no longer concerned with the financial standoff that lurked beneath his injury report status.

"It didn't get done, it didn't happen," Porter said of his desired contract extension, adding he did not request a trade. "That's really just old news for me now. It's mainly just focus on what I've got ahead of me and just really getting back to 100%."

Mike Macdonald says Sam Darnold is 'on a good track' to return from his glute injury | CBS Sports

"I don't know what 'fully healthy' means," Macdonald said when asked whether Darnold is fully healthy, per ESPN.com. "I think we'll make a decision at some point before Friday's over. I don't think we'd go into the weekend not knowing if he's going to play. But it's on a good track right now, assuming today goes well."

It at first seemed as though Darnold might miss extended time with the injury, but the healing process has apparently gone better than expected. It's entirely possible that he misses only one week of action and returns this Sunday against the Commanders.

Is Week 3 in Miami a trap game for the Chiefs?

"I haven't talked to [my teammates] about it," Mahomes declared. "I think we've been so focused on just getting better and going to this next opponent and playing against a team that's hungry and ready to play. There're a lot of Texas Tech guys too. It gives me some more motivation to go out there and compete because I was going to watch these guys play and talking to them in the locker room. Now, they'll be playing against me, so I know they'll be hungry to go up against me as well."

title: ‘It’s crazy for teams to deal with that’: Frustrating presidential policy sparks reactions before Donald Trump appearance
description: United States President Donald Trump is set to attend Saturday afternoon’s showdown between the Tennessee Volunteers and the Texas Longhorns in Knoxville. It’s widely known that the president’s attendance at any public event causes a lot of logistical challenges, but it’s safe to say that not many people knew about how Trump’s appearance could directly…
fullText:
United States President Donald Trump is set to attend Saturday afternoon's showdown between the Tennessee Volunteers and the Texas Longhorns in Knoxville. It's widely known that the president's attendance at any public event causes a lot of logistical challenges, but it's safe to say that not many people knew about how Trump's appearance could directly impact the game itself.

As the Longhorns prepare for the road showdown with Tennessee, Texas head coach Steve Sarkisian gave some rather unique insight into one of the challenges that come along with Trump attending games, and the sports media world was stunned by his revelations.

During his Thursday press conference, Sarkisian revealed that this actually is not the first time that he will be involved in a game that Trump has attended. Sarkisian was the offensive coordinator at Alabama under Nick Saban when Trump attended the College Football Playoff National Championship following the 2017 season.

Given this experience, Sarkisian has some unique insight that he was able to share.

Sarkisian revealed that whenever the president moves throughout the stadium, all communication throughout the stadium has to be shut down, including the communication between the coordinators in the booth and the sideline as well as the in-helmet comms for the players.

"One thing we have to be aware of is when the President goes to a game, any time he enters, leaves or changes locations within the stadium, they cut all communication," Sarkisian said during his Thursday Zoom press availability, via 247Sports. "They cut all communication, so they cut your headsets to coaches and they cut headsets with coach-to-player communication."

Sarkisian added that this can happen without any warning, even for something simple like the president using the restroom.

"So, you have to have a plan for that, if and or when it happens and you don't get any warning," Sarkisian said. "It just cuts out. So, you have to have a plan for that and adjust. If he comes in the middle of the first quarter and leaves in the fourth quarter or if he decides use the restroom, whatever it is, you have to be prepared for that."

Sarkisian went on to reveal that the Miami Hurricanes and the Indiana Hoosiers actually had to deal with these issues during the national championship game.

Needless to say, Sarkisian's revelation seemingly caught the sports world off guard, as several high-profile sports commentators, analysts, and personalities had no idea that this was even an issue.

"Have to admit, didn't know this one…" wrote former ESPN star Gene Wojciechowski.

"I did not realize football helmet communication gets shut off if the president gets up to go to the bathroom," wrote Chris Vianni of The Athletic.

"So if the president decides to go pee during an important 3rd down or a late offensive possession the comms go out and they have to signal in the plays? Seems like a big deal," wrote Geoff Schwartz of Fox Sports.

"I get why that's in place, but it's CRAZY for teams to deal with that. Wonder how the Lions/Commanders navigated that last year," wrote Detroit Lions beat writer Jeremy Reisman of Pride of Detroit.

"That's actually kind of wild," wrote NFL insider Albert Breer.

"It's gotta be like using your phone on the NYC subway with this president's bladder," joked broadcaster and journalist Master Tesfatsion of Bleacher Report and Amazon Prime Video.

It's certainly a unique challenge. We'll have to see whether or not it comes into play on Saturday.

title: Atalanta’s Charles De Ketelaere reveals PSG talks
description: Atalanta forward Charles De Ketelaere (25) has revealed that he held talks with Paris Saint-Germain this summer, before the reigning European champions ultimately set their sights on Spain’s Ferran ...
fullText:
Atalanta forward Charles De Ketelaere (25) has revealed that he held talks with Paris Saint-Germain this summer, before the reigning European champions ultimately set their sights on Spain's Ferran Torres (26).

PSG refreshed their attack this summer. Out went Bradley Barcola, Randal Kolo Muani, Lee Kang-in, and Goncalo Ramos, and in came Mika Godts, Maghnes Akliouche, and Torres. The latter has started in spectacular form, scoring seven goals since making the move from Barcelona. However, things could have been different.

De Ketelaere, speaking in an interview with La Dernière Heure, has revealed that he joined PSG instead of Torres. "There were clubs interested, but when you see the prices being paid in the current market, it isn't always easy to leave," said the former AC Milan forward. "I know that Atalanta were asking for a lot, I think it was around €50m."

That fee is what Les Parisiens paid to sign Torres, just weeks after he netted the winner for Spain in the FIFA World Cup final. "You have to find a team that will pay it," De Ketelaere continued. "In the Premier League, there are several teams that can do it, but it didn't happen. I spoke with PSG but they ultimately chose Ferran Torres. I am happy at Atalanta. I know how important it is to be a starter following my adventure at AC Milan."

At PSG, De Ketelaere likely would have been a rotation option and perhaps sparsely used in the big UEFA Champions League fixtures, although Torres' strong start saw him also start their UCL opener against Slovan Bratislava, during which he netted a hat-trick.

title: Theranos founder reportedly to be transferred to halfway home next year
description: Holmes was sentenced to 11 years in prison in 2022 but has seen her sentenced reduced several times
fullText:
Holmes was sentenced to 11 years in prison in 2022 but has seen her sentenced reduced several times

Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of blood testing startup Theranos, will reportedly be transferred from a minimum security prison to a halfway home next August.

In 2022, Holmes, 42, was sentenced to more than 11 years in prison for defrauding Theranos investors out of hundreds of millions of dollars and ordered to pay restitution. The company falsely promoted its technology as being capable of detecting diseases, including types of cancer, from drops of finger-pricked blood.

The Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP) informed Holmes’s victims of the upcoming move to the Austin transitional center in Del Valle, Texas, according to ABC News. The New York Times and NBC News confirmed ABC’s reporting.

While Holmes has been incarcerated at the federal prison center in Bryan, Texas, her prison term has been reduced several times.

The US district judge Edward Davila wrote in court filings that her shortened sentence did not diminish the weight of her fraudulent behavior. “Holmes’s revised sentence continues to reflect a just punishment for her serious offense and serves as a reminder that the scales of justice will balance,” Davila said, according to ABC News.

She is set to leave prison in February 2030, BOP records show.

ABC News reported that Holmes plans to reside in Austin after her release.

Holmes has faced renewed interest as the subject of comedian Nathan Fielder’s upcoming documentary You Can See Everything. The enigmatic project follows Holmes and her partner Billy Evans before her prison term and through the start of her incarceration.

In May, NPR reported that Evans had raised millions for a new medical testing startup, a revelation that fueled speculation over Holmes’s post-prison plans.

Agririgo builds a living digital twin of your farm, where every field, tunnel, pump, solar array and sensor is an object with state and history. Rigo AI reads that twin and tells you where to act, ranked, with the reason it is saying so. Built for commercial farms in Zambia and South Africa.

Open models and open data, so what we compute can be checked rather than taken on trust.

Agririgo connects every source a farm already has into one structure, where the things on the farm are objects with state and history. Rigo AI reads that structure and returns ranked actions, running on the farm's own machine, with consent.

Fields, tunnels, pumps, solar arrays, sensors, vehicles, herds and stores. Not rows in a spreadsheet: objects with a state right now and a record of what they were before.

A field belongs to a farm, carries a crop, runs through a season, is watched by a sensor and watered by a pump. Agririgo's ontology holds those relationships, so the farm exists in one place instead of nine.

Every observation, every intervention and what came of it, season after season. This is the part that compounds, and the reason an answer in year two is better than the same answer in year one.

Not a label on a photograph. A ranked list of where to act, what to optimise, where the drone should fly and what is ready for the supply chain, each with the evidence behind it.

Agririgo connects them, and remembers every field.

One ontology, models fine-tuned on African conditions, and engineers who come to the farm and map the operation before anything is built.

Tunnels, pivots, solar, herds and drones stop being separate systems. Each has a state today and a history behind it, and Rigo AI reads them together.

One twin. Every object connected, and remembered season after season.

Readings shown are illustrative

Market access, not just transparency

Traceability stopped being a goodwill exercise. For a growing list of crops, an importer in the EU or the US cannot legally accept your consignment without records you are expected to produce on demand. RigoTrace is built to hold exactly those records, per lot, from the day you plant.

Applies to coffee, cocoa, soy, palm oil, cattle, rubber and timber entering the EU. Operators must hold plot-level geolocation for the land the commodity was grown on, plus a due-diligence statement proving it was not linked to deforestation.

What RigoTrace holds: field and plot identification per lot, chain of custody through aggregation, and an exportable record for your due-diligence filing.

Applies to foods on the FDA Food Traceability List, including many fresh fruits and vegetables. Anyone in the chain must keep Key Data Elements at each Critical Tracking Event and produce them to the FDA within 24 hours of a request.

What RigoTrace holds: harvest, packing, and shipping events with lot codes and dates, exportable as a sortable spreadsheet.

Compliance dates for both regimes have been amended more than once and differ by company size. Confirm the deadline that applies to you with your importer or the official register before you plan around it. Agririgo holds the records; it does not file on your behalf and is not a substitute for legal advice.
