title: Education, Barcelona & Basque culture - why Spain are dominating football
description: Spain go into Saturday's Nations League match against England on a 38-match unbeaten run - and with a host of honours to their name. Why are they so good?
fullText:
World champions. European champions. Olympic champions. Undefeated in two and a half years. Spain are the dominant force in men's world football.

Of the past 10 major international tournaments, they have won five.

Going into Saturday's Nations League meeting with England at Wembley (19:45 BST), they are on an international record 38-match unbeaten run. They have not lost since a 1-0 defeat by Colombia in a 2024 friendly.

And the success does not stop with the senior men's team. During that time, Spain have also won:

Six Under-19 European Championships

Three Under-21 European Championships

At club level, Spanish teams have won half of all available Champions League and Europa League titles since 2009.

Spain football expert Guillem Balague told BBC Radio 5 Live there are "three pillars" that explain Spain's coaching culture and its unprecedented success.

"The first one was university, and in particular something called the National Institute of Physical Education," he said. "University entered physical education in Spain a long time ago, in the 1990s, and they created physical coaches and football coaches with a deep understanding of learning and training processes.

"Some of those fitness coaches became really big managers, like Rafa Benitez or Marcelino Garcia Toral. They came from learning and studying what football was about ahead of anybody else.

"The second pillar is the Basque culture. The Basque Country represents historically a special reference within Spanish football because they relate to work ethic, massive work ethic, daily effort.

"And the third pillar is what everybody knows: the Barcelona influence, Johan Cruyff and the tactical revolution that followed through him."

Eight players from Barcelona's La Masia academy were in the Spain squad who won the 2010 World Cup under Vicente del Bosque, and another eight were in Luis de la Fuente's group as they lifted the trophy again this summer.

Barcelona won their first European Cup in 1992 under Cruyff playing total football - a style pioneered by the Netherlands team of the 1970s in which he played, and later mirrored at the Nou Camp under Pep Guardiola's management between 2008 and 2012.

That was a period where Barcelona won three consecutive La Liga titles, while Spain won back-to-back European Championships in 2008 and 2012 either side of their 2010 World Cup triumph.

Xavi, Andres Iniesta and Sergio Busquets were brought through in a system where players learn the art of ball possession and positional play in its purest form.

Jordi Gratacos, Barcelona's international director of academies from 2009 to 2011, and then from 2016 to 2020, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "The number one thing is to understand the tactical meaning of the technical action. What I mean is to create intelligent players [who are] very good in technical aspects.

"In this level, all players are very good in the technical aspects. The most important are these players who always decide the best option inside the field and make others better.

"The main objective is to prepare the players to take the position. It's an open education when you create some scenarios, context and ecosystem where the player needs to decide, and the coach needs also to say: 'This was the best option - next time, take the other option.'

"The most important thing is that they need to decide inside the game."

In his first two seasons as Barcelona manager, Hansi Flick repeated what Guardiola did - and not only in the sense of winning two La Liga titles in a row.

Academy products form the engine of his project - with Lamine Yamal, Dani Olmo and Pau Cubarsi proving key players at both club and international level - just as the generation of 2008-12 did.

Spain have found the formula to repeat success, and Barcelona are at the heart of it.

If Barcelona and Catalonia represents the artistry of Spanish football, the Basque Country represents its character.

Five players in the 2026 World Cup squad were from the region and came through at either Athletic Bilbao or Real Sociedad - clubs where eight players were playing at the time Spain won Euro 2024.

Then there is Mikel Merino, who scored a quarter-final winner against Germany at Euro 2024, before going on to score six goals in six games in World Cup qualifying, and late winners against Portugal and Belgium over the summer.

Although not Basque, Merino is from Pamplona in the autonomous community of Navarre - a region that has a significant influence of both Spanish and Basque culture.

Just five kilometres away from Pamplona is Zizur Mayor - the town where former Chelsea captain and Spain international Cesar Azpilicueta grew up.

When asked to describe Basque culture, Azpilicueta told BBC Radio 5 Live: "The discipline, the culture of working hard, of not giving up or being resilient, not very flashy.

"Normally, people want to display this culture of fight, being tough - like English football - more duels, more physical, less technical.

"But also in terms of tactical approach, more compact, great knowledge of knowing where to go, and with the ball keep it simple and try to go forward as quick as possible."

The five Basque players from the 2026 squad have formed an important part of Spain's recent success and are an embodiment of what Cruyff thought of players from that region.

Cruyff once said: "The first thing I did as a coach, was to sign four players from the Basque region. They are not afraid of anything."

For current Spain boss De la Fuente in 2026, Unai Simon played in goal, with former Manchester City defender Aymeric Laporte a key cornerstone of a defence that conceded just one goal in eight matches all tournament.

Nico Williams assisted the winning goal for Ferran Torres in the final against Argentina, Martin Zubimendi made a positive impact from the bench in both the Euro 2024 and World Cup finals, while Mikel Oyarzabal has scored 18 goals in his past 20 Spain appearances.

This influence stretches beyond the pitch as Basque coaches are in charge at four of England's biggest clubs - Mikel Arteta at Arsenal, Unai Emery at Aston Villa, Xabi Alonso at Chelsea and Andoni Iraola at Liverpool.

On to the final pillar - education.

Former Liverpool boss Rafael Benitez explained: "We were creating in Spain a group of fitness coaches who knew about football.

"I went to Liverpool John Moores University to see the programme of the sports scientists and they didn't have the knowledge in football that we had.

"They were really good in fitness, but with the ball and on the pitch, they didn't know how to manage. So you didn't have in England, this professional, this specialist in football, sports medicine and everything that we were studying in university.

"That was a crucial part of the formation of why Spain was improving and has been improving since then."

title: FA Cup qualifying tie to be replayed after ref's error
description: Mulbarton Wanderers are "deeply upset" after being told they must replay their FA Cup qualifying tie with Woodford Town because of a referee's error.
fullText:
Mulbarton Wanderers are "deeply upset" after being told they must replay their FA Cup qualifying tie with Woodford Town because of a referee's error.

Mulbarton won 2-1 at Essex Senior League side Woodford in the second qualifying round on Saturday but the home team then lodged a protest with the Football Association following a decision in the 30th minute.

Woodford scored a penalty but the referee disallowed the goal for encroachment by a number of Woodford players and awarded Mulbarton an indirect free-kick.

Law 14 in the laws of the game, external states that the referee should have ordered the penalty to be retaken.

The FA initially said that a protest for misapplication of the rules was not permissible.

The matter was then reviewed by an FA sub-committee, which found there had been a technical error by the referee and ordered the match to be replayed.

This time Mulbarton will host the game on Tuesday, 29 September, with the tie to be decided on the night.

Mulbarton, who play in the Isthmian League North, said that the decision is "final and binding and there is no right of appeal".

The eighth-tier side from Norfolk added: "The club is deeply upset and disappointed by this decision, the impact that it will have upon our football club, and the potential wider implications regarding the finality of results for any FA Cup match in the future played by any team and the integrity of the game as a whole."

Redbridge-based Woodford, who play in the ninth tier, said: "Woodford Town FC would like to thank the FA for its thorough consideration of the matter, and for reaching a decision that ensures the tie can be concluded in accordance with FA Cup rules."

The winners will host Gloucester City of the Southern League Premier Division South in the third qualifying round on Saturday, 3 October.

The seventh-tier side initially thought they would be visiting Mulbarton so said: "We understand that this situation will be frustrating and disappointing for our supporters, particularly those who have already made plans around the scheduled fixture. We share that frustration."

They added: "We thank all of our supporters for their patience and understanding while the situation is resolved."

A non-league fixture in 2006 is thought to be the first in English football that was ordered to be replayed, external because of a referee's error. That was also when a successful penalty should have been retaken.

An FA Vase tie was also replayed last season after a referee's error over a penalty shootout.

title: The FA Cup final assistant ref whose life was turned upside down by tumour discovery
description: Dan Robathan tells BBC Newsbeat how his career as a Premier League assistant referee was brought to an end by the discovery of spinal tumours.
fullText:
It was May 2025 and life was good for Premier League and Fifa assistant referee Dan Robathan.

Years of climbing the football ladder had paid off and he was running the line at the FA Cup final between Crystal Palace and Manchester City.

But just months after this career highlight, symptoms Dan thought were sciatic nerve pain and wear and tear were revealed to be benign tumours in his spine, which needed to be operated on immediately.

"I saw a neurosurgeon who told me I had two tumours, initially I thought it was one, but it was two," Dan tells BBC Newsbeat.

"It was compressing nerves, there was a chance it could affect a motor nerve which means it could affect function in my leg.

"I needed to go home, lay down and not move. I did that for 15 days, my life turned upside down overnight."

BBC Newsbeat met Dan at a football pitch in Norwich, close to where he lives, where he revealed the struggles he has had in trying to regain his fitness and mobility.

Dan picked up his first flag at 10 years old, working his way up from grassroots football to the lines at more than 200 Premier League clashes and World Cup qualifiers.

Speaking at the time of the FA Cup final, Dan said it was "a privilege to stand there on behalf of over 37,000 referees across the country".

The chances of becoming an elite level referee are low.

The FA describes Fifa match officials, external as the "pinnacle of the officiating ladder".

And in his social media posts, Dan gives a glimpse of everything you would expect from an official at elite level - from the roar of fans to sprinting to be in the right place during split second decisions.

To the outside world, all looked well.

"I started having quite bad problems with sexual dysfunction or bladder issues where I'd have to sit down to urinate and I couldn't stand up," he explains.

"It got to a point in September [2025] where something's not right at all."

A neurosurgeon confirmed to Dan he had two tumours in his spine – and his life ground to a halt.

"It was fear, anxiety, not knowing how long it will take me to get back.

"What would my life look like? Will I be a normal man? Will I walk again?"

Surgeons removed one tumour and left one alone, which was deemed safe.

The tumours were non-cancerous, but have caused significant damage to Dan, who describes his post-operation recovery as "brutal".

Yet there was "no doubt" in his mind that he would return.

But by Christmas 2025, Dan was still feeling fatigued and struggling to lift his heel, walk, or feel his calf.

"The surgeon said I had under a 10% chance of ever getting back on the field but even then I was like I don't care I will prove everyone wrong," Dan recalls.

Yet despite fighting "like mad", he was unable to regain his fitness levels.

This week, Dan was forced to medically retire, saying in effect "the decision was made for me".

The 38-year-old says he still has days where he struggles to walk, or where his back feels "on fire".

"My body just can't do what I want it to do," he says.

Dan underwent testing to confirm his tumours weren't linked to genetics, which was reassuring, but still leaves him facing the unknown.

"It's a loss of identity. I've been 'Dan the ref' since I was 10 years old.

"It's 28 years of being who I am, it's my personality.

"When you have the recognition that that sort of life is over, psychologically it is really tough."

Dan is now working with a psychologist to decide the path forward.

"I feel like a 16-year-old who's just left school and trying to work out what I want to do with my life," he jokes.

"I have a few options, staying in football.

"[But] I don't know if I will be able to with the mental health problems I've had.

"Can I stay involved in a sport that I loved but can't do myself?"

One thing he is certain of, is going into the future with his family.

"I want to put my son, fiancée, my stepchildren first. I want to try and advocate for men's mental health, for men speaking about health issues.

"If I can help one or two men in the process, I've done my job."

And Dan accepts that if he gets back into football it would need to be for the right reasons.

"I need to get that fire my belly."

title: Chelsea charged by FA over discriminatory chanting
description: Chelsea are charged by the Football Association over alleged discriminatory behaviour by fans during their win at Fulham in August.
fullText:
Chelsea have been charged by the Football Association over alleged discriminatory behaviour by fans during their win at Fulham at the start of the Premier League season.

Chelsea wrote to supporters following the 3-2 victory at Craven Cottage on 24 August, acknowledging receiving "multiple reports of sectarian chanting from a small portion" of fans.

The Blues said they do not condone any discriminatory chants, and that fans found guilty would face "the strongest possible action".

A statement from an FA spokesperson read: "Chelsea FC has been charged with breaching FA Rule E21 during the ninth minute of its Premier League fixture against Fulham FC on 24 August.

"It's alleged that the club failed to ensure its spectators and/or supporters did not behave in an improper, offensive, abusive or insulting way.

"It's further alleged that this behaviour was discriminatory in that it included a reference, whether express or implied, to religion or belief."

In 2021 Chelsea condemned the actions of a fan who was seen on social media aiming sectarian abuse at Aston Villa's Scottish international John McGinn.

The Blues are 10th in the Premier League on seven points after the opening five games.

title: Our son's death could have been prevented by FA - Billy Vigar's parents
description: Billy Vigar's parents say the Football Association could have prevented their son's death.
fullText:
"You swing from sadness to anger because you just feel it could have been prevented."

That is the view of Camilla Vigar, whose son Billy, a former Arsenal academy player, died a year ago today from a "significant brain injury", five days after colliding with a concrete wall surrounding a pitch.

The 21-year-old striker was playing for Chichester City at Wingate and Finchley FC in north London.

In their first broadcast interview since their son's passing, the Vigar family accuse the Football Association of doing "nothing" after previous similar incidents.

"[Billy] had his whole life ahead of him. He was 21 years old and he lost it playing football when he didn't need to," she told BBC Sport.

"I personally feel that the FA could have stopped Billy losing his life because they had so many warnings."

They give the example of amateur footballer Ben Hiscox, who died in 2015 after colliding with a clubhouse near Bristol.

After the coroner warned the FA about the risk of future deaths, padding was added to Stoke Gifford United's clubhouse and the run-off between it and the pitch was increased.

The Vigars also point to the life-changing injuries sustained by Alex Fletcher in 2022.

Fletcher fractured his skull when colliding with concrete barriers next to the pitch at Bath City's ground, and was forced to retire in 2024.

The FA conducted a review of clubs after that incident.

"As far as I'm aware, nothing was done with that information and it just sat there. One of the clubs as far as I'm aware that was highlighted as being one of the high-risk clubs was Wingate [and Finchley], where Billy then lost his life," said Camilla Vigar.

When asked by the BBC what was done with the information it had gathered, the FA provided no comment.

At the time of Vigar's accident, the FA's stadium accreditation criteria, which applies to the National League System in men's football and the Women's National League, said clubs needed to have a "permanent" barrier around the pitch "of sound construction (eg concrete and steel)".

In light of what happened to Vigar, the FA launched a safety review of more than 900 clubs, which was conducted by independent experts.

As a result, the stadium criteria was updated last month and "no longer permits solid brick, breeze block or concrete barriers around pitches".

The BBC has been told 169 clubs in the men's National League System and women's National League were notified they would need to make changes "as soon as is reasonably practicable".

Where walls are structural, they must be "covered with suitable protection", such as padding.

The FA said: "This important work is under way, and we will continue to fully support the clubs involved."

Funding is being provided by the FA and the Premier League.

BBC Sport approached hundreds of affected clubs in an effort to gauge their views on the changes and understand the status of their remedial work.

Bromsgrove Sporting near Birmingham, which has a concrete wall surrounding its pitch, told BBC Sport the changes were "completely understandable and long overdue". It added: "We are fully supportive of this and are grateful for the 100% funding from the FA."

The club said it had been given a deadline of the end of this season but "being high risk it would be good to complete this side of Christmas".

Meanwhile, Sheppey United, in Kent, has a concrete supporting wall around two sides of its 3G pitch, which will be covered in padding.

Asked for their thoughts on the changes, the club said: "There is always an element of risk in all sports and they can't all be mitigated, unfortunately in this instance the remedial works are more a reactive response rather than a proactive one. If the funding wasn't in place I think it would make it difficult for some clubs to fund this."

Bath City, where Fletcher's incident happened, has solid perimeter walls on all sides of its pitch.

The club told BBC Sport: "We welcome the ruling as it seeks to improve player safety and recognises that funding needs to be available to support clubs to implement this fundamental change to the ground grading regulations."

Keith Vigar, Billy's father, said: "I work in the health and safety industry, and the main thing is you don't go to work and expect to get injured, let alone even die at work in the workplace."

The Vigars want the regulations extended above and below the National League.

"It needs to change basically at all levels, not just at the levels that have changed," said Keith Vigar.

That is a view shared by Fletcher, who said the FA had "ignored" his years of campaigning on the issue of pitch perimeter safety.

"It wasn't until Billy's passing that [the FA] came to the table on this issue," he said.

"So for me, that is a complete dereliction of duty on their part, and there should be accountability for that failing."

Fletcher also said he is worried the ban on concrete, breeze block and brick walls does not cover all levels of the game and wants that explored urgently by the authorities.

"There could be still situations where football is being played at some level, to some degree, organised football in this country, with these unsafe pitch perimeters. I would like to see that guidance, or the regulation, extended to consider all of football."

Compared to many youngsters, Billy Vigar joined the football system late - and yet his talent was still recognised.

He was scouted by Arsenal while playing for local club Hove Rivervale in Sussex, and joined the Premier League side's academy.

"It was just an amazing feeling," said his father.

"Sort of like your son's been chosen. And I'd always promised him a decent pair of football boots if he joined an academy. So yeah, since then it's cost me a fortune.

"He was something different, Billy. I think most, even at Arsenal, they saw something different in him. He was a great athlete, basically. And that started from an early age with his brother, who quickly learned there's not much point trying to challenge him because he wanted to win."

Injuries followed, and Vigar was recuperating from one such setback while playing for Chichester City FC, where he had made an instant impression.

Darin Kilpatrick, the club's first-team manager, said: "He was so coachable, he would run in behind, he would drop in short. His hold-up play was excellent and obviously he had an eye for a goal which all strikers have to have.

"To be fair, the way Bills was playing in his last couple of games that we had him, we would probably have only been able to keep him another six months before we moved him on into the higher levels where he belonged."

Asked what level he was aiming for with Billy, Kilpatrick said: "He would have gone into the National League or [English] Football League, without a doubt."

Watching football again has been difficult for Keith Vigar.

"It did become less important, far less important to start with, the struggle to get back into it," he said. "When we went to see Chichester in that sense, first off, it's hard because you're just thinking, 'Billy should be out there, Billy should be playing' and that sort of thing. That's been hard."

The Vigars said Chichester FC have been "amazing" during the past year, including designing a kit that makes moving but subtle references to their son.

They want accountability and answers. They are awaiting the inquest, which is likely to take place next year.

But today, as they mark the one-year anniversary of their son's tragic accident, they will pour all their focus into climbing Snowdon with their children Phoebe and Ollie, and the family of Billy's girlfriend Lois.

"I think it just gives us something to focus on and gives us a challenge to do," Keith Vigar said. "And I know he'd have liked to do that. I'm sure he will be with us somewhere, looking over us in some way or form, having a laugh at us, no doubt, in the rain."

Vigar's death was 'entirely preventable'

title: NHL's Kuzmenko returns to Russia after father killed by bear
description: Pittsburgh Penguins forward Andrei Kuzmenko returns to Russia before the start of the NHL season after his father was killed by a bear.
fullText:
Pittsburgh Penguins forward Andrei Kuzmenko has returned to Russia before the start of the NHL season after his father was killed by a bear.

Kuzmenko's father Alexander, who was an ice hockey coach in Russia, was on a fishing trip along the Krasnaya River in Southern Siberia with a group of seven others when a bear attacked from the trees.

The 62-year-old suffered severe facial injuries in the attack.

A member of the fishing party called for an ambulance but the dense forest made it difficult for emergency services to reach the area.

Kuzmenko was taken by river downstream for four hours before then being airlifted to hospital, where he was later pronounced dead.

Penguins president Kyle Dubas said the team was "deeply saddened" by the death.

"Our deepest thoughts and sympathies are with the Kuzmenko family and their loved ones as they grieve the loss of Alexander. We ask that the privacy of Andrei and the Kuzmenko family be respected at this time," the team said in a statement.

"Andrei chose to be surrounded by his team-mates and practice with the team this morning before returning to Moscow to be with his family this afternoon. Andrei and the Kuzmenko family have the full support of the Penguins organisation during this time."

The 30-year-old signed a one-year contract with the Penguins this summer and is about to compete in his fifth season in the NHL, following previous stints with the Vancouver Canucks, Calgary Flames, Philadelphia Flyers and Los Angeles Kings.

The NHL season begins on 29 September.

title: You are the new Scotland boss - what would you do?
description: Put yourself in the shoes of the new Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli as he picks his first XI.
fullText:
Nations League: Slovenia v Scotland

Saturday 26 September, 14:00 BST

It is a new era for the Scotland men's side as head coach Sebastien Pocognoli takes charge of his first game on Saturday against Slovenia, live on the BBC.

The Belgian included eight uncapped players in his first squad before releasing Findlay Curtis and James Wilson to the under-21s, which means the line-up and approach to the Nations League match in Ljubljana is unpredictable.

However, you can try your best to assess what the new Scotland boss might do with our team selector below, while we have also picked out some key issues for Pocognoli to wrestle with.

When manager of Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco, Pocognoli generally favoured a 3-4-2-1 formation and its variations.

That means Scotland are likely to line up with three centre-backs on Saturday afternoon, with five named in the squad.

Jack Hendry and Scott McKenna are the experienced survivors from Steve Clarke's World Cup group and, given Pocognoli said he is keen to strike a balance between new and old faces "to keep the cohesion in the team", they both appear likely starters.

Especially given they have the physical profile to play the aggressive style the head coach wants.

That would leave Swansea City's Stephen Welsh, Stoke City's Luke Graham and Brondby captain Luis Binks to fight it out for the final spot.

Welsh is the only right-footed one of the three, which might give him the edge if McKenna were to play on the left and Hendry in the middle.

However, Graham has been playing on the left of a back three for Stoke, which could allow McKenna to sit in the middle and shift Hendry to the right.

It all depends what balance Scotland are looking for.

With captain Andy Robertson a certainty to win his 98th cap at left wing-back, and Aaron Hickey surely in prime position to start on the other side, where does that leave Scotland's wide attacking options?

Ben Gannon-Doak was so key for Scotland under Clarke due to his speed and ability to beat players. Josh McPake has shown a similar ability for Hearts on the same side.

However, with Pocognoli often deploying two narrow attackers either side of a centre forward and using the wing-backs for width, could Scotland's wingers be squeezed out?

One of those forward places would surely be reserved for John McGinn, given his goal threat for Scotland, running power and experience of occupying a similar role on the left. He also offers more off the ball.

Ryan Christie might be another candidate for one of those roles, assuming Scotland only play two holding midfielders from their deep pool - Lewis Ferguson and Billy Gilmour. The Bournemouth midfielder is also relentless out of possession.

Could Gannon-Doak or McPake play further in the pitch closer to a striker? And do they have the defensive instincts to play more centrally when Scotland don't have the ball?

Gannon-Doak was named as a forward in the squad, while McPake, interestingly, was named as a midfielder. Who knows if that means anything, but it will be fascinating to see what Pocognoli thinks.

Pocognoli has 'positive nervousness' for Scotland debut

From leaving Rangers to La Liga - Scotland is next step for Ure

Well-travelled Binks eager to make mark for Scotland

Kieron Bowie, Robbie Ure and Oli McBurnie are the striker options in the squad and all three are in good form and confident.

Ure and McBurnie are yet to score for their clubs this term, but the former just got a morale-boosting move to Sevilla after his exploits in Sweden and faced Barcelona only a week ago.

The latter is playing well for Hull City in the Premier League and grabbed 19 goals in their promotion charge last term.

McBurnie is the oldest and comfortably the most experienced of the options in the squad but has never impressed in his 16 previous caps.

Now, it's a clean slate and he says he has a point to prove after a few years in the international wilderness.

It would be the ultimate vote of confidence from Pocognoli if he were to start McBurnie in the face of a few Tartan Army grumbles.

title: Why schoolboys have become a huge part of football's transfer market
description: BBC Sport explores why clubs at the top of English football are increasingly trading academy players and what the impact is on the youngsters themselves.
fullText:
A 15-year-old growing up in the UK faces many tough personal decisions about their future - which school subjects to study, which social circle suits them, and where their priorities lie in life.

But in the past few weeks the choices teenage Manchester United striker JJ Gabriel has been making about his future in football have drawn huge public attention in sports media and online.

Gabriel has informed United he wants to leave the club and join another. BBC Sport has reported that he has stayed away from training and begun talking to other clubs because he and his representatives are unhappy with United's handling of the 15-year-old's progress.

That a transfer saga involving a footballer so young could generate so much interest highlights a truth that to many is uncomfortable - money is changing how the football transfer market works, and children are increasingly deemed to be among its most valuable commodities.

So what is behind the rise in transfers involving boys who in some cases are not even old enough to have taken their GCSEs, what kind of influence can the money on offer have on agents and parents, and what exactly are the country's top football clubs getting out of it?

"It's crazy when you think about it," says Ryan Cardwell, former youth scout at Liverpool and Southampton.

"In what other kind of world would 15 and 16-year-olds be spoken about in the media like this?"

This summer alone, all six of the Premier League's wealthiest clubs either signed a highly-rated academy player from another, or lost a youngster to a direct rival.

"It is such a competitive market," Cardwell explains. "There are now tens of transfers between the elite academies every summer, when it used to be the case that if you were already at one of those, you would likely stay the course.

"The race for talent is huge – you look at what teams are spending on transfers for senior players and it's enormous, so if you can spot a player earlier and offset some of that financial risk, you're going to do so."

Some inside football claim that the transfer of Rio Ngumoha - the now 18-year-old winger who was called up to this month's senior England squad - from Chelsea to Liverpool at the age of 15 in 2024 ushered in a new era of competition for academy players among the nation's elite.

One of the major factors is Brexit. Before 2021 English clubs were allowed to sign academy players over the age of 16 who held European Union passports.

Since the UK left the EU, foreign players cannot join English clubs until they reach 18.

"Heathrow and Gatwick [airports] on a Friday night were inundated with scouts going to other countries to look for young players", says Caldwell.

"Belgium and the Netherlands were full of scouts for Premier League clubs.

"Now it's the competition between English clubs that has increased, looking at each other's players, including the old-school 'top six' but also the likes of Southampton, Aston Villa, and Fulham."

Young players have further added financial value - youth signings don't count towards the Premier League's squad cost ratio rules, and any future sale counts as 'pure profit' in club accounts.

Advances in video technology and data analysis mean more young players are being identified, tracked and approached by rival clubs than ever before.

Players can de-register from their academy at the end of their under-12, under-14 and under-16 seasons if they wish to explore options elsewhere.

They can be offered paid scholarship contracts from the season in which they turn 14, and can sign professional deals from the season in which they turn 16.

Some pundits and fans have criticised Gabriel's family over the controversy in recent weeks.

Gabriel can potentially join clubs in Europe because he has an Irish passport.

"It's a really tough world - players and families want the best for their kids and you can't give them stick without knowing what their motivations are," says Phil Jagielka, whose son Zac left Liverpool in 2024 and signed a scholarship deal at Hull City at 16.

"The harsh reality is that if a young player fails to progress, or gets a bad injury, teams will stop being interested in them. So there is an element of strike while the iron's hot."

When a club signs a player from a rival academy, they pay a set compensation fee based on how long they had been trained there.

Depending on the player's age, the fee can reach millions of pounds.

The increasing allure of signing young academy players from rivals means some parents are now compiling data packs on their sons to give to potential clubs, and more and more children are represented by football agents.

"There are good agents and bad agents," Cardwell says.

"You certainly speak to some and think 'that's completely the wrong idea', or, ' this player is going to be misguided'. Sometimes they push for a move when a player isn't ready.

"The contracts can be enormous and [money] can be a huge motivation to move. It could set a young player's family up for life.

"I would quite like to see some form of financial cap. My fear for some of the young players is they're on the biggest salaries they'll ever have, because if they don't make it at the top level, they can go from being on tens of thousands (of pounds) a week to one or two thousand lower down the pyramid."

In decades gone by, development of academy players would be combined with menial tasks around the training ground.

The idea was to keep young footballers grounded and make them feel a part of the wider club.

But the Gabriel case demonstrates the significant changes football has undergone.

"We would clean boots, sweep floors, tidy the changing rooms," says Jagielka, who came through Sheffield United's academy in the late 1990s.

"I fully back that system. It taught us responsibility and discipline. It was a way of getting to know the first-team players, and you would get a proper telling off if you didn't do your jobs properly.

"There was nowhere near as much outside influence on young players back then. Now there is an entourage, people wanting to play the long game with, 9, 10, 11-year-olds because of the millions of pounds of commission if they turn out to be a superstar.

"There are far more people out there now who are prepared to rock the boat between the different clubs."

The public scrutiny on young players has increased significantly, and the elite clubs' desire to succeed in the market means that high-profile youth transfers involving big money seem to be here to stay.

"Young players now have such a big platform on social media that intrigue is part of day-to-day life for them," says Cardwell.

"When you're in elite sport you have to grow up really, really fast. Teenagers are expected to cope with the pressure and naturally some people fall into the trap of thinking 'well, he's a young man already' and forget about everything else.

"The race for talent is never, ever going to change."

Youth star JJ Gabriel, 15, on brink of leaving Man Utd

'I never looked back' - Ngumoha on his rise over the past year

title: George Lombard Jr.'s late go-ahead homer punctuates Yankees' 6-4 comeback win over Rays
description: Cam Schlittler made his final start of a season worthy of the AL Cy Young, while George Lombard Jr. powered the Yankees to a 6-4 come-from-behind win over the rival Tampa Bay Rays.
fullText:
In the final game of their four-game home series against the Tampa Bay Rays (96-63), the Yankees (92-67) came back from 4-0 down to win 6-4.

-- In the second inning, after allowing a walk to Jonny DeLuca and a single to Richie Palacios with two outs away, Yankees starter Cam Schlittler struck out Ryan Vilade to strand Rays baserunners on first and third and preserve a scoreless tie.

-- The following inning, Taylor Walls drew a leadoff walk. Walls came around to score on the very next at-bat, a single by Yandy Diaz, which became an unearned RBI double when right fielder Heliot Ramos' throw to third base intended to tag out Walls skittered away. Then, Rays star third baseman Junior Caminero laced an RBI single to double the damage in the inning.

-- With the Rays having clinched the AL East division title, Yankees manager Aaron Boone made it clear that he would be limiting the number of pitches his starters throw during the team's remaining regular season games to ensure their arms are fresh for the postseason. Accordingly, with the Yanks still trailing 2-0, he pulled Schlittler for right-handed reliever Michael Fulmer, who opened the fourth inning with a clean frame to work with. Caminero knocked Fulmer out of the game with one out away in the fifth, mashing an RBI double off the left field wall, which scored Diaz. Tim Hill relieved Fulmer and worked into - and more importantly, out of - a bases-loaded jam to hold the Rays to their 3-0 lead.

-- With Luis Gil on the mound for the sixth inning, the Yankees couldn't complete a double play when Gil dropped George Lombard Jr.'s on-target throw to first base. A run scored as a result. In the bottom half of the frame, Austin Wells clubbed a solo homer to cut Tampa's lead to 4-1. Gil pushed onward to record a scoreless seventh inning.

-- Lombard singled home Ben Rice in the bottom of the seventh with a one-out double, before the shortstop added another run thanks to a wild pitch with an acrobatic slide-turned-hop-turned tag of home plate, beating out Rays catcher Liam Hicks. With two outs and Yankees baserunners on second and third, Paul Goldschmidt completed the comeback and tied the game, 4-4, with a single to center field. Cody Bellinger grounded out with runners on the corners to end the inning.

-- Rookie reliever Bradley Hanner handled the eighth for the Yankees. After allowing a leadoff double, he battled back to record a scoreless inning.

-- With the score still tied, one runner on base, and two outs in the inning, Lombard cranked a pitch down the left field line, a moonshot that stayed fair and gave New York a 6-4 lead.

-- Hanner closed the door in the ninth inning, earning his first career win as well as his first career save, sealing the series win for the Yankees, 6-4 the final on Thursday night.

-- Following his brief start on Thursday night, Schlittler's final stats for the 2026 regular season were set in stone. Across 33 starts, Schlittler pitched to the tune of a 1.95 ERA and 0.92 WHIP. He tallied 239 strikeouts and just 47 walks in 193.2 IP. Time will tell whether his sensational season is rewarded with the AL Cy Young Award.

The rookie shortstop was the hero on Thursday night. He tallied three RBI on two hits - a double and a two-run homer, his seventh in just 41 career games thus far - and showcased his athleticism on his improvisational slide, which allowed him to score from third on a wild pitch.

A solo homer for Austin Wells to lead off the bottom of the 6th and the Yankees are on the board pic.twitter.com/woyBnJ9Bqq

An RBI double for George Lombard Jr.! pic.twitter.com/wIBriD3grw

What a slide by George Lombard Jr.!

The Yankees cut it to 4-3! pic.twitter.com/XNl2G2oOzn

Paul Goldschmidt comes through and then Yankees tie the game! pic.twitter.com/4secEoz1uP

GEORGE LOMBARD JR. CLUTCH 2-RUN HOMER FOR THE LEAD! pic.twitter.com/c2nuoMyhqW

The Yankees kick off the final series of their regular season, a three-game set at home against the Baltimore Orioles on Friday.

Due to the forecast of sustained inclement weather on Saturday, Friday will see the Yanks and O's play a doubleheader.

The first game is set to begin at 4:05 p.m. and the second game will start no earlier than 7:05 p.m.

New York's starting pitcher in that first game is yet to be announced.

Baltimore will send out Trevor Rogers (4.07 ERA, 1.18 WHIP in 165.2 IP).

title: He is the ATP player who became world number one despite losing six first round matches in a row
description: There have been 29 different men who have held the number one singles ranking on the ATP Tour. Jannik Sinner is the 29th of those...
fullText:
There have been 29 different men who have held the number one singles ranking on the ATP Tour.

Jannik Sinner is the 29th of those world number ones, with his current ongoing reign lasting 24 weeks, having topped the ATP rankings for a total of 90 weeks across his three spells.

Despite this, Sinner is under threat of losing his number one to Alexander Zverev, who has won two Grand Slams this year and is currently on track to end the year as the top-ranked player in men's tennis.

Zverev is now in a similar position to what Yevgeny Kafelnikov was in back in 1999, but he will be hoping that if he does become world number one, it happens in a more successful fashion than it did for the Russian 27 years ago.

Kafelnikov came into the 1999 season as the world number 11, but had previously been ranked as high as world number three.

The Russian very quickly returned to the top 10, as Kafelnikov won the Australian Open, his second Grand Slam title after Roland Garros in 1996.

This propelled Kafelnikov back up to his previous career-high of world number three, as he closed in on the world number one ranking, which was then held by Pete Sampras, who did not play the Australian Open due to physical and mental fatigue.

Kafelnikov continued this form into the indoor season, where he won the title at the Rotterdam Open after beating a young Roger Federer, as well as British players Greg Rusedski and then Tim Henman in the final.

This placed Kafelnikov as the world number two heading into the sunshine double of Indian Wells and the Miami Open, but neither tournament went to plan for him.

Kafelnikov lost his only match at both Indian Wells and the Miami Open, and after winning two matches in the Davis Cup, he was hoping to rediscover his form upon his return to the ATP Tour for the clay court season.

This did not happen for Kafelnikov, who lost in the first round of all four of his next clay-court tournaments. Three of these four players Kafelnikov would lose to were ranked outside the top 60, including then world number 196 Ivan Ljubicic beating him in Monte Carlo.

Despite Kafelnikov losing in the first round of six tournaments in a row, he became world number one after being beaten by world number 72 Richard Fromberg and overtook Sampras, who dropped 144 points after being absent due to a back injury, at the top of the ATP rankings.

Yevygeny Kafelnikov's losing streak before becoming No.1

Gustavo Kuerten beat Kafelnikov, 0-6 7-6(4) 6-3

Vincent Spadea beat Kafelnikov, 6(6)-7 7-6(4) 6-2

Andrei Pavel beat Kafelnikov, 6-3 2-6 6-3

Franco Squillari beat Kafelnikov, 6-2 6-4

Ivan Ljubicic beat Kafelnikov, 6-1 6-2

Richard Fromberg beat Kafelnikov, 6-4 2-6 6-4

Kafelnikov ended his run of six successive first-round losses at his next tournament in Rome, but his relatively poor form still continued after becoming world number one.

In his four tournaments as world number one, Kafelnikov won just six of his 10 matches, which culminated after losing in the first round of the Queen's Club Championships.

Sampras won the title at Queen's, and therefore dethroned world number one Kafelnikov, who dropped down to world number three after also falling below Pat Rafter.

Tournaments Kafelnikov played as world number one

Third Round – Lost to Gustavo Kuerten (No.14)

Hypo Group Tennis International (St.Poelten)

Semi-final – Lost to Mariano Zabaleta (No.26)

Second Round – Lost to Dominik Hrbaty (No.30)

First Round – Lost to Sargis Sargsian (No.74)

Kafelnikov's one and only run as world number one lasted a total of six weeks, which is one of the lowest in ATP history, equal to Marcelo Rios and Thomas Muster.

Only Carlos Moya (2) and Rafter (1) have had short reigns as world number one, with both also taking place during the 1999 season.

title: QB Marcus Washington Jr. commits to Kentucky Football
description: Kentucky secure a commitment from sophomore quarterback Marcus Washington following the team's upset of Texas A&M.
fullText:
The momentum from Kentucky Football's huge upset win over No. 9 Texas A&M continues for the Wildcats and head coach Will Stein, as the Wildcats have landed a commitment from 2029 3-star quarterback Marcus Washington Jr.

Washington does not currently have a national ranking, as he is only a sopho

The 6-foot, 165-pound quarterback plays for Cajon High School in San Bernardino, California, and chose Kentucky over programs including Arizona, Arizona State, Michigan, North Carolina, Texas A&M, and others.

Kentucky first offered Washington in May and brought him to Lexington for an unofficial visit on Sept. 12. It appears the Wildcats made a strong first impression, with Kentucky's 31-21 upset of Texas A&M helping further solidify Washington's interest in the program.

The Wildcats also have a promising quarterback pipeline for the coming years. Kenny Minchey is expected to lead the team this season and next, while Matt Ponatoski could take over in 2028. 4-star 2027 quarterback Jake Nawrot is also committed to Kentucky, giving the Wildcats another highly regarded quarterback in the pipeline.

Of course, Kentucky could still add another quarterback to its 2028 recruiting class, but the future of the position is already looking bright under Stein.

Washington's recruitment is not necessarily over, and plenty can change during the recruiting process. However, his commitment gives Stein and the Kentucky staff another young quarterback to develop as they continue building the program for the future.

title: Durfee football wins with heavy heart: 'Everything we do moving forward is for Marvins.'
description: Durfee football players honored late teammate Marvins Antoine with an emotional victory. "Everything we do moving forward is for Marvins."
fullText:
FALL RIVER — Matt Sherry and the Durfee High football team played with a heavy heart on Thursday, Sept. 24 against Somerset Berkley.

The Hilltoppers wore the emblem 'MA4' on their helmets in memory of former teammate Marvins Antoine, who was killed in a stabbing last weekend.

For 48 minutes, the Durfee team and Sherry played hard for Antoine.

"Mentally the whole team was in a rough place, especially coming after that news in the morning" Sherry said after the Hilltoppers defeated the Raiders 28-7. "I feel like it defintely brought us together this week. Everything we do moving forward is for Marvins."

Watch MA high school football on NFHS

Sherry threw two touchdowns and ran for another to account for most of the Hilltoppers offense. Sophomore running back Ahliy Cantave rushed for his third straight 100-yard game. He finished with a game-high 134 yards on 18 carries and scored a 47-yard touchdown.

"It has been a tough week for the program," Durfee head coach Taylor Brown said. "We went through real life situations this week. I'm happy for the kids with they way they responded all week. We were only able to practice two days this week. We knew it wasn't going to be easy because Somerset plays until the end. I told the kids to play for Marvins because he was always super competitive when he was out there."

The Raiders (0-3) responded after the Hilltoppers drove the field for a touchdown — a Sherry keeper from 2 yards out — on their first possession. Senior Gavin Gooch took it in from 16 yards out to tie the game at 7-7 with a 1:50 remaining in the first quarter.

The only problem, SBR went scoreless for the last three quarters.

"You can shoot yourself in the foot," Raiders first-year head coach Chris Santos said. "We were playing behind the sticks, penalties and stuff like that. It makes life difficult. I thought my boys played hard. Those guys (Durfee) was playing with a little extra fire today."

Catave's long touchdown run late in the second quarter enabled the Hilltoppers (2-1) to take a 14-7 lead. Sherry then completed a long 45-yard pass to Landyn Nogueira for a touchdown with 39 seconds before halftime to give Durfee the lead at 21-7.

Sherry finished off his brilliant night with 21-yard touchdown strike to James Gondre with 3:59 left in the third quarter.

There was a moment of silence prior to the game to pay homage to Antoine, who lost his life last weekend in Providence, Rhode Island. He was 18 years of age. Since the COVID season, the Raiders hold a 3-2 advantage over the Hilltoppers entering Thursday's contest. Both of Durfee's win came at Somerset Berkley Regional High School.

title: Houston Rockets jersey history No. 32 - Pete Chilcutt (1994-96)
description: During his time suiting up for the Rockets, Chilcutt wore only jersey No. 32 and put up 3.9 points, and 3.3 rebounds per game.
fullText:
The Houston Rockets have had players donning a total of 52 different jersey numbers (and have one not part of any numerical series for Houston assistant coach and general manager Carroll Dawson) since their founding at the start of the 1967-68 season, worn by just under 500 players in the course of Rockets history.

To honor all of the players who wore those numbers over the decades, Rockets Wire is covering the entire history of jersey numbers and the players who wore them since the founding of the team all those years ago right up to the present day.

With seven of those jerseys now retired to honor some of the greatest Rockets of all time to wear those jerseys, there is a lot of history to cover.

And for today's article, we will continue with the seventh of 14 who wore the No. 32, Pete Chilcutt. After ending his college career at UNC, Chilcutt was picked up with the 27th overall selection of the 1991 NBA Draft by the Sacramento Kings.

The Sumter, South Carolina native played the first 3 seasons of his pro career with the Kings. He also played for the Detroit Pistons before he signed with the Houston Rockets in 1994. His stay with the team lasted until he was dealt to the (then) Vancouver (now, Memphis) Grizzlies in 1996

During his time suiting up for the Rockets, Chilcutt wore only jersey No. 32 and put up 3.9 points, and 3.3 rebounds per game.

title: JJ Redick addresses Lakers starting lineup then drops viral quote
description: Who will join Luka Doncic, Austin Reaves and Walker Kessler in the Lakers starting lineup this season?
fullText:
The 2026-27 NBA season is quickly approaching, and Los Angeles Lakers coach JJ Redick still has questions to answer before training camps begin Monday, Sept. 29.

Redick and Rob Pelinka, the team's President of Basketball Operations, spoke reporters to address where things stand from a roster reconstruction standpoint within the organization.

Redick was clear that guards Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves along with center Walker Kessler are all penciled in as starters for the upcoming season, but position battles remain.

As for the rest of the starting lineup? Redick joked, "The other spots will not be two white guys."

More: Did Lakers lose or win free agency? Grading massive roster overhaul.

Pelinka stated that the team has three clear objectives for the roster this offseason.

The first was re-signing Reaves, who agreed to a four-year, $180 million max contract in July. The team also had aspirations of acquiring a "franchise center" to play alongside Dončić.

Kessler signed a four-year, $130 million deal with the Lakers, but in order to secure the big man, the Lakers needed to send multiple draft assets to the Utah Jazz as part of the trade, including unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and 2033 and first-round swaps in 2028 and 2030.

Los Angeles went with a youth movement after LeBron James, the NBA's oldest active player and arguably still the league's biggest star, departed and signed as a free agent with the Philadelphia 76ers.

Kessler is 25 years old, and wing Ziaire Williams is 24. Guard Quentin Grimes is 26, while guard Collin Sexton and forward Sandro Mamukelashvili are both 27.

Quentin Grimes is expected to serve as the small forward in the lineup while Jake LaRavia and Sandro Mamukelashvili will compete for the role as the starting power forward.

title: Seahawks safety Julian Love an NFL leader in key stat

title: It should have happened years ago. Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua are finally ready
description: Talk about the fight between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua has shifted from if the heavyweight bout will happen to what it might look like Dec. 11.
fullText:
Tyson Fury will try to keep Anthony Joshua on his back foot with the jab, predicts Grey Johnson of BoxRec, the official database for pro boxing. Maybe sneak in an uppercut and hurt Joshua.

Joshua, by contrast, will try to box carefully for a bit to get his confidence going, said BoxRec's Johnson. Maybe get in some counters and then he can push Fury around.

In abrupt and welcome fashion, talk around the heavyweight boxing match between Fury (36-2-1, 25 KOs) and Joshua (30-4, 27 KOs) finally shifted from if it will happen to what might happen during a fight between two former world champions.

It's on, and it's a win for boxing.

No gimmicks. No influencers. Just two British heavyweights capable of slugging it out.

Let's get the details out of the way:

Where: Principality Stadium in Cardiff Wales of the United Kingdom.

Time: 2 a.m. local time. 9 p.m. ET.

Streaming: Netflix (free with a monthly subscription.)

Joshua stands 6-6 and for his last fight weighed in at 251 pounds.

Fury stands 6-9 and for his last fight weighed 261 pounds.

In December, Joshua broke Jake Paul's jaw in two places during a sixth-round knockout victory. In July, Joshua knocked out Kristian Prenga in the second round.

In July, Fury's opponent, Mariusz Wach did not bother coming out for the eighth round.

Both Fury and Joshnua are equipped to stop the other with one punch.

Ideally, they would have fought seven years ago. In recent years, both fighters have showed their age.

Joshua, 36, got knocked down twice in the first by Prenga in July before he staved off near-disaster with his second-round KO. He also suffered a brutal knockout loss to Daniel Dubois in 2024.

Fury, 37, got knocked down in 2023 by Francis Ngannou, the former UFC champion who was making his pro boxing debut.

Both Joshua and Fury also have lost two fights to Oleksandr Usyk, the former undisputed heavyweight champion.

Fury and Joshua remain two of the biggest and most charismatic stars in boxing. They have the size and the skill to deliver an electric fight, in front of an expected sellout crowd of 73,000 in Principality Stadium and a global audience on Netflix.

Tyson is the early favorite, and the line could shift before something becomes clear about this fight.

title: Concerning news for Knicks as $276 Million Finals Star Hits Contract Stalemate
description: The New York Knicks are preparing to defend their first NBA championship in 53 years, but a key player faces an uncertain future. Karl-Anthony Towns helped New York beat the San Antonio Spurs in the Finals, but his contract situation remains unsettled before training camp. Towns is eligible for a four-year extension worth up to [...]
fullText:
The New York Knicks are preparing to defend their first NBA championship in 53 years, but a key player faces an uncertain future. Karl-Anthony Towns helped New York beat the San Antonio Spurs in the Finals, but his contract situation remains unsettled before training camp.

Towns is eligible for a four-year extension worth up to $276 million. ESPN's Shams Charania reported that talks have stalled and that an agreement is unlikely before training camp begins.

The Knicks and Towns discussed an extension for much of the offseason, but little progress has been made recently. Talks could continue during the season, although ESPN reported that a deal is not expected soon.

The timing adds pressure to the situation. Towns is entering the final guaranteed year of his contract and will earn $57 million this season. He also has a $61 million player option for the 2027-28 season.

New York has also set a clear financial limit. Owner James Dolan has repeatedly said the Knicks want to avoid the NBA's second apron, which restricts how expensive teams can build and change their rosters. That approach has already come at a cost, as backup center Mitchell Robinson left for the Boston Celtics during the offseason.

Towns enters the contract talks after a strong postseason. He averaged 15.9 points, 10.6 rebounds and 4.9 assists while shooting 55 percent during the playoffs. That production helped New York finish 16-3 and win the championship.

His playoff performance gives him a strong case for a major extension. However, the Knicks also face other costly contract decisions. Josh Hart is eligible for an extension, while Jalen Brunson and OG Anunoby could become eligible next offseason.

New York must now balance two goals. The Knicks want to keep their championship team together, but they also want to avoid pushing the payroll beyond the limit they have set.

Towns remains under contract with the Knicks for the coming season. The main question is whether New York can find a number that keeps its championship core together without crossing its financial line.

title: California high court rules sheriff's seizure of 650,000 ballots was unlawful
description:
Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco arrives at the Supreme Court of California in San Francisco on Aug. 24 for a hearing about his seizure of more than half a million 2025 election ballots. (Noah Berger / Associated Press)
The California Supreme Court excoriated Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco over his seizure of hundreds of thousands of Proposition 50 ballots earlier this year, ordering the former gubernatorial candidate to immediately hand over all remaining materials in a pair of scathing decisions Thursday. 
“We hold that the seizure of the ballots was unlawful,” wrote Chief Justice Patricia Guerrero. “While allegations of election improprieties are a very serious matter, our Elections Code contains numerous established mechanisms for investigating and proving misconduct that do not compromise the integrity of voted ballots — contrary to the means employed here.
fullText:
The California Supreme Court excoriated Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco over his seizure of hundreds of thousands of Proposition 50 ballots earlier this year, ordering the former gubernatorial candidate to immediately hand over all remaining materials in a pair of scathing decisions Thursday.

"We hold that the seizure of the ballots was unlawful," wrote Chief Justice Patricia Guerrero. "While allegations of election improprieties are a very serious matter, our Elections Code contains numerous established mechanisms for investigating and proving misconduct that do not compromise the integrity of voted ballots — contrary to the means employed here."

California voters overwhelmingly passed Proposition 50 in a special election last fall, blessing a new congressional map that all but eliminated Republican districts in response to gerrymandering efforts in Texas and other deep-red strongholds.

Bianco, a popular MAGA personality and former Republican candidate for governor, doggedly pursued claims the Riverside County returns were fraudulent, seizing on a discrepancy between the registrar's voluntary hand tally and the official vote count to commandeer the ballots as evidence of a crime — a move the court roundly rejected.

"A criminal prosecution commences only upon the occurrence of certain events — none of which has occurred in this case — and may only be initiated by a public prosecutor," Guerrero wrote. "But even if a criminal prosecution had commenced, allowing for a court-ordered production, [the law's] plain text prohibits the removal of the ballots from the registrar's physical custody."

The ruling comes less than two weeks before Californians will start casting ballots in the race for governor and a handful of bitter congressional contests — nationally-watched elections that would be vulnerable to similar interference unless the court gave clear orders, advocates warned at oral arguments last month.

"It's bound to be repeated again," said Chad W. Dunn of the UCLA Voting Rights Project, which led the first of two related suits against Bianco.

California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta, who brought the other suit, cheered Thursday's rulings as an important electoral safeguard.

"The Court has now made clear that this kind of defiance cannot stand," Bonta said in a statement following the twin decisions. "I encourage Californians to make their voices heard and vote early in the fast-approaching November 3 midterm elections, with the confidence of knowing that their voted ballots will never again be subject to physical seizure by rogue county sheriffs."

Bianco did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Bianco has long flirted with President Trump's election fraud conspiracy movement. Though the ballot seizures in February were widely seen as a campaign stunt, the legal theory behind them — that local lawmen can commandeer voter materials from elections officials, and that sheriffs are unanswerable to officials who outrank them, including attorneys general — belongs to a larger "constitutional sheriffs" ideology.

California's seven Supreme Court justices appeared by turns perplexed by and incredulous of those theories during oral arguments last month.

"You are walking into a very dense thicket of very specific laws that govern elections in particular and I think it's a very established cannon of interpretation that the specific trumps the general," said Associate Justice Goodwin H. Liu.

Thursday's rulings effectively short-circuited Bianco's efforts to keep the ballot probe alive.

"Bianco presumably could have used traditional investigatory tools, within the bounds of the law, to obtain other evidence of election-related crime," Guerrero wrote.

Further, the court said, Bonta's authority to stop both the seizure and the ad hoc recount was unequivocal.

"Respondents' arguments all boil down to the unsustainable view that the state's chief law enforcement officer ... must remain a mere bystander to an unprecedented sheriff's investigation of undeniable statewide significance," Guerrero wrote. "As we have explained, that is not the case."

In a footnote, justices also took a swipe at Bianco's initial effort to have the case tossed for lack of standing — a move apparently undertaken on the legal advice of an elaborate AI hallucination, reminding lawyers of their "professional duties of competence and candor."

The ballot battle emerged from a Riverside County pilot program meant to boost voter confidence — a handwritten tally that ultimately fell about 46,000 votes short of the official count, sparking claims of fraud.

The registrar of voters met with the county board of supervisors and the citizens' group behind the claim and carefully explained how the discrepancy emerged. Yet, Bianco pursued warrants to seize more than 650,000 ballots, alleging they were evidence in an investigation of wide-ranging misconduct.

When he learned of the warrants, Bonta ordered Bianco to stand down. Instead, the sheriff accelerated his plans, dispatching armed deputies from Riverside County's Special Investigations Bureau, Emergency Response Team and SWAT unit to sweep up the votes.

Later, Bianco directed his underlings to begin counting those ballots by hand — a potential felony under state law, which forbids anyone other than election officials from so much as touching a ballot container.

When Bonta again ordered him to stop, Bianco argued the attorney general had no authority to command him, later claiming in court that the law conferred only an "advise and consent" role.

Spurred by the Riverside dustup, lawmakers in Sacramento recently passed a "raft of additional legislation" to shore up ballots and empower elected officials to protect them in the future.

"It is a lot to ask of our election officials that they not only do their jobs competently but also stand ready to sue anyone who unlawfully interferes with their duties. Yet here we are," Liu wrote. "For our democracy to flourish, our elections must be conducted in accordance with the law."

A. Times and beyond in your inbox six days a week.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times.

fullText:
Nolan Wells died after going on a boat trip with friends on the 4th of July.

The family of Nolan Wells on Thursday released the Mississippi State Medical Examiner's autopsy report, which found that the cause and manner of death are "undetermined."

"This 18 year old male was found face down in the water at Horn Island. Because the circumstances surrounding this death are unknown, the cause and manner of death are best classified as undetermined," the state autopsy report states.

The state autopsy report indicated that the pathologist found "evidence of injury" to the back on Wells' head that is described as "two dark red-purple subcutaneous scalp contusions."

The report did not conclude how this injury occurred. It also found that there were "no external scalp injuries" and "no fractures" in the skull.

The State Medical Examiner's office report comes after a grand jury reviewing the evidence in Wells' death found that no criminal charges are warranted at this point, according to the report released on Monday night.

The state autopsy report's conclusion matches the findings of the private autopsy commissioned by Wells' family, which was released in July. It preliminarily ruled his cause and manner of death as "undetermined pending investigation," with the independent pathologist acknowledging multiple limitations in the report.

"Losing a child, it truly breaks your heart ... especially someone like Nolan, who brought so much joy and light and life to everyone," Wells' mother, Christine Wonsley, told reporters in July.

"The only question we have is, what happened to our son?" she said.

The circumstances surrounding Wells' death garnered national interest after the college football player went missing on the 4th of July after going on a boat trip with friends to Horn Island. Officials said it appeared Wells stayed behind on the island after his friends left.

The teen's body was recovered on July 6, and authorities said they suspect he drowned.

Jackson County Sheriff John Ledbetter said there was no initial indication of a crime, but he stressed that investigators were "working diligently to determine exactly what occurred."

Ledbetter also said the sheriff's office welcomed the family's independent investigation.

ABC News' Sabina Ghebremedhin contributed to this report.

description:
, Trevor Hunnicutt and David Brunnstrom 
   WASHINGTON, Sept 24 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday, with talks on trade and artificial intelligence and the growing strategic rivalry between the countries all in the spotlight during an elaborate state visit. 
   Here are some major takeaways from ‌the talks: 
   TRADE DEAL EXTENDED, FOR NOW 
   The US secured an extension of its trade truce this week - but only a short one.

fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 24 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday, with talks on trade and artificial intelligence and the growing strategic rivalry between the countries all in the spotlight during an elaborate state visit.

Here are some major takeaways from ‌the talks:

The US secured an extension of its trade truce this week - but only a short one.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the two sides agreed ‌to extend by two months a trade agreement that ended last year's trade war and was due to expire in November. The extension would give Washington and Beijing "more time to see what we can do on the economic front," he said.

But ​rather than locking in a durable agreement, the extension appears to push the central questions — tariffs, Chinese purchases, rare-earth supplies and technology restrictions — into the next round of negotiations.

Bessent said on Wednesday that Beijing was meeting its requirement in the earlier agreement to buy 25 million tons of soybeans but was lagging on its pledge to buy $17 billion in other agricultural goods. US officials have said rare-earth deliveries were also falling short, another sign that significant gaps remain.

For companies, the result is a familiar form of instability: tariff rates remain lower for now, but decisions must still be made against a shifting policy backdrop.

For ‌Trump, Xi's White House visit was an opportunity to show off ⁠a Washington being remade in his image.

After Xi treated Trump in Beijing to a tour around a Ming dynasty temple and a walled-off garden retreat rarely opened to foreigners, the US president returned the favor with a different kind of spectacle: Troops wearing wigs and tri-corner hats marched in formation and played music in ⁠a Rose Garden redesigned to look like a Trump golf club.

Fighter jets and bombers roared overhead during ceremonies staged on Wednesday and Thursday, one so loud it caused Trump to flinch.

When the White House press corps was called to cover the two leaders, it wasn't to hear them talk about the weighty affairs of state. Instead, it was to watch them tour the Marine One helicopter and the recently redesigned South Lawn of the ​White ​House, replete with a large helipad emblazoned with the presidential seal.

Speaking to reporters, Trump brushed away questions about ​their policy discussions.

"He loves good granite," Trump said of Xi. "Great meeting."

XI WANTS US 'PRUDENCE' ‌OVER TAIWAN

As expected, Xi pressed Trump on the Taiwan issue, saying, according to China's official news agency, that China hoped the United States would "handle the Taiwan question with prudence."

The agency's English-language service also wrote that Xi hoped the US would oppose Taiwan independence.

That would be a tougher version of Washington's long-standing formulation that it does not "support" independence. There are no signs that the Trump administration plans to change its wording.

There was no immediate White House readout of the exchange, but US officials have long avoided explicitly stating opposition to Taiwanese independence. Any shift in language would raise questions about Washington's resolve to defend the island and provoke opposition in Congress.

Xi, not for the first time while meeting Trump, invoked the "Thucydides Trap", an academic theory that competition between a rising power and an established one tends ‌toward war.

While the Chinese leader said the risk "can be overcome," his reference underscored how concerns about a potential US-China ​military conflict continue to shadow relations between the world's two largest powers.

Xi argued that both nations stand to gain from ​cooperation and lose from confrontation, and he called for regular military dialogue and stronger crisis-prevention ​mechanisms.

Trump, for his part, drew on the two nations' shared history to emphasize the potential for cooperation. They could accomplish much by pursuing common interests, he ‌said, invoking their wartime alliance against Japan.

The two leaders expressed diverging ​views about artificial intelligence.

Trump, who has declared that AI ​should be called super intelligence, or SI, said in a social media post that he wants to "to leave it exactly where it is" and rely on the US Department of Justice rather than impose any new guardrails. He insisted that China held the same position.

But Xi said on Thursday that, as leading nations on AI, China and the US must ​manage its growth.

"We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and ‌manage AI for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people," Xi said.

Some of the biggest ​names in AI were expected to attend Trump's state dinner at the White House on Thursday for Xi, including Alphabet's (GOOGL.O) Sundar Pichai, OpenAI's Sam Altman and Nvidia's (NVDA.O) Jensen Huang.

(Reporting ​by Simon Lewis, David Brunnstrom and Trevor Hunnicutt; Editing by Ross Colvin, Alistair Bell and Sanjeev Miglani)
